Introduction to Ephesians

[1]. Metzger (1972: 10) comments, “There is scarcely an illustrious personality in Greek literature or history from Themistocles down to Alexander, who was not credited with a more or less extensive correspondence.” Cf. the list in Rosenmeyer 2001: 194. For the texts of many of these letters, see Hercher 1873; and for a more accessible sampling, see Malherbe 1977.

[2]. Bury (1961: 607) points out that the authentic Plato spelled this name “Archytes.”

[3]. A similar deception may lie behind the opening of Ep. 13 (which follows “Plato’s” trademark epistolary greeting, “Do well”): “Let this greeting not only commence my letter but serve at the same time as a token that is from me” (trans. Bury 1961).

[4]. E.g., “Mneson of Amphipolis was introduced to me in Potidaea” (Ep. 3.1; Malherbe 1977: 229, trans. S. K. Stowers).

[5]. E.g., “You have not understood correctly if you think that Socrates would do something for money which he had not already decided to do without charge” (Ep. 1.21–23; Malherbe 1977: 221, trans. S. K. Stowers; cf. Rosenmeyer 2001: 208).

[6]. This is not the letter mentioned in the Muratorian Canon, since it shows no hint of Marcionism. On the date and identity of the letter, see J. K. Elliott 1993: 544. I have used Elliott’s translation.

[7]. Whether the fifth-century Epistle of Titus, the Disciple of Paul was intended to deceive is difficult to tell. On one hand, the only aspect of the text that renders it either pseudepigraphic or a letter is its title and subscription. On the other hand, it is easy to think that the author of such an emotional screed against sexual intimacy—with its frequent misrepresentation of the meaning of Scripture, lavish use of spurious texts, and unscrupulous scare tactics—would also try to deceive readers into thinking that the text originated with “Titus, the Disciple of Paul.” It is clear, in any case, that this is a highly polemical document, desperate to win a victory in the battle to keep ascetic practice alive among Christians.

[8]. Suetonius seems to view it as an unusually cruel punishment.

[9]. Cf. also Exod. 1:15–22; Josh. 2:2–7; 6:25; James 2:25. See Speyer 1971: 94n4; Best 1998: 12.

[10]. Clement is only the first known in a long line of other church fathers who also defended the “necessary lie” (Speyer 1971: 94–95).

[11]. Cf. Fischer 1973: 15: “A serene tranquility appears to lie over the whole letter. In this, the letter to the Ephesians is essentially different from all other writings that critical research regards as pseudepigraphs.” (Ein heiterer Friede scheint über dem ganzen Brief zu liegen. Darin unterscheidet sich der Epheserbrief wesentlich von allen anderen Schreiben, die innerhalb der kritischen Forschung als Pseudepigraphen angesehen werden.) Fischer is talking about supposedly pseudepigraphical writings in the NT.

[12]. The author of the Sentences of Pseudo-Phocylides, according to many scholars, wrote pseudonymously to show Jewish readers that their traditional customs were compatible with the best ethical teaching of the Hellenistic world (W. Wilson 2005: 3–8). If this was the author’s intention, then he clearly wrote deceptively at the same time that he encouraged truthfulness (lines 7, 16–17, 48, 50), and he did not write to address any obviously polemical situation. These characteristics might provide an analogy to a pseudonymous Ephesians, especially if the purpose of Ephesians was to ease tensions between Christians and their Greco-Roman environment. Apart from the difference in literary genre (one text is a poem and the other a letter), however, the purpose and deceptive intent of Pseudo-Phocylides is far from certain. Moreover, the idea that the household code in Ephesians was written to ease tensions between Christians and the wider society (MacDonald 2000: 159–69, 337–38; Osiek and MacDonald 2006: 118–43; cf. Merz 2000: 132, 146) runs aground on the countercultural nature of the household code itself (5:25; 6:9) and of the letter generally (2:1–3; 4:17–19; 5:3–14).

[13]. This is true even if, for the sake of argument, we assume that the five other disputed letters in the NT Pauline corpus are pseudonymous.

[14]. Chrysostom uses ὑπέρογκος elsewhere to mean “difficult” (PGL 1440), and this is a common meaning of the term in the LXX (Exod. 18:22, 26; Deut. 30:11; 2 Sam. 13:2). In the NT, ὑπέρογκος is used of “bombastic” speech (Jude 16; 2 Pet. 2:18; BDAG 1034). Cf. Theophylact, PG 82:1033.

[15]. What constitutes a sentence varies from editor to editor, and the Nestle-Aland text is generous with periods. Most interpreters would recognize 1:3–14, for example, as a single sentence, since it contains no independent clauses, but the Nestle-Aland text punctuates it with four periods.

[16]. These examples come from Holtzmann 1872: 5–6. Διάβολος appears in the Pastoral Epistles (1 Tim. 3:6, 7, 11; 2 Tim. 2:26; 3:3; Titus 2:3), but Holtzmann believed those letters to be pseudonymous. The vocabulary of Ephesians falls well within the Pauline range, but some scholars have observed that among the forty words appearing only in Ephesians in the NT and the fifty-one words that do not appear elsewhere in the undisputed Pauline letters, “many” also appear in early Christian writings composed after Paul’s time (Schnackenburg 1991: 26; cf., e.g., Lincoln 1990: lxv). Schnackenburg lists twelve such words and adds to this list five others that appear elsewhere in the NT but “predominate in the late writings.” Yet sixteen of these seventeen words appear reasonably frequently in Greek literature dating, at the latest, from the fourth century BC. Only κυριότης (Eph. 1:21; Col. 1:16; 2 Pet. 2:10; Jude 8) is not well attested before the first century AD (BDAG 579).

[17]. Several of these examples come from R. Wilson 2005: 13.

[18]. For evidence that the borrowing went in the other direction, see Best 1997b. Complex theories about the redaction of both Ephesians and Colossians on the basis of each other or even the missing letter to the Laodiceans (Col. 4:16), although improbable, reflect the inability of the prevailing theory to explain all the evidence. See, e.g., Holtzmann 1872; Muddimann 2001.

[19]. See, e.g., Dunn 1996: 186–87; R. Wilson 2005: 225.

[20]. Οἰκονομία appears once in Colossians (1:25), and πλήρωμα twice (1:19; 2:9).

[21]. Οἰκονομία appears in 1 Cor. 9:17, and πλήρωμα in Rom. 11:12, 25; 13:10; 15:29; 1 Cor. 10:26; Gal. 4:4.

[22]. See the exegesis of Eph. 3:5 below.

[23]. For the same general point with respect to Ephesians, see Witherington 2007: 2.

[24]. It is also possible, as Witherington (2007: 4–25) argues, that Paul dictated the letter in a more Asiatic style than was his custom because he was writing to the province of Asia, where the most famous practitioners of Asiatic rhetoric had flourished (e.g., Hegesias of Magnesia). Hellenistic Jewish authors did sometimes compose in the Asiatic style (see Wifstrand 1948: 217–19, who cites Prov. 20:9; 22:13 LXX; T. Levi 4.1; and T. Gad 3.2–3 as examples), and the long sentences, redundancy, coinage of new words, and wordplays in Ephesians would fit the Asiatic profile (Sellin 2008: 64, 85n61). It is important, however, to be cautious on this point. Most of Ephesians does not have the studied, self-conscious quality of Asiatic rhetoric. The long sentences and sometimes broken syntax of Ephesians betray the voice of someone who could have composed in the Asiatic style if time were available, but who did not have the luxury to sort out the details of its complex techniques in this particular letter.

[25]. At first it might seem that the general nature of Ephesians counts against its authenticity, but after a careful study of ancient pseudepigraphical letters, Bauckham (1988: 488) observes that “not many pseudepigraphal writers wished to produce generalized didactic works, and those who did preferred other genres [than the letter], such as wisdom literature.”

[26]. Ὄντας αὐτοὺς ἰδιαζόντως ὠνόμασεν εἰπών· τοῖς ἁγίοις τοῖς οὖσι καὶ πιστοῖς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ.

[27]. See, e.g., Theodore of Mopsuestia (Swete 1882: 112–18); Theodoret of Cyrus (R. Hill 2001: 2.31–33); Severian of Gabala (Staab 1933: 304–5).

[28]. Cf. van Roon 1974: 81; Lincoln 1990: 4; Best 1997a: 5; Dahl 2000: 170–72.

[29]. As early as the fifth century, interpreters of Ephesians debated whether Paul wrote Ephesians before or after his ministry in the city. Severian of Gabala (Staab 1933: 304) and Theodore of Mopsuestia (Swete 1882: 112) favored the idea that Paul wrote Ephesians before visiting Ephesus. Theodoret of Cyrus argued against it (R. Hill 2001: 2.31).

[30]. Following Schnabel’s chronology (2004: 1262, 1267, 1270), these would have been the periods from summer 57 to autumn 59, winter 59–60, and spring 60–62 respectively.

[31]. On Ignatius’s reasons for doing this, see Richards 1991: 72.

[32]. Rapske (1994: 177–91) argues that Paul was under such light custody because the case against him was weak. This means that Philippians, where Paul is uncertain about the outcome of his imprisonment (1:19–26; 2:23–24), was probably written not at the end of Paul’s Roman imprisonment but either at its beginning (Lightfoot 1896: 30–46) or, perhaps, during an otherwise unknown imprisonment in Ephesus five years earlier (Thielman 2003).

[33]. The Romans identified Artemis with the Italian hunting goddess Diana. Ancient images of Artemis depicted her with a number of smooth, oval objects attached to her chest. According to Trebilco (2004: 21–24; cf. Schnabel 2004: 1212), however, they are probably not breasts, and Artemis was not a fertility goddess, as early Christian polemic sometimes claimed. She seems to have been connected with benevolence, protection, and power over other supernatural beings.

[34]. Pace Strelan (1996: 86–88), it is reasonable to associate Artemis with magical practices. In addition to Arnold 1989: 22–24, see Trebilco 2004: 21n64, 150n206.

[35]. On the whole theme, see Zanker 1988: 297–333.

[36]. Here I follow the translation and interpretation of these inscriptions in Friesen 2001: 32–36, 123–26.

[37]. On the use of the term αἰών on coins and in inscriptions to stress the eternality of the emperor and of Rome, see Nock 1934: 85–86.

[38]. Cf. his use of the terms οἱ ἄρχοντες and ἐξουσίαι in a political sense in 1 Cor. 2:6; Rom. 13:1–3; and Titus 3:1. The argument here is not that Paul believed spiritual powers controlled the governments of the various nations (e.g., Cullmann 1951: 192–93; Caird 1956: 1–30), although this view was certainly current during his time, and it is possible that he held it (Deut. 32:8–9 LXX; Dan. 10:13, 20–21; Jub. 15.31–32; 3 En. 14.2; 26.12; Luke 4:6; Rev. 12:18–13:1; Origen, Cels. 8.63; Wink 1984: 26–35; Schwindt 2002: 363–64). Nor is the argument that Paul has begun to “demythologize” the powers and view them as symbols “of the real determinants of human existence” (Wink 1984: 61–63; cf. Caird 1976: 46–47). Paul is saying instead in Eph. 1:20–22a that God has made Christ victorious over every power that seeks to harm God’s people or to claim ultimate sovereignty over them. Paul is thinking of powers located “in the heavenly places” (1:20; cf. 3:10; 6:12), but among these powers would be the demonic forces that Rome identified with the deified members of the imperial household. As Revelation shows, from the perspective of persecuted Christians, the power of these demonic forces to create havoc in the world made itself felt among Christians most forcefully in the reigning emperor and in the cultic, military, and political machinery through which he ruled the empire.

[39]. Ephesians probably does participate in the general movement in late antiquity away from Greek rationalism and toward “higher wisdom through revelation” (Hengel 1974: 1.210–18). Its participation in this movement, moreover, probably explains its use of concepts and language that later became popular within gnostic religions (cf. Schwindt 2002: 508).

[40]. MacDonald follows S. Wilson 1995 at this point.

[41]. Cf. Chadwick’s view (1960: 148) that Ephesians links Judaism to Christianity because of “einer apologetischen Notwendigkeit” (an apologetic necessity).

[42]. For the chronology, see Acts 20:3, 6, 16; 24:27; 27:9; 28:11, 30; 1 Cor. 16:8; and the discussion in Schnabel 2004: 1220, 1223, 1257, 1262, and 1267.

[43]. If 2 Timothy was written to Ephesus (Trebilco 2004: 206–9), then it would provide further evidence for continued suffering among Christians there (2 Tim. 1:8; 2:3, 11–13; 3:12; 4:5).

[44]. On the large increase in the numbers of Christians through Paul’s work in Ephesus, see Trebilco 2004: 134–52.

I. Prescript and Greeting (1:1–2)

[1]. See also the third-person prayer-wishes for peace and grace at the end of the letter (6:23–24). This is the only Pauline letter in which the concluding grace-wish is not formulated in the second person.

[2]. In his essay “A Slip of the Tongue in Greeting” Lucian (Laps. 2) says that although by his time (second century AD) the greeting χαίρειν was used only in the morning, in ancient times it was used at any time of day. His easy movement back and forth between face-to-face and epistolary greetings in his discussion reveals his assumption that the epistolary greeting arose from the oral salutation. Tertullian comments on the similarity between the greetings in Paul’s Letters and the custom that Jews observed even in Tertullian’s own time (early third century AD) of saluting each other with “Peace!” (Marc. 5.5). Cf. Lieu 1985: 162–67.

[3]. Εἰρήνη ὑμῖν πληθυνθείη is Theodotian’s rendering of the Aramaic greeting שְׁלָמְכֹון יִשְׂגֵּא in the letters from Nebuchadnezzar and Darius in Dan. 4:1 (3:31 MT) and 6:25 (6:26 MT, Theod.).

[4]. Milgrom (1990: 360–62) has gathered evidence for the antiquity and wide-ranging influence of the priestly benediction (e.g., Mal. 1:8–10; 1QSb 3.1–5) and observes that it seems to have even influenced social greetings (e.g., Ruth 2:4).

II. Blessing God Who Has Blessed His People in Christ (1:3–14)

[1]. For the elements of the tractate that probably predate AD 70, see Instone-Brewer 2004: 41–119. For ancient Jewish prayer generally and the importance of benedictory prayers specifically, see, in addition to Instone-Brewer’s treatment, Bonsirven 1935: 141–58; Cohen 1987: 62–73; E. Sanders 1990: 72–77; 1992: 195–208.

[2]. The regular prayers are the Shema and the Tefillah. The Shema is not actually a “prayer” but a confession that comprises Deut. 6:4–9; 11:13–21; Num. 15:37–41. The Tefillah is the Shemoneh Esreh, or Eighteen Benedictions. See Danby 1933: 2n1, 796–97nn38 and 46.

[3]. Paul may allude to the blessing that should accompany each course in a meal when he cites Ps. 24:1 in 1 Cor. 10:26. Cf. t. Ber. 4.1 and the discussion in Instone-Brewer 2004: 72–74.

[4]. Clement of Alexandria (Strom. 1.21) also refers to this correspondence but does not quote it. Josephus, Clement, and Eusebius apparently relied on the mid-first-century-BC historian Alexander Polyhistor, who seems to have quoted Eupolemus fairly closely. See F. Fallon, OTP 2:861–62.

[5]. According to F. Fallon, OTP 2:862, Eupolemus’s name Σούρων (Sourōn, Souron) comes from the Hebrew חוּרָם (ḥûrām, Huram, as in 2 Chron. 2:3 [2 MT]). Curiously, it also resembles צוֹר or צֹר, the Hebrew words for Tyre.

[6]. Cf. 2 Macc. 1:10–12, which, however, may also be part of a fictional letter (Goldstein 1983: 157–67) and uses the phrase “we give much thanks to him [i.e., God]” rather than “Blessed be the Lord. . . .”

[7]. Sellin (2008: 85n61) calls this wordplay figura etymologica and says that it is a characteristic of Asiatic rhetoric.

[8]. Trans. García Martínez and Tigchelaar 1998. Cf. 4Q502 and 4Q512, which, although briefer and more fragmentary, seem to follow the same pattern.

[9]. Merkel (1987: 3224–26) lists twenty, and Hoehner (2002: 154–57, 160–61) lists forty-three attempts to explain the organization of the passage.

[10]. In Greek poetry, a “period” is a continuous string of rhythmic sounds after which there is a pause. It is similar to a sentence in prose composition. A “colon” (the singular of “cola”) is the basic unit of which a period is made, not more than twelve syllables long, with a regular, often well-known rhythm or meter. It corresponds to a phrase in prose composition. See West 1982: 5–6. Lohmeyer did not attempt to apply classical standards of poetry to Eph. 1:3–14, which he viewed as “eine eigentümliche Mischung griechischen und semitischen Sprachstiles” (a peculiar mixture of a Greek and Semitic style of speech; 1926a: 122; 1926b: 233–34). Lohmeyer (1926a: 120–21) did, however, refer to the passage as a “period,” found that it had “ein überraschend regelmässiges Gebilde” (a surprisingly regular structure), and divided it into four stanzas composed of small triadic “strophes,” the first three stanzas with four strophes each and the final stanza with three strophes.

[11]. Fischer (1973: 113–14) omits from the “hymn” elements that are either reminiscent of the theological distinctives of the rest of the letter or disruptive of its symmetry. Coutts (1957: 120–24) similarly tries to reconstruct the original baptismal liturgy on which he thinks the passage is based by eliminating the author’s afterthoughts, comments, interruptions, rearrangements, and small changes to the wording. Fischer comments that his reconstruction is “natürlich sehr unsicher” (naturally very uncertain; 1973: 114), and Coutts (1957: 120) describes his own effort as “a rash undertaking.” Cf. Lang (1969: 12–13), who distills part of a baptismal liturgy from 1:11–14.

[12]. Schlier’s idea (1957: 39) that three main verbs—ἐξελέξατο (v. 4), ἐχαρίτωσεν (v. 6), and ἐπερίσσευσεν (v. 8)—form the structural framework for verses 4–10 seems to ignore the presence of other important indicative verbs, such as ἔχομεν in verse 7 and προέθετο in verse 9.

[13]. Cf. Deichgräber 1967: 66–67. Some scholars (e.g., Coutts 1957: 115–27; Lang 1969: 12–16; Dahl 2000: 327–28) suggest that the prayer, or at least part of it, arose out of a baptismal setting. This seems unnecessarily speculative, however, since nothing in the prayer explicitly refers to baptism.

[14]. See the discussion of m. Ber. 4.4 and b. Ber. 34a in Instone-Brewer 2004: 57–59.

[15]. This matches exactly the arrangement of the passage in the NA27, which departed from all previous editions in arranging the text this way. Cf. the appeal to K. Aland in Krämer 1967: 40n1 to make such a change.

[16]. The ninth-century bishop Photius of Constantinople captured this element of the benediction in his comment on the passage:

He blessed us through the Son; he chose us through the Son; he adopted through the Son; he shed favor through the Son. And how through the Son? O marvelous thing! “Through his blood,” he says. Do you see the richness of grace? And how exceedingly abundant and unutterable the mercy? And not only these things, but also, “He made known to us the mystery of his will.” Through what means? Even this came through his Son—everything came through the Son, whose good pleasure agrees in every way with the Father. (Staab 1933: 611, my trans.)

A. Praise to God for His Grace in Making Believers His People (1:3–6)

[1]. Cf. Tob. 13:17 NRSV: “‘Blessed be the God of Israel!’ and the blessed will bless the holy name for ever and ever”; 13:18 Sin.: εὐλογητὸς ὁ θεὸς τοῦ Ισραηλ· καὶ εὐλογητοὶ εὐλογήσουσιν τὸ ὄνομα τὸ ἅγιον εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα. See also 4Q403 28–29: “Blessed be the Lord, the king of all, above all blessing and p[raise. And may he bless all the ho]ly ones who bless him, [and proclaim him just] in the name of his glory. And he will bless those permanently blessed” (trans. García Martínez and Tigchelaar 1998).

[2]. Apart from the Pauline Letters, it appears in Biblical Greek only in 1 Pet. 2:5 (2x) and in Rev. 11:8, where it takes the adverbial form πνευματικῶς.

[3]. In the early church, see, e.g., Origen (Heine 2002: 81–84); Chrysostom (Hom. Eph., hom. 1; NPNF 13:50–51; PG 62:12); Jerome (Heine 2002: 82); and cf. Pelagius (Souter 1926: 345). In more recent times, see Westcott 1906: 7.

[4]. This notion so offended those who preserved the textual tradition represented by 𝔓46 that they left the phrase out of 6:12 (Schwindt 2002: 360n48). The notion was common in ancient Jewish literature (Job 1:6; 1 En. 61.10), however, and sometimes involved conflict between the two sides (Dan. 10:13, 21; Rev. 12:7; 19:11; Lincoln 1973: 474). Ephesians also assumes the presence of conflict in the heavenly places (6:12), but the outcome of this conflict has already been decided (1:20–22).

[5]. Chrysostom interprets Paul’s understanding of election in 1:4 in precisely the wrong way, therefore, when he says that God not only chose believers out of his love but also because he saw in advance that their moral excellence and mettle would make them the best choice out of the various options (Hom. Eph., hom. 1; NPNF 13:51; PG 62:12). Cf. Origen’s comments on 1:4, especially as Jerome uses them (Heine 2002: 85, 276).

[6]. On the scarcity of the word κατενώπιον, see BDF §214.5. That ἄμωμος was a live metaphor for virtuous conduct in the first century is clear from Philo’s statement that Moses speaks of sacrificing “to God the abominations of Egypt [Exod. 8:26], meaning thereby the virtues, these offerings unblemished [ἄμωμος] and most worthy, which are the abominations of every fool” (Sacrifices 51).

[7]. Alford 1857: 69; Hoehner 2002: 184; cf. Lightfoot 1895: 313; Westcott 1906: 9; Barth 1974: 79–80; Lincoln 1990: 17. Pace Cambier 1963: 72–74.

[8]. For the translation “adoptive sonship,” see Byrne 1993: 293; 1996: 252.

[9]. For the idea that υἱοθεσία in Rom. 8:23 refers to the future bodily resurrection of believers, see Rom. 8:11 and the comments of Byrne 1979: 109.

[10]. Cf. Col. 1:16b, 20; Schlier 1957: 54; Gnilka 1971: 73.

[11]. Cambier (1963: 76) hits the mark: “Toute la théologie paulinienne souligne que le Père constitue le point de départ et le point d’aboutissement de toute l’action salvifique divine.” (All Pauline theology emphasizes that the Father constitutes the departure point and concluding point of all the saving action of God.)

[12]. In these passages, the term is always the verbal adjective ἀγαπητός rather than the participle of ἀγαπάω found in the other passages and in Eph. 1:6, but the meaning is virtually identical.

[13]. Cf. Sir. 18:17, which describes a gracious man as ἀνδρὶ κεχαριτωμένῳ, literally, “a man who has been made gracious.”

[14]. On Chrysostom’s text and comments, see Haupt 1902a: 13; Best 1998: 128.

B. Praise to God for His Grace in Redemption and Revelation (1:7–10)

[1]. Morris 1955: 11, 39 observes that in Dan. 4:24 OG (4:27 Eng.) Daniel instructs the king to redeem (λύτρωσαι) his wickedness with almsgiving and concludes that when Nebuchadnezzar later says, καὶ ἐπὶ συντελείᾳ τῶν ἑπτὰ ἐτῶν ὁ χρόνος μου τῆς ἀπολυτρώσεως ἦλθε (And at the completion of seven years my time of redemption came; 4:30c OG, NETS), he is referring to this purchase of his deliverance with alms to the poor. Nebuchadnezzar, however, does not explicitly make this connection, and his use of ἀπολύτρωσις rather than λύτρωσις diminishes the likelihood that the reader should make this connection.

[2]. On the “genitive of price,” see BDF §179; Wallace 1996: 122.

[3]. Cf. also the comments of Origen (Heine 2002: 91); Theophylact (PG 124:1037); Ellicott 1859: 10.

[4]. Origen thought that human beings had sold themselves into the devil’s captivity and thus God had to pay the price of Christ’s death for their release. Augustine claimed that God paid the price to himself to satisfy the need for justice. Anselm argued that human sin was basically a failure to give God the honor that was his due and that God’s honor could be restored only by the payment of a penalty, a payment that Christ’s death satisfied. For a brief review of these theories, see Colleran 1969: 42–48.

[5]. In addition to Photius, see, e.g., the comments of Origen (Heine 2002: 91) and Theophylact (PG 124:1037) on this text.

[6]. Cf. also Exod. 15:13; Deut. 7:8; 2 Sam. 4:9; 2 Esd. 11:10 LXX (Neh. 1:10 MT, Eng.); Pss. 25:22; 77:15.

[7]. Col. 1:14 reads ἐν ᾧ ἔχομεν τὴν ἀπολύτρωσιν, τὴν ἄφεσιν τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν. The phrase is identical to Eph. 1:7a except that it does not have διὰ τοῦ αἵματος αὐτοῦ, and instead of παραπτωμάτων it has ἁμαρτιῶν.

[8]. The relative pronoun ἧς at the beginning of Eph. 1:8, although genitive rather than accusative, is the direct object of ἐπερίσσευσεν. It has been attracted into the case of its antecedent χάριτος. See BDF §294; Wallace 1996: 338–39.

[9]. Abbott 1897: 15; Westcott 1906: 12; Lincoln 1990: 17, 29; Schnackenburg 1991: 56–57; Pokorný 1992: 64; O’Brien 1999: 107; Hoehner 2002: 212.

[10]. Origen (Heine 2002: 93–97); Chrysostom (PG 62:14–15); Theodore of Mopsuestia (Swete 1882: 127); Alford 1857: 72–73; Eadie 1883: 44–49; Gnilka 1971: 77; Best 1998: 132–33; Sellin 2008: 99–100.

[11]. Sellin (2008: 100) thinks it goes with both verbs.

[12]. Some have objected to this way of taking ἐν πάσῃ σοφίᾳ καὶ φρονήσει because the adjective πᾶς with a singular abstract noun that does not have the article regularly means “every kind of” and, if the phrase referred to God, would imply that God’s wisdom might be incomplete. He would not have all wisdom, only all kinds of wisdom (e.g., Ellicott 1859: 12; Abbott 1897: 15; Hoehner 2002: 212). Πᾶς with an anarthrous abstract noun can, however, mean simply “all,” as is probably the case in Matt. 3:15; 28:18. See Moule 1959: 94–95.

[13]. Paul’s reference to “the beautifully complex wisdom of God” in Eph. 3:10, however, diminishes the usefulness of trying to decide the question on the basis of references to wisdom later in the letter.

[14]. See, e.g., Origen and Jerome (Heine 2002: 96); Ellicott 1859: 12; Hoehner 2002: 215.

[15]. Cf. also Paul’s use of the noun πρόθεσιν in 3:11, where the qualifying phrase τῶν αἰώνων seems to give it temporal connotations.

[16]. The thought is similar to that expressed in Matt. 11:26 (Luke 10:21), where Jesus says that it was God’s “good pleasure” (εὐδοκία) to reveal the significance of Jesus’s mighty works to his disciples although they were mere babes in comparison to the “wise [σοφοί] and intelligent [συνετοί]” people who rejected Jesus.

[17]. This is the conclusion of the overwhelming majority of commentators. See, e.g., Alford 1857: 73; Ellicott 1859: 13; Abbott 1897: 17; Caragounis 1977: 94–95; Lincoln 1990: 31; Best 1998: 139; Muddiman 2001: 75. For the use of εἰς with προτίθημι to indicate the purpose of the action, see Rom. 3:25.

[18]. This is the majority position among commentators (e.g., Schlier 1957: 63; Gnilka 1971: 79n4; Lincoln 1990: 31–32; Best 1998: 138–39; Hoehner 2002: 217–18; cf. Lindemann 1975: 94), although not of Eadie 1883: 51 (“an arrangement, . . . a compact and symmetrical system of perfect harmony, . . . a plan”); Lightfoot 1895: 319 (“system or method of administration”); or BDAG 698 (“plan of salvation”).

[19]. Cf. Dan. 4:37 Theod.; 2 Bar. 40.3; cf. 2﻿ Bar. 81.4; Schnackenburg 1991: 59; Lincoln 1990: 32. Paul may also mean that God has measured out the length of time before he acts decisively to rescue his people and that this measure has now been filled up. In Christ, God’s historical purposes have come to a climax. Cf. Gal. 4:4; 2 Esd. (4 Ezra) 4:35–37. Pace Lindemann (1975: 95), however, this would not mean “the elimination of history generally” (die Ausschaltung von Geschichte überhaupt). It is difficult to think that for the author of Ephesians, Christians would need to be vigilant against “the strategies of the devil” (6:11) in a period when history had ceased to exist.

[20]. See, e.g., Polybius, Hist. 24.5.2; 3 Macc. 2:27; and Rom. 1:13. Haupt (1902a: 16) comments that if we do not take the infinitive as an expression of the content of the mystery of God’s will, then it might be attached to εὐδοκία (it was God’s good pleasure to sum up all things in Christ) or to προέθετο (God planned to sum up all things in Christ, and this was his good pleasure), or it could explain more fully the meaning of the phrase οἰκονομίαν τοῦ πληρώματος τῶν καιρῶν (God administered the fullness of the times by summing up all things in Christ). All three of these other possibilities, he says, ultimately yield the same sense.

[21]. See, e.g., John Chrysostom, PG 62:16; Schlier, TDNT 3:682; Masson 1953: 145; Schlier 1957: 65; Cambier 1963: 86–89; Schnackenburg 1991: 60–61.

[22]. Cf. Luke’s procedure in Acts 1:1–2 and Josephus’s procedure in Ag. Ap. 2.1. For the use of a participial form of the verb to refer to the concluding summary of an oral declamation, see Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Lys. 9.16. Chrysostom (Hom. Eph., hom. 1), in his comments on this passage, defines the infinitive ἀνακεφαλαιώσασθαι as meaning συνάψαι (synapsai, to join together), a term that could be used of drawing a conclusion from a logical argument (LSJ 1698). He defines the noun ἀνακεφαλαίωσις as a “pulling together in a brief space things spoken at length and to say concisely all the things spoken in many words” (PG 62:16; cf. NPNF 13:54).

[23]. Pace Harvey (1980: 327), who believes that μυστήρια here refers to “the moral and ascetic discipline of the just man.”

[24]. The term μυστήριον appears three times in the Synoptic Gospels in parallel passages, four times in Revelation, and eleven times in the Apostolic Fathers (seven of these in the Epistle to Diognetus). The term appears twenty-one times in the Pauline corpus (a figure that assumes μυστήριον rather than μαρτύριον is the right reading in 1 Cor. 2:1); of these uses, six occur in 1 Corinthians, four in Colossians, and six in Ephesians. This makes the concentration of the term in Colossians and Ephesians about the same (and about the same as in the Epistle to Diognetus). This concentration of uses is far heavier than in 1 Corinthians, which is more than four times the length of Colossians and nearly three times the length of Ephesians.

[25]. On this understanding of μυστήριον in 1 Corinthians, see Bockmuehl 1990: 157–66.

[26]. Cf. also 1 Cor. 9:17, where the same idea occurs without the use of the term μυστήριον.

[27]. Cf. Col. 1:25–26, where Paul describes his role as one who proclaims the mystery of God’s word as that of a “servant” (διάκονος).

C. Praise to God for Making His People Heirs and Giving Them Hope in Christ (1:11–12)

[1]. Through the centuries a few interpreters have claimed that Paul means “we have been appointed by lot.” On this reading, Paul pictures God metaphorically as casting lots to determine who would be his people, and the lot fell on “us.” Yet Paul used this expression to emphasize the sovereign grace of God in choosing his people—his choice came to them completely unmerited by anything in them—and then guarded against the conclusion that God’s choice was arbitrary by immediately qualifying the verb ἐκληρώθημεν (we have been chosen by lot) with the participle προορισθέντες (having been predestined).

[2]. Haupt 1902a: 26; Masson 1953: 146; cf. Foerster, TDNT 3:784.

[3]. So, correctly, Muddiman (2001: 77), without, however, adopting his ingenious idea about what motivated this string of references to predestination. Muddiman suggests that an interpreter of Paul, anticipating the supposed reference to Jewish Christians who “hoped beforehand in Christ” in verse 12, may have tried to forestall any notion that Paul had denied Jewish privilege in his authentic correspondence by piling up references to God’s predestination of the belief of Jewish Christians. As Muddiman points out, in Rom. 9:4–5 Paul had already done something to prevent this misunderstanding, and we might add, also in Rom. 1:16; 3:2; 10:1; 11:1–32.

[4]. Westcott (1906: 15–16) and Barth (1974: 132) think that the word refers to Jews who believed in the promises of “the Deliverer” or “the Messiah” before his actual coming (cf. Aletti 2001: 77–79). Robinson (1904: 34–35) is undecided as to whether the reference is to Jewish Christians or to Jews who hoped in the coming of the Messiah before hearing the gospel (cf. Muddiman 2001: 77). Bengel 1860: 4.68–69; Alford 1857: 75–76; Ellicott 1859: 16; Eadie 1883: 60; Abbott 1897: 21; O’Brien 1999: 116–17; and MacDonald 2000: 203–4 believe that the term refers to the hope of Jewish Christians.

[5]. Cf., e.g., Haupt 1902a: 26–27; Masson 1953: 146; Lincoln 1990: 37; Best 1998: 144–45; Hoehner 2002: 231–33.

[6]. The subject of προηλπικότας in 1:12b is identical to the subject of προορισθέντες in 1:11a.

[7]. As in, e.g., Posidippus of Cassandreia, frag. 27.8 (cf. Athenaeus of Naucratis, Deipn. 9.20); Galen, In Hippocratis prorrheticum I commentaria iii [Kühn 1821–33: 16.822, 838]; Publius Herennius Dexippus, frag. 2a; Gregory of Nyssa, Vita sanctae Macrinae 9; Themistius, Or. 5.65a.

[8]. Paul’s use of the perfect active participle here in 1:12 is similar to the use of the perfect active participle προηλπικώς in a fragment from the new comedy poet Posidippus (frag. 27.8) from the third century BC. Posidippus compares the plight of a cook who faces a hungry, drunken crowd to that of a general facing the surging mass of enemy combatants. This crowd, he says, has been “anticipating” dinner for fifteen days (ἐκ πέντε καὶ δέχ’ ἡμερῶν προηλπικὼς τὸ δεῖπνον). The anticipation of the crowd is on the verge of ending with a satisfying meal, but they are still hungry. The perfect tense allows the reader to view this anticipation closely: it is not anticipation pure and simple but a complex state built up over the course of fifteen days.

[9]. The thought is therefore similar to that of Rom. 8:19.

D. Praise to God for the Conversion and Future Salvation of Paul’s Readers (1:13–14)

[1]. Three verbs have been proposed: ἠλπίκατε (ēlpikate, you hoped), ἐκληρώθητε (eklērōthēte, you were made heirs), and, most often, ἐστέ (este, you are). See the surveys in Alford 1857: 76; and Eadie 1883: 63. Origen (Heine 2002: 101), who read the text in his native tongue, comments on the strange repetition of the second ἐν ᾧ but does not suggest supplying a verb to remedy the situation. This implies that the phrase could not be construed according to the normal rules of Greek syntax.

[2]. Cf. Rom. 2:17–22; 5:6; 2 Cor. 4:6; Gal. 2:4, 6; 1 Tim. 1:3–4; and the comments of both BDF §467 and Schlier 1957: 68.

[3]. Yet see Rom. 1:16; 8:24; and 2 Cor. 6:2.

[4]. Ancient Jewish literature sometimes compares circumcision to a seal (Fitzer, TDNT 7:947–48), just as Paul does in Rom. 4:11, and Christian literature beginning in the early second century makes a similar comparison between baptism and sealing (Herm. Sim. 9.16.3–4). Some interpreters have argued that Eph. 1:13 also has baptism in view. Gnilka (1971: 86), for example, believes that the metaphor speaks of baptism itself, and Schlier (1957: 70) suggests that it could refer to “die Handauflegung, . . . durch die das Pneuma vermittelt wurde” (the laying on of hands, . . . through which the Spirit was mediated). If Ephesians was known to the author of the Shepherd of Hermas, then this interpretation may be very ancient. Herm. Sim. 9.17.4, with its sequence of hearing (ἀκούσαντα), believing (πιστεύσαντα), and receiving the seal (τὴν σφραγῖδα) of baptism (cf. 9.16.3–4), may echo this text. Although ancient, this interpretation reads too much into the text. Paul says nothing explicit about baptism here, and if he had intended to refer to it as a critical element in his readers’ conversion, he probably would have made the reference explicit.

[5]. See the full footnote on this in Schlier 1957: 70–71.

[6]. According to Kerr (1988: 93), a service provider who failed to render the promised services was required to repay twice the amount of the ἀρραβών.

[7]. Pace Lightfoot (1895: 324) and Kerr (1988: 97), who argue that Paul’s use of the metaphor also implies that those who have received the “down payment” of the Holy Spirit have an obligation to God that they must fulfill.

[8]. On the relationship of the Acts passages to the prophetic promises of the Spirit listed here, see Fitzmyer 1998: 259.

[9]. Compare Luke’s use of περιποιήσασθαι in Luke 17:33 with his use of σῴζω in the virtually identical saying in 9:24.

[10]. See, e.g., Cambier (1963: 96), who in a footnote mentions the three lexical options—“conservation, acquisition (sens subjectif), propriété”—but discusses the meaning of the term as if only the last two options are possibilities for this passage. In their helpful review of the history of the interpretation of this text, Lyonnet and Sabourin (1970: 116) describe three opinions on the meaning of περιποίησις: the people acquired for God by the blood of Christ (cf. v. 7), an act of acquisition that believers engage in, and God’s “most precious possession.” If we are thinking of the meaning of the term itself, however, we can collapse the first and second of these interpretations into the single category of those who think the word refers to the action of acquiring something, whether God’s acquisition of believers through Christ’s redemption or believers’ acquisition of an inheritance at the time of their redemption. Once again, that leaves basically two interpretive options.

[11]. Most interpreters take this approach. See, e.g., John of Damascus, PG 95:825; Ellicott 1859: 20; Eadie 1883: 70; Robinson 1904: 148; Percy 1946: 188–89n15; Cambier 1963: 96–97; Lincoln 1990: 41–42; Pokorný 1992: 74; O’Brien 1999: 122; Muddiman 2001: 80; Hoehner 2002: 244; Spicq, TLNT 3:100–101; BDAG 804. For the idea that περιποίησις is a technical term meaning “God’s special people,” see Haupt 1902a: 32; and Gnilka 1971: 87.

[12]. See, e.g., Abbott 1897: 23; Masson 1953: 148n6; and Best 1998: 153.

[13]. See also, e.g., Jerome (Heine 2002: 104–5); Dibelius and Greeven 1953: 62–63; Masson 1953: 148; Schlier 1957: 71–72; Best 1998: 152–53.

[14]. Cf. NIV, NJB, and the similar idiom in Xenophon, Cyr. 4.4.10, where Cyrus uses the verb when he speaks to captives taken in war and whom he intends to spare because they have surrendered to his army. He says to them, ἄνδρες, . . . νῦν τε ὅτι ἐπείθσεσε τὰς ψυχὰς περιεποιήσασθε (“My men, . . . you have now saved your lives by your submission”; trans. Miller 1914).

[15]. Taking σωτηρίας as a genitive of apposition.

[16]. It is true that the Hebrew text of Mal. 3:17 echoes the covenant promise of Exod. 19:5 that if Israel obeys God and keeps his covenant, they will be his “treasured possession” (סְגֻלָּה), but there the LXX uses λαὸς περιούσιος to translate סְגֻלָּה. The translator of Mal. 3:17 may have purposely switched the expression λαὸς περιούσιος for περιποίησις thinking that περιποίησις was more appropriate for a context in which one group is spared in a time of judgment.

III. Thanksgiving for Conversion and Intercession for Understanding (1:15–23)

[1]. Reports of thanks to a god or the gods are not common in the extant correspondence from antiquity. Schubert (1939: 172–73, 181) suggests that this is because the conditions of intimacy and genuinely shared religious feeling that are common to most thanksgiving prayer reports were rare in private correspondence and even rarer in official letters.

[2]. Hunt and Edgar 1932: 303, 317, and 319 respectively. The thanksgiving or intercessory prayer report could also occur at other places in the letter besides the beginning. See, e.g., P.Oxy. 1481 (White 1986: 158), where the thanksgiving to the gods comes at the letter’s conclusion, and 1 Macc. 12:11, which records an intercessory prayer report in the middle of an official letter. Cf. the comments of Richards 2004: 132n36.

[3]. See the often-cited letter of Isias to Hephaistion from 168 BC, which can be found in White 1986: 65–66; and Hunt and Edgar 1932: 283. See also the commentary on the letter in both Schubert 1939: 160–63; and Murphy O’Connor 1995: 56–57.

[4]. See 1 Thess. 1:2–5; 2 Thess. 1:3–4; 1 Cor. 1:4–9; Phil. 1:3–6; Rom. 1:8; Col. 1:3–5; Philem. 4–5; 2 Tim. 1:3–5; cf. 1 Tim. 1:12–14.

[5]. 2 Thess. 1:11–12; Phil. 1:9–11; Rom. 1:9–12; Col. 1:9–14; Philem. 6.

[6]. Cf. 2 Macc. 1:10–17, where elements of thanksgiving (1:11) and benediction (1:17) are mixed together. This makes it difficult to see how Schubert’s claim (1939: 44) can be sustained that the thanksgiving in Ephesians “is superfluous” after the benediction and therefore the mark of a pseudonymous author who wanted “to omit nothing which he considered formally essential in Pauline epistolography” (cf. Schnackenburg 1991: 71).

[7]. It is also difficult to identify the precise epistolary genre of many of Paul’s letters, including Ephesians. They blend the intimate quality of private correspondence, noticeable especially in those with thanksgiving prayer reports (although not as noticeable in Ephesians), with the authoritative quality of official correspondence, obvious from their length, their wide publication, and certain formal elements such as Paul’s identification of his apostolic office, his mention of cosenders (although not in Ephesians), and the address of his letters to entire communities. See Schubert 1939: 182; Stirewalt 2003: 25–55; and Richards 2004: 122–40.

[8]. Prior to 3:21, πίστις and its cognates appear in the letter seven times (1:1, 13, 15, 19; 2:8; 3:12, 17). After 3:21, they appear in the body of the letter only at 4:5, 13 and 6:16. After 3:21, ἀγάπη and its cognates appear twelve times (4:2, 15, 16; 5:1, 2 [2x], 25 [2x], 28 [3x], 33), whereas prior to 3:21 the terms appear only seven times (1:4, 6, 15; 2:4 [2x]; 3:17, 19). In the letter’s conclusion, πιστός and ἀγαπητός appear together in a description of Tychicus (6:21; cf. Col. 4:7), and εἰρήνη, ἀγάπη, πίστις, χάρις, and ἀγαπάω show up in the benediction (6:23–24). These concluding occurrences of the two concepts together with other important themes from the letter seem to have a summarizing function similar to that of 1:15.

A. Thanksgiving for Faith and Love, and Intercession for Illumination (1:15–19)

[1]. The more common translation “I also” for κἀγώ does not work here since the notion that Paul also gives thanks in addition to his readers or some other person or group is unsupported by the surrounding context and thus reads too much into the word. On this, see the still-valuable comments of Eadie 1883: 72–73. For the translation of κἀγώ as “I in particular,” see BDAG 487, although it does not adopt this meaning for Eph. 1:15, preferring instead to see the contraction simply as a synonym for ἐγώ.

[2]. The peculiarity of the remark was already discussed in the mid-fifth century. Theodoret comments, “From this remark some commentators surmised that the divine apostle wrote the letter without having yet laid eyes on them” (R. Hill 2001: 2.36).

[3]. Why would the author of Ephesians, if he were following Colossians, have expressed the second-person-plural possessive with the phrase καθ᾿ ὑμᾶς rather than with the simple genitive ὑμῶν? Why, with his greater interest in the connection between Gentile Christianity and Israel, would he have replaced the Χριστῷ of Col. 1:4 with κυρίῳ? And why would he have described his readers’ “love for all the saints” with the attributive use of a prepositional phrase rather than with a relative clause? Explanations can be offered for these changes (see Sellin 2008: 124–25), but it is at least as reasonable to think of the same author producing all three letters as it is to think of the author of Ephesians making the minute editorial decisions that these changes would involve.

[4]. Cf., e.g., 1 Thess. 1:3; 3:5, 6, 10, 12; 4:9–10, 13; 1 Cor. 1:4–8; 12:1–14:40; Phil. 1:3–4; 4:10–20; Rom. 1:12; 14:19; 15:5, 7, 14.

[5]. Here, then, ἵνα functions not as the introduction to a purpose clause but merely as a conjunction meaning “that” (BDAG 476; Wallace 1996: 475).

[6]. Something similar happens in 2 Cor. 1:3, where Paul begins his opening benediction with the statement Εὐλογητὸς ὁ θεὸς καὶ πατὴρ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ and then continues by dividing the designations θεός and πατήρ between two further descriptions: ὁ πατὴρ τῶν οἰκτιρμῶν καὶ θεὸς πάσης παρακλήσεως.

[7]. See, e.g., Exod. 24:17; Isa. 4:2; 35:2; 60:2, 13, where in each instance the LXX uses δόξα or δοξάζω.

[8]. Westcott (1906: 22) gives a much longer list of the occurrences of πνεῦμα in similar constructions and claims that they all refer to “the influence and temper” that allows a certain “principle or power or feeling or characteristic” to become effective in the person. Many of the references he lists, however, probably refer to the Holy Spirit rather than to a human spirit.

[9]. Cf. Isa. 11:2, where “the spirit of the LORD” rests on the coming Davidic king and is further identified with “the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and the fear of the LORD” (NRSV). As Fee (1994: 675) says, the “spirit” here is clearly the Spirit of God.

[10]. Cf. the use of ἐπίγνωσις in Phil. 1:9; Col. 1:9–10; and Philem. 6. Each of these statements, like Eph. 1:17, appears in the intercessory prayer report of a captivity epistle. On this, see O’Brien 1999: 133.

[11]. Winer 1881: 572. See examples in Eph. 1:18; 4:1–2; Col. 2:2; 3:16.

[12]. Cf. the expression ἠνεῴχθησαν ἡμῶν οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ τῆς καρδίας in 1 Clem. 36.2 (cf. 59.3), which may (Hoehner 2002: 261) or may not (Best 1998: 165) reflect a dependence on Ephesians.

[13]. Cf. the LXX of, e.g., Deut. 32:9; 1 Sam. 10:1; 26:19; 2 Sam. 14:16; 20:19; 21:3; 1 Kings 8:53 [8:12–13 MT, Eng.], 51; 2 Kings 21:4; Pss. 28:9; 33:12; 78:62, 71; 94:14; 106:40; Isa. 19:25; 47:6; Joel 2:17; Mic. 7:18. Also see Add. Esth. C (13:15–17); F (10:12); Sir. 24:12; Pss. Sol. 14:5.

[14]. Some commentators (e.g., Schnackenburg 1991: 75; Pokorný 1992: 79–80; Best 1998: 167–68; MacDonald 2000: 218) believe that οἱ ἅγιοι here refers to heavenly beings with whom the readers of the letter are, or will be (Sellin 2008: 133), spiritually united. In the Judaism of Paul’s time, the term could certainly refer to “holy ones” in the heavenly world (Ps. 88:6, 8 LXX; Sir. 42:17; Tob. 12:15; Jub. 31.14; 1 En. 1.9; 12.2; 14.23; 39.5; 47.2; 57.2; 61.10, 12; cf. Dan. 8:13; Tob. 11:14; Jude 14), and Paul may use it this way in 1 Thess. 3:13. The Qumran community offers precedent for thinking that God’s people on earth dwell in the company of such beings (1QHa 3.10; 11.21–22; 1QM 12.1–2, 4), and in 1QS 11 the speaker describes how his “eyes” have observed “wisdom, . . . knowledge and prudent understanding,” that these have been “a well of strength,” and that the community to which he belongs has “an inheritance in the lot of the holy ones.” The “holy ones” here are then defined as “the sons of the heavens” to whom the earthly community is united (lines 5–8, trans. García Martínez and Tigchelaar 1997). Despite these significant similarities with the language of Ephesians, we should probably understand Paul’s use of οἱ ἅγιοι here in 1:18 through the lens of his use of the term in 1:1; 3:18; 4:12; 5:3; and 6:18, and in those places it must refer to earthly Christians. See also Lincoln 1990: 60; Aletti 2001: 99; and Muddiman 2001: 86.

[15]. The phrase ὁ πλοῦτος τῆς δόξης τῆς κληρονομίας αὐτοῦ, with its string of genitives, is similar to the phrase ἔπαινον δόξης τῆς χάριτος αὐτοῦ in 1:6. Like that phrase, this one has the rhetorical effect of slowing the discourse and lending solemnity to the ideas it expresses.

[16]. The thought is similar to that of 1 Clem. 29, which speaks of God as “our gentle and compassionate Father, who has made us his chosen portion [ἐκλογῆς μέρος] for himself” and then quotes Deut. 32:8–9, which speaks of Israel as God’s “inheritance” (κληρονομία); cf. Deut. 4:34.

[17]. On this use of κατά, see BDAG 512, and on the appropriateness of this meaning here, see Hoehner 2002: 269.

[18]. Distinguishing carefully between the meanings of κράτος and ἰσχύς in this passage has a long interpretive history. See, e.g., Calvin 1965: 135; Alford 1857: 82; Ellicott 1859: 26–27; Abbott 1897: 31; and Westcott 1906: 25.

[19]. Cf. Theodoret (R. Hill 2001: 2.37; PG 82:517), “This is surely the reason that the divine apostle is quite carried away [ὑπεραγασθείς]: he first praises the surpassing greatness of his power, then the operation of the power of his might; and he looks for terms capable of expressing the baffling character of the reality.”

[20]. See, e.g., Westcott (1906: 22), who offers no reasons for his decision to read the optative; Robertson (1923: 309, 326, 983, 994), who correctly abandons the notion that this is the optative after final ἵνα but limits his arguments primarily to finding precedent for “the optative of future wish” following ἵνα in classical Greek; and Gnilka (1971: 89), who believes that the author’s use of the optative betrays an affinity with early patristic modes of prayer (cf. 1 Clem. 64; Barn. 21.5).

[21]. Some scribes (B, 1739, 1881, and a few other manuscripts) shortened δώῃ to the more familiar form δῷ. Cf. the same variation in the manuscript tradition of 2 Tim. 2:25.

[22]. Pace Gnilka (1971: 89), therefore, a comparison of the author’s δῴη to 1 Clem. 64 and Barn. 21.5 is not evidence that the author of Ephesians wrote in the subapostolic period.

[23]. Cf. Barn. 21.5: Ὁ δὲ θεός, ὁ τοῦ παντὸς κόσμου κυριεύων, δώῃ ὑμῖν σοφίαν, σύνεσιν (“And may God, who rules over the whole world, give you wisdom, understanding,” trans. Holmes 2007: 440–41). As Prostmeier (1999: 571–72n45) explains, whether to read δῴη or δώῃ is also a problem here. The manuscript tradition does not make clear whether the understood ι should go beneath the ω or the η. Prostmeier believes that Barnabas is echoing Eph. 1:17 at this point, but it seems equally likely that both Paul and Barnabas were independently echoing the language of 1 Chron. 22:12.

B. God’s Great Power Displayed in Christ and for the Church (1:20–23)

[1]. Paul most often uses ὁ Χριστός simply as a name for Jesus in Ephesians, but because in 1:20 it appears within an allusion to Ps. 110:1, it probably carries its literal royal meaning, “the Anointed One,” or in Hebrew, “Messiah.” Cf. BDAG 1091.

[2]. Ἐγείρας and καθίσας are adverbial participles of means. See the comments on identifying this kind of participle in Wallace 1996: 629; cf. Hoehner 2002: 274.

[3]. See Mark 12:35–37; Matt. 22:41–46; Luke 20:41–44; and Jesus’s conflation of Dan. 7:13 with Ps. 110:1 (109:1 LXX) in Mark 14:62; Matt. 26:64; and Luke 22:69.

[4]. Yet cf. 1 Cor. 15:25; Heb. 10:13, where the words of Ps. 110:1b (109:1b LXX) explicitly appear. See the discussion in Lincoln 1982: 41–42.

[5]. See, e.g., Mark 10:30; Matt. 12:32; Luke 18:30; 2 Esd. (4 Ezra) 6:9; 7:12–13; 8:1; m. Peʾah 1.1; m. Qidd. 4.14; m. Sanh. 10.3; m. ʾAbot 4.1, 17; 5.19. Cf., e.g., 1 Cor. 10:11; Rom. 8:38; 2 Bar. 48.50. Cf. Schürer 1979: 537n86.

[6]. 1 Cor. 1:20; 2:6, 8; 3:18; Gal. 1:4; 2 Cor. 4:4; Rom. 12:2; 1 Tim. 6:17; 2 Tim. 4:10; Titus 2:12.

[7]. For the house graffito, see Trebilco 2004: 34n151; for the Assos inscription, see Sasse, TDNT 1:207, citing SIG 797.9.

[8]. Paul in Eph. 1:22: καὶ πάντα ὑπέταξεν ὑπὸ τοὺς πόδας αὐτοῦ

Paul in 1 Cor. 15:27: πάντα γὰρ ὑπέταξεν ὑπὸ τοὺς πόδας αὐτοῦ

LXX of Ps. 8:7 (8:6): πάντα ὑπέταξας ὑποκάτω τῶν ποδῶν αὐτοῦ

MT of Ps. 8:7 (8:6): כֹּל שַׁתָּה תַחַת־רַגְלָיו

[9]. On the relationship between Ps. 8 and Egyptian conceptions of a connection between the king and the divine, see Kraus 1993a: 183–84.

[10]. The earliest Christians probably also considered themselves the “vanguard” (Vorhut) of the eschatological ἐκκλησία τοῦ θεοῦ. Cf. the use of the phrase קהל אל in 1QM 4.10 and the perspective of Stuhlmacher 1992: 357, taken up and expanded in Gehring 2004: 160. Horbury (1997: 13) observes that the word is used in the LXX both for Israel in its entirety and for other assemblies. This varied usage, he says, may have made it an especially appropriate term for the church, with its elements both of continuity and discontinuity with historic Israel.

[11]. The early Pauline letters often use the word ἐκκλησία to refer to the individual gatherings of God’s people in a particular house, city, or region. Paul can speak of the “church” that meets in the house of Prisca and Aquila (Rom. 16:5), to the church that meets in Philemon’s house (Philem. 1:2), and the “church” (in the singular) in the cities of Thessalonica (1 Thess. 1:1; 2 Thess. 1:1), Corinth (1 Cor. 1:2; 2 Cor. 1:1), and Laodicea (Col. 4:16). When he moves to the regional level, he speaks of the “churches” (plural) in Judea (1 Thess. 2:14; Gal. 1:22), Galatia (1 Cor. 16:1; Gal. 1:2), Asia (1 Cor. 16:19), and Macedonia (2 Cor. 8:1).

[12]. As Best (1998: 626; cf. 190–91) comments, Colossians forms something of a bridge between the two groups of letters since it speaks both of the local church (1:2; 4:15) and of the church universal (1:18, 24). Gehring (2004: 154–55) observes helpfully that if Nympha’s church was located in Laodicea (and the context makes this probable), then Col. 4:15–16 shows us that Paul considered οἱ ἀδελφοί in Laodicea to constitute the whole church in that city and considered the church that met in Nympha’s house (ἡ κατ’ οἶκον αὐτῆς ἐκκλησία) to be one expression of that church. Cf. 1 Cor. 14:23; Rom. 16:23 (written from Corinth); and the analysis of Gehring 2004: 155–65.

[13]. See, e.g., Calvin 1965: 138; Barth 1974: 157–58; Dunn 1992: 153n1; BDAG 242; RSV; NRSV; TNIV.

[14]. This is the majority position among commentators. See, e.g., Alford 1857: 83; Ellicott 1859: 30; Eadie 1883: 104–5; Abbott 1897: 34; Gnilka 1971: 97; Caird 1976: 48; Lincoln 1990: 66; MacDonald 2000: 220; and Hoehner 2002: 85.

[15]. “Head” and “foot” were commonly used together in antiquity to describe the whole physical person, just as they are in the English expression “from head to foot” (Lev. 13:12 LXX; Job 2:7 LXX; Homer, Il. 23.169). They also formed a natural pair when used in figures of speech (1 Cor. 12:21) and could be used together to mean “completely everything.” See, e.g., Aristophanes, Plut. 649–50: τὰ πράγματα ἐκ τῶν ποδῶν εἰς τὴν κεφαλήν σοι πάντ’ ἐρῶ (I will tell you everything from feet to head). Cf. LSJ 945; Schlier, TDNT 3:674–75; LEH 338. Dawes (1998: 141n68) observes correctly, however, that Paul does not use the feet metaphor from Ps. 8 in the same way that he uses the head metaphor: “Christ has feet, but he is the head.”

[16]. Cf. the exegesis of, e.g., Howard 1974: 353; Lincoln 1990: 67–68; Dawes 1998: 141, 245–46; O’Brien 1999: 145–46; and Aletti 2001: 103–4. A warm debate surrounds whether κεφαλή sometimes means “source” in the NT, particularly in relation to Paul’s figurative use of the term in 1 Cor. 11:3 and Eph. 5:23, where the husband is said to be “head” of the wife. Here in Eph. 1:22, however, the term must mean “a being of high status” or “superior rank” (BDAG 542; Best 1998: 630–31; Dawes 1998: 139).

[17]. On the two elements of the metaphor, the church as a harmoniously working body of many parts and the church as the body of Christ, see Dunn 1992: 148–53.

[18]. The metaphor moves, therefore, in the opposite direction to its movement in 1 Corinthians, where, as we have just seen, the idea of a harmoniously working body of many parts is more prominent than the idea of the church as the body of Christ. See Best 1998: 192–93.

[19]. Cf. Roose (2005: 138–41), who sees this as a post-Pauline development of 1 Cor. 15:27 and one that breaks the boundaries of Pauline theology. In 1 Corinthians and Romans, she argues, the metaphor is used in a “democratizing” way to emphasize the unity and equality of all believers, but in Ephesians the church, as Christ’s body, is given hegemony over the entire cosmos (Roose 2005: 117–20, 140–41). If the “all” of Eph. 1:22 refers primarily to the evil powers listed in 1:21, however, the change in emphasis is less dramatic and more understandable as an organic development from the way the metaphor is used in the undisputed letters. It has simply been employed in a situation where the letter’s audience was tempted to fear the inimical powers and needed to be reassured that their incorporation into Christ had given them victory over these powers.

[20]. Best 1998: 184; Hoehner 2002: 298. In opposition to this argument, Lincoln (1990: 77) claims that Paul can use καρποφορέω (active) in Col. 1:10 and καρποφορέομαι (passive) in Col. 1:6 with no apparent difference in meaning (cf., e.g., Moule 1957: 50; O’Brien 1982: 23). It is not clear, however, that this example proves Lincoln’s point (Lightfoot 1879: 135; Haupt 1902a: 9).

[21]. It is significant that Origen, himself writing in Greek, simply assumes that the participle is passive (Heine 2002: 116–17).

[22]. This is the conclusion of a number of interpreters. See, e.g., Lightfoot 1879: 263; Dawes 1998: 237–48; Hoehner 2002: 299–301.

[23]. Cf. Col. 3:11, where πάντα seems to function as a predicate nominative (“Christ is all things”) and ἐν πᾶσιν as an adverbial prepositional phrase (“in all kinds of people”). Pace Hoehner (2002: 295–96), an adverbial use of the entire phrase does not seem to be a viable option in either 1 Cor. 12:6 or 15:28. See also T. Ab. 13.14 (rec. A), τὰ πάντα ἐν πᾶσιν ἐν πυρὶ καὶ ζυγῷ δοκιμάζονται, which Allison (2003: 275) translates as “all things in everybody are tested by fire and balance.”

[24]. There may be some precedent for this in Dio Chrysostom, De philosopho (Or. 71) 1, εἰσιν οἵ φασι δεῖν πάντα ἐν πᾶσιν εἶναι περιττὸν τὸν φιλόσοφον, which might be rendered “There are some who say that it is necessary for the philosopher to be excellent in every way.” The phrase is slightly different from what we find in Ephesians, since πάντα lacks the article, but the similarity is still close.

[25]. For alliteration with the letter p, see, e.g., the frequently recurring phrase πολυμερῶς καὶ πολυτρόπως or its equivalent (Philo, Drunkenness 170; Heb. 1:1a; Maximus of Tyre, Dialexeis 1.2b) and the use of words with initial p in Melito of Sardis, Peri Pascha (e.g., §§1, 4, 17). Cf. Attridge 1989: 37n17; Witherington 2007: 245–46; Sellin 2008: 154n211.

IV. From Children of Wrath to New Creation (2:1–10)

[1]. Cf. Hoehner’s title (2002: 305) for the section: “New Position Individually.”

A. Children of Wrath Like All the Rest (2:1–3)

[1]. Cf. 1:13–14, where Paul applies the blessings of God described in 1:3–12 directly to his readers and again shifts into second-person address.

[2]. This original sentence was probably similar to Col. 1:13 or Eph. 2:5a.

[3]. Verse 2: ἐν αἷς ποτε περιεπατήσατε κατὰ . . .

Verse 3: ἐν οἷς καὶ ἡμεῖς πάντες ἀνεστράφημέν ποτε ἐν . . .

[4]. He does not, however, mean “you Gentiles” (Barth 1974: 211–12; Bruce 1984: 280; O’Brien 1999: 156), since at this point in the letter Paul has not yet started to distinguish between his readers as Gentiles and Jews. See the comments above on 1:12 and 1:13. Gombis (2004: 404–5, 407, 410) believes that in 2:1–16 the author is defending his claim in 1:20–23 that Christ has been exalted to the status of king and victor over his enemies, following the pattern of divine-warfare narratives in the ancient Near East. If this were correct, however, we would probably find a more explicit indication in 2:1 that Paul is defending his claim in 1:20–23 against those who might doubt it.

[5]. For this understanding of Matt. 8:22 and Luke 9:60, see Bultmann, TDNT 4:893; and Fitzmyer 1983: 835–36.

[6]. Later, in 1 John 3:14, John says that this movement from death to life proves itself in love for fellow Christians.

[7]. The νεκρὰ ἔργα of Heb. 6:1 and 9:14 are probably also deeds that deserve death because they are sins. See Attridge 1989: 164.

[8]. So far, Paul has used the following phrases:

1:4 ἁγίους καὶ ἀμώμους

1:5 τὴν εὐδοκίαν τοῦ θελήματος αὐτοῦ

1:8 σοφίᾳ καὶ φρονήσει

1:11 τὴν βουλὴν τοῦ θελήματος αὐτοῦ

1:17 σοφίας καὶ ἀποκαλύψεως

1:19 τὴν ἐνέργειαν τοῦ κράτους τῆς ἰσχύος αὐτοῦ

Schlier (1957: 101) is probably correct that the phrase is a “redundancy typical of preaching” (ein predigtmässiger Doppelausdruck).

[9]. See the LXX of Ps. 18:13–14 (19:12–13 Eng.); Ezek. 3:20; 18:24; and cf. Rom. 5:20.

[10]. Origen and Jerome (Heine 2002: 120), for example, believed that παράπτωμα referred to the beginning of sin and ἁμαρτία to the complete act. Eadie (1883: 118–19) suggests that the two terms refer to flagrant sin and sinful thoughts respectively. Seeing the two terms as synonymous receives confirmation in Col. 2:13, which makes basically the same point as Eph. 2:1 and uses almost identical language to do so: καὶ ὑμᾶς νεκροὺς ὄντας [ἐν] τοῖς παραπτώμασιν. Instead of following this phrase with καὶ ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις ὑμῶν, however, Col. 2:13 has καὶ τῇ ἀκροβυστίᾳ τῆς σαρκὸς ὑμῶν. In Ephesians, Paul will take up the issue of his readers’ status as the ἀκροβυστία later (2:11). Here he is concerned simply with their sin against God’s law. For Gentile knowledge of τὸ δικαίωμα τοῦ θεοῦ and culpability for disobeying it, see Rom. 1:32; 2:14–16.

[11]. Porkoný (1992: 97) and Hübner (1997: 156) claim that these uses of the plural are only in “citations” or “traditional material.” For all but three of them (1 Cor. 15:3; Rom. 4:7; 11:27), however, that is a matter of debate. It would be very difficult to make a case for the use of traditional material in Rom. 7:5.

[12]. It appears thirty-three times in the Pauline corpus, and every use is metaphorical. In the rest of the NT, only John comes close to this with two metaphorical uses in the Gospel and ten in the Epistles. Cf. the use of הָלַךְ in the OT in such passages as Isa. 33:15 and Ps. 15:2 (HALOT 1:247).

[13]. The relative pronoun αἷς is feminine, to agree with the closest of its two antecedents, ἁμαρτίαις.

[14]. On this element of Paul’s theology in Romans, see Dunn 1998b: 111–14.

[15]. I have used, but slightly modified, the translation of Babbitt 1927–36.

[16]. My trans.; text in BDAG 23. Cf. the second-century-BC treatise De universi natura (On the Nature of the Universe), which divides the world into the heaven, where the gods live; earth, where human beings live; and the “airy place” (ἀέριον), where the demons live.

[17]. I have used, but modified, the translation of Hicks 1980.

[18]. See Arnold (1989: 60–61), who quotes from PGM 4.2699: “Protect me from every demon of the air.”

[19]. Cf. 1 Tim. 3:6–7, 11; 2 Tim. 2:26; 3:3; and Titus 2:3. In addition to ὁ διάβολος (ho diabolos, the devil) Paul uses the names ὁ σατανᾶς (ho satanas, the Adversary, Satan; 1 Thess. 2:18; 2 Thess. 2:9; 1 Cor. 5:5; 7:5; 2 Cor. 2:11; 11:14; 12:7; 1 Tim. 1:20; 5:15), βελίαρ (Beliar, Beliar; 2 Cor. 6:15), and ὁ πειράζων (ho peirazōn, the tempter; 1 Thess. 3:5) for this spiritual being. Cf. Arnold 1989: 65.

[20]. The phrase οἱ υἱοὶ τῆς ἀπειθείας (also present in 5:6; cf. 5:8) preserves a Semitic use of the noun בֵּן to mean “one of a group or type, with a certain destiny” (HALOT 1:138). See, e.g., Num. 17:25 MT (17:10 Eng.); 2 Sam. 3:34; and Hos. 10:9; 1 Thess. 5:5.

[21]. E.g., Calvin 1965: 141; Abbott 1897: 43; Robinson 1904: 49; Westcott 1906: 30; Dibelius and Greeven 1953: 66; Barth 1974: 116–17; Bruce 1984: 283; Porkorný 1992: 100; Hübner 1997: 159–60; O’Brien 1999: 161; cf. Muddiman 2001: 105–6; Yee 2005: 46–56.

[22]. Hoehner 2002: 317–18; cf. Alford 1857: 87–88; Ellicott 1859: 35; Eadie 1883: 130–31; Haupt 1902a: 53; Lincoln 1990: 97; Schnackenburg 1991: 92; Best 1998: 207–8.

[23]. Although the two clauses ἐν αἷς (v. 2a) and ἐν οἷς (v. 3) are rhetorically parallel to one another, the relative pronoun οἷς does not refer back to παραπτώμασιν (v. 1) in the same way that αἷς refers back to ἁμαρτίαις. The antecedent of οἷς is instead the much closer noun υἱοῖς (v. 2b).

[24]. 1 Thess. 4:5; Gal. 5:16, 24; Rom. 1:24; 6:12; 7:7–8; 13:14; Col. 3:5; Eph. 4:22; 1 Tim. 6:9; Titus 2:12; 3:3; 2 Tim. 2:22; 3:6; 4:3.

[25]. See Schrenk (TDNT 3:53), who points to the use of the term in PGM 4.1521 (cf. 1532): τὰ ἐμὰ θελήματα πάντα ποιείτω, ta ema thelēmata panta poieitō, let her perform all my desires). In the NT, θέλημα occurs in the plural only here in Eph. 2:3 and in the quotation of Isa. 44:28 in Acts 13:22 (Hoehner 2002: 321), but the idiom ποιεῖν θελήματα occurs fairly frequently in the LXX: Isa. 44:28; 58:13; 2 Macc. 1:3.

[26]. In Rom. 12:2 Paul uses the term νοῦς (nous, mind). Cf. Abbott 1897: 44; Bruce 1984: 284; and Marshall 2004b: 320n22.

[27]. This is confirmed by the other uses of the term σάρξ in Ephesians, all of which regard σάρξ as either neutral (2:11; 6:5, 12) or positive (2:14; 5:29, 31). Best (1998: 209) sees a difference between Ephesians and the undisputed letters in the use of the personal pronoun (our) with σάρξ here in 2:3. Paul, he argues, rarely if ever (Rom. 7:18?) uses σάρξ with a personal pronoun when he connects σάρξ with sin. The author uses the personal pronoun here, he says, to make clear that σάρξ is not a cosmic power outside of human beings. Dunn (1998b: 66–67) observes perceptively, however, that in Rom. 7–8 there is a close connection between the “I” and the “flesh,” and yet Paul makes clear that it is “sin,” not the “I” (and therefore not the “flesh”), that stands outside of humanity and pushes human beings to rebel against God. If Dunn is correct, then there is agreement between Romans and Ephesians on this very subtle point, an agreement that actually favors the authenticity of Ephesians.

[28]. On the “genitive of destination,” see Wallace 1996: 101. The expression “children of wrath” probably preserves the Semitic use of בֵּן to refer to “one of a group or type, with a certain destiny” (HALOT 1:138). See note 20 above and 1 Sam. 26:16; Pss. 79:11 MT, Eng. [78:11 LXX]; 102:21 MT [101:21 LXX; 102:20 Eng.]; 2 Thess. 2:3; and 1 Pet. 1:14. For hesitations about seeing the expression with τέκνα as a Semitic idiom, see Jobes 2005: 115.

[29]. See, e.g., Gal. 2:15 (φύσει Ἰουδαῖοι, Jews by birth); Sophocles, Oed. col. 1295 (φύσει νεώτερος, younger by birth); Aj. 1301 (φύσει . . . βασίλεια, a queen by birth); and Herodotus, Hist. 7.134.2 (φύσι . . . γεγονότες εὖ, noble by birth).

[30]. The term φύσει sometimes referred to someone’s origins “by birth” (φύσει) in contrast to who they were “by adoption” (θέσει; Diogenes Laertius, Vit. phil. 9.25). In light of the important role that “adoption” (υἱοθεσία) plays in the benediction (1:5; cf. 1:11, 14), it is tempting to find an implicit contrast here with the status of believers as adopted children of God.

[31]. Among the texts listed in BDAG 32, see especially T. Benj. 11.3; 1 Cor. 1:20; 2:6; 3:18; Gal. 1:4; 2 Cor. 4:4; Rom. 12:2; 1 Tim. 6:17; Titus 2:12; 2 Tim. 4:10; Ign. Eph. 17.1; 19.1; SIG 797.9.

[32]. By the first century AD, the Hebrew term עוֹלָם and the Aramaic term עָלְמָא could mean both “age” and “world,” and the use of αἰών with these two senses in the NT may originate with this development. See Sasse, TDNT 1:204.

[33]. Epiphanius wrote in the late fourth century AD, and the earliest manuscript of the Alexander Romance comes from the third century AD. Stoneman (1991: 8–17) argues forcefully that the Alexander Romance contains much ancient material, and he believes that the section describing Alexander’s establishment of the worship of Serapis at Alexandria (which also mentions the cult of “Aion”) dates to the early Ptolemaic period (30.6). As Stoneman says, however, the Alexander Romance was the object of much editorial activity over many centuries. Any early dating for the reference to organized worship of “Aion” must, therefore, remain very uncertain.

[34]. W. Oldfather (1925–28) translates the relevant phrase, “For I am not eternal, but a man.”

[35]. On Ignatius’s use of the word, see Schoedel 1985: 63n2, 91n24.

[36]. According to Yee (2005: 49–53), the author uses αἰών in an “ethnographic” sense as if it were the national god of the Gentiles, who stands in contrast to the true, Jewish God.

B. Objects of God’s Mercy (2:4–7)

[1]. LXX: Exod. 34:6; Num. 14:18; 2 Esd. 19:17 (Neh. 9:17 MT, Eng.); Pss. 85:5, 15 (86:5, 15 MT, Eng.); 102:8 (103:8 MT, Eng.); 144:8 (145:8 MT [גדל חסד], Eng.); Joel 2:13; Jon. 4:2; Sir. 2:11; 3 Macc. 6:9; 1QS 4.4; 1QHa 15.27; 19.28; 20.14; 23.5. Cf. 1 Pet. 1:3 (κατὰ τὸ πολὺ αὐτοῦ ἔλεος). For the translation of πολυέλεος as “very merciful,” see LSJ 1438 and LEH 505. On the parallels between the language of abundant mercy in Ephesians and the Qumran texts, see especially Kuhn 1968: 119; and on the terms ἐλεέω and ἔλεος generally, see TLNT 1:471–79.

[2]. It is possible that 1:4; 3:17; and 5:1 also belong in this category.

[3]. Robertson (1934: 478) further specifies this as a cognate accusative of “inner content,” meaning that the accusative form is not the object of the verb but the means of its accomplishment. In these instances, the addition of “with” in English translation is appropriate. Cf. Eph. 4:1, τῆς κλήσεως ἧς ἐκλήθητε, although here the accusative relative pronoun has been attracted to the genitive case of its antecedent.

[4]. Eph. 2:1 καὶ ὑμᾶς ὄντας νεκροὺς τοῖς παραπτώμασιν καὶ ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις ὑμῶν

Eph. 2:5 καὶ ὄντας ἡμᾶς νεκροὺς τοῖς παραπτώμασιν

Col. 2:13 καὶ ὑμᾶς νεκροὺς ὄντας [ἐν] τοῖς παραπτώμασιν καὶ τῇ ἀκροβυστίᾳ τῆς σαρκὸς ὑμῶν

[5]. Ellicott 1859: 37–38; Schnackenburg 1991: 94. The καί, then, is probably ascensive (“even when we were dead”), as, e.g., Eadie 1883: 141; Abbott 1897: 47; Porkorný 1992: 102; and Hoehner 2002: 329 believe. Others have taken it as concessive (Aletti 2001: 126–27), as a simple repetition of the καί in 2:1 (Dibelius and Greeven 1954: 67), as part of an early Christian liturgical phrase that also appears in Col. 2:13a (J. Sanders 1965: 220, 222–23), or as simply a reformulation, like Eph. 2:1, of Col. 2:13a (Best 1997a: 78).

[6]. The articles on the word in LSJ 1670 and BDAG 954 imply this, and a search of the TLG seems to confirm it.

[7]. Dan. 7:9; 2 Tim. 2:12; Mark 10:37; Matt. 19:28; Luke 22:30; Rev. 3:21; 4:4, 10; 11:16; 4Q521 2.7; cf. Wis. 3:8; 1 Cor. 6:2–3.

[8]. Col. 2:12–13 and 3:1–2 express similar ideas, but mention of the believer’s heavenly reign with Christ is unique to Ephesians. See Allen 1986: 105.

[9]. The following example, from Ephesus sometime after AD 14, is typical: “By the favor ([χάρι]τι) of Caesar Augustus God from the holy revenues which he himself gave to the goddess the road was made level in the proconsulship of Sextus Appuleius” (Harrison 2003: 49). The goddess is Ephesian Artemis.

[10]. This understanding of the background for Paul’s use of grace terminology in 2:5, 7–8 seems more plausible than the specifically Ephesian background that Harrison 2003: 242–47 finds for it in magic and the cult of Artemis.

[11]. Campbell (2008a: 107) comments, “Sometimes the context can create stative Aktionsart even if the lexeme is not itself stative. Stative perfects are normally present in their temporal reference.”

[12]. If the disputed letters are included in the analysis of the evidence, however, this perspective is less unusual. See 2 Tim. 1:9 and Titus 3:5.

[13]. When Paul touches on the believer’s resurrection from the dead elsewhere in his letters, he never refers to it explicitly as an event that has already taken place, even when he correlates it with the resurrection of Christ (1 Cor. 6:14; 2 Cor. 4:14; Rom. 6:5, 8; 8:11; Phil. 3:10–11). He speaks of it only as a future event (1 Thess. 4:16; 1 Cor. 15:12–58; 2 Cor. 4:16–5:10; Rom. 8:23, 29; 11:15; Phil. 3:21; 2 Tim. 2:18).

[14]. See especially Lincoln 1983: 621–22.

[15]. Cf. 1 Thess. 2:14–15; 1 Cor. 1:18–2:5; 4:8–17; 5:7–8; 6:7; 9:19–23; 10:31–11:1; Gal. 2:19; Phil. 3:10; 2 Cor. 4:7–12; 8:8–9; Rom. 6:5–6, 11; Philem. 1 (“a prisoner of Christ Jesus”).

[16]. If, as is likely, we should read φορέσωμεν rather than φορέσομεν at 1 Cor. 15:49, moreover, Paul instructs the Corinthians to bear the image of the heavenly last Adam in the present.

[17]. See further Ridderbos 1975: 537–39 and Arnold 1989: 148.

[18]. See already Origen (Heine 2002: 126) and many commentators after him, e.g., Jerome (Heine 2002: 127); Alford 1857: 90; Westcott 1906: 32; Bruce 1984: 287; and O’Brien 1999: 171n72.

[19]. As I. Marshall (1996: 344–45) says, the mistake in the notion that the soteriology of Ephesians differs from that of the undisputed letters lies in “assuming that the thrust of Paul’s thought is towards the future rather than being firmly rooted in what God has done in Christ.”

[20]. Out of the fifteen uses of ἐνδείκνυμι and its cognate noun ἔνδειξις in the NT, only two (Heb. 6:10, 11) fall outside the Pauline Epistles.

[21]. The word ἐπέρχομαι can refer to the coming of a disaster or attack (BDAG 361–62). For this understanding of the phrase, see, e.g., Dibelius and Greeven 1953: 67 and Lindemann 1975: 129–30; cf. Schlier 1957: 112–18 and Barth 1974: 222–23. Best (1998: 198) takes this interpretation very seriously, and at one point seems to adopt it, although eventually he concludes that “there is no easy solution” to the proper reading of the phrase (1998: 223–24). The idea seems to have its origins in Reitzenstein (1921: 234–37), who interprets the αἰῶν and αἰῶνες in Eph. 2:2, 7; 3:9 and in Ign. Eph. 8.1 and 19.2 as personal powers. He believes this religious concept is indebted to Persian mysticism and dualism, a theory that, as we saw above in the additional note on 2:2, is unlikely to be correct.

[22]. Admittedly, as Lindemann (1975: 129) and Best (1998: 223) observe, the phrase in these instances is in the singular, whereas in Eph. 2:7 it is in the plural. The plural expression ἀπὸ τῶν αἰώνων καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν γενεῶν appears in Col. 1:26, however, and as the term γενεῶν indicates, the whole phrase should probably be understood temporally (R. Wilson 2005: 176–77). Cf. also Jude 25 and 1 Tim. 1:17 (Abbott 1897: 50).

[23]. See Philo Sacrifices 27; Virtues 84; Moses 1.249 (Weiss, TDNT 9:490). Jerome describes χρηστότης as “a mild, tender, tranquil virtue, prepared to share its goods; it invites to friendship; it is sweet in its speech. . . . [It differs from goodness] in that goodness can be a bit somber, frowning in moral austerity, no doubt doing good and giving what is asked but without being sweet and without attracting people by its mildness” (PL 26:420, as quoted and translated in Spicq, TLNT 3:515n20). The definition “simplicity, silly good nature” in LSJ 2007 seems to be based on a mistaken reading of Pseudo-Plato, Def. 412e. The editors of LSJ believe that this passage defines χρηστότης as ἤθους ἀπλαστία μετ’ ἀλογιστίας (simplicity of character with thoughtlessness), but the text of Definitiones here actually says the opposite: ἤθους ἀπλαστία μετ’ εὐλογιστίας (simplicity of character with prudence).

[24]. Pace Lindemann (1975: 119), who accepts ἐν τῷ Χριστῷ as original.

[25]. Barth (1974: 220) surprisingly says that this variant merits “some consideration,” although he does not conclude that it is correct.

[26]. Gnilka (1971: 118n5) thinks that the motivation was rather to specify the grace as the grace of Christ.

C. The Nature and Consequences of God’s Grace (2:8–10)

[1]. For this understanding of γάρ, see Schlier 1957: 115.

[2]. Since τοῦτο is neuter, Paul was perhaps thinking of the neuter form τὸ σωτήριον (which he uses at 6:17) or already looking ahead to his use of the term δῶρον in the next clause. That the antecedent of τοῦτο is not πίστεως in 2:8a (as some earlier commentators thought) is clear from 2:9a, where Paul denies that τοῦτο is ἐξ ἔργων (ex ergōn, from works). It makes much better sense to say that “salvation” is not from works than to say that “faith” is not from works. See the especially thorough discussion in Eadie 1883: 152.

[3]. Cf. Rom. 5:15, 17, where, however, Paul uses the term δωρεά (cf. Eph. 3:7; 4:7) rather than δῶρον. This is the only use of δῶρον in the Pauline corpus.

[4]. Even Titus 3:4–7 occurs in a context of polemics against οἱ ἐκ τῆς περιτομῆς (1:10).

[5]. Ephesians 2:10 gives the grounds for all of 2:8b–9 (καὶ τοῦτο οὐκ ἐξ ὑμῶν, θεοῦ τὸ δῶρον· οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων, ἵνα μή τις καυχήσηται; Eadie 1883: 156; Abbott 1897; Best 1998: 229) and not merely for 2:9b (ἵνα μή τις καυχήσηται; Schnackenburg 1991: 98).

[6]. Cf. Aelian, Nat. an. 153, who thinks that the goat may be a “creation of [the god] Prometheus” (ποίημα Προμηθέως). Philo is fond of calling God “the Maker” (ὁ ποιητής; e.g., Creation 7, 9, 21, 53, 77, 88; Worse 86, 124) and at one point (Worse 125) develops an elaborate analogy between God and a poet, in which he calls the works of God’s creation the “poems of God” (θεοῦ ποιήματα). Paul’s use of the term, however, is not metaphorical and thus stands closer to Aelian’s use. Pace Lincoln 1990: 114; O’Brien 1999: 178; and Muddiman 2002: 112, the term is never used unambiguously in the LXX of God’s work at creation, although it is used of God’s work generally.

[7]. Eadie (1883: 156) argues against this idea, claiming it is based on an “unwarranted assumption,” but something must account for Paul’s sudden introduction of this theme, and this idea at least has some historical precedent elsewhere in Pauline and other early Christian literature.

[8]. See, e.g., Lincoln 1990: 115; Schnackenburg 1991: 99; Best 1998: 231; MacDonald 2000: 234.

[9]. This counts appearances of both ἀγαθά and καλά with ἔργα.

[10]. Admittedly, 2 Tim. 2:14 occurs within one of the disputed letters. See BDAG 366; BDF §235.4; Moule 1953: 50; and Zerwick 1963: 43.

[11]. The relative pronoun οἷς is dative rather than accusative (ἅ) because it has been attracted to the case of its antecedent ἔργοις (Winer 1881: 149, 163; Robertson 1934: 716).

[12]. See the use of πρό in 1:4, προορίσας in 1:5, προέθετο in 1:9, and προορισθέντες . . . πρόθεσιν in 1:11, and cf. the use of πρόθεσιν in 3:11.

V. From Existence without God to Membership in the People of God (2:11–22)

[1]. Christ’s death, however, is still not a demonstration of weakness, such as we find in 1–2 Corinthians, but a powerful death that kills the enmity between God and human beings, whether Jewish or Gentile (v. 16).

[2]. See the discussion of L. Johnson (2001: 148–49, 164, 174) on the use of the term in 1 Timothy.

A. The Special Plight of the Gentiles and God’s Response (2:11–13)

[1]. On this, see Winter 1994: 123–43; Hardin 2008; and the introduction to the commentary.

[2]. The two uses of ὅτι do not represent two separate, grammatically equal clauses. The second ὅτι resumes the first ὅτι after the lengthy interruption of 2:11 (cf. 2:5a). Rhetorically, then, much of 2:11 (οἱ λεγόμενοι ἀκροβυστία ὑπὸ τῆς λεγομένης περιτομῆς ἐν σαρκὶ χειροποιήτου) is a parenthesis (see NAB; NJB). Conceptually, however, the two clauses beginning with ὅτι describe two main components of the Gentiles’ plight (see TNIV; NRSV; ESV).

[3]. See the use of (ἡ) περιτομή in Gal. 2:7–9; Phil. 3:3; Rom. 3:30; 4:9, 12; 15:8; and Col. 3:11 and of οἱ ἐκ περιτομῆς in Gal. 2:12; Col. 4:11 (οἱ ὄντες ἐκ περιτομῆς); Titus 1:10; and Acts 11:2. Cf. Acts 10:45; Justin, Dial. 1.3; m. Ned. 3.11.

[4]. Pace Lincoln (1987: 619–20), the perspective is not unlike that of Rom. 9:1–5 and 9:30–10:21.

[5]. Pace Barth (1959: 125; 1983: 46), but also pace Lincoln, whose 1987 article is organized around a polemical interaction with Barth. Although Lincoln would agree (against Barth) that the author assumes a distance between non-Christian Jews and Christians here, Lincoln nevertheless sees a coolness and detachment in the description of circumcision that reveals a post-Pauline setting.

[6]. Eadie 1883: 163–64; Schlier 1957: 120; Gnilka 1971: 135; Best 1998: 241; Hoehner 2002: 356.
