[7]. See Paul’s use of Ps. 110:1 in Eph. 1:20–22; his possible allusion to Exod. 17:1–7 and Num. 20:2–13 in 1 Cor. 10:4; his echo of such Scriptures as Isa. 11:1, 10 and Ezek. 34:23–24 in Rom. 1:2–4; and his possible allusion to Gen. 15:6 and Hab. 2:4 in Rom. 3:21.

[8]. On the messianic expectations of some Jews in Second Temple Judaism, see Collins 1995, and on the occasional interpretation of Ps. 110:1 in a messianic sense in non-Christian Jewish texts, see Juel 1988: 137–39.

[9]. Pace Yee 2005: 98–99. On the difficulty of distinguishing the two constructions, see Wallace 1996: 647n83.

[10]. See Heine 2002: 132, although Heine’s rendering “commonwealth” for both πολιτεία (Origen) and conuersatio (Jerome) obscures this nuance. “Way of life” seems to have been the most common meaning for πολιτεία among the Greek-speaking church fathers (PGL 1113–14). LSJ 1434 think that this is “perhaps” the meaning of the term in Eph. 2:12.

[11]. As in 3 Macc. 3:21, 23; Josephus, Ant. 12.119; Acts 22:28. See, e.g., Haupt 1902a: 71; Pokorný 1992: 114; Hoehner 2002: 256–57; MacDonald 2004: 438n42 (a change from her 2000: 242). Cf. Aletti 2001: 142–44.

[12]. As in Plato, Resp. 10.619c; Appian, Bell. civ. 2.19.138. See, e.g., Abbott 1897: 57–58; Eadie 1883: 164–65; Robinson 1928: 159; Lincoln 1990: 137; O’Brien 1999: 189; MacDonald 2000: 242; BDAG 845. Cf. Best 1998: 241.

[13]. The genitives, both here and in the previous clause, are genitives of separation (BDF §180.1; BDR §180.1n2).

[14]. Here I am following Cohen 1999: 110–19, 125–29 and the application of Cohen’s discussion to Eph. 2:12 in Aletti 2001: 143–44.

[15]. Cf. 4:18, where the Gentiles’ alienation (ἀπηλλοτριωμένοι) from “the life of God” seems to mean alienation from the way of living that God requires and that leads to life.

[16]. Cf. Schlier 1957: 120–21; Best 1998: 242. This approach is not uncontroversial. Some commentators believe that Paul (or the author) refers to a series of covenants with various people such as Abraham, Isaac, Israel, Jacob (e.g, Gnilka 1971: 136; Lincoln 1990: 137; Aletti 2001: 143; Muddiman 2001: 121). Others think that he refers only to covenants in which God unilaterally promises blessing without any condition: the Abrahamic covenant, the Davidic covenant, and the new covenant (Hoehner 2002: 359).

[17]. Eadie (1883: 166) and Schnackenburg (1991: 110) believe that Paul refers to the Messiah. Cf. Muddiman 2001: 121.

[18]. A small percentage of Gentiles had access to Israel’s Scriptures and Israel’s hope through attendance at the synagogue (e.g., Luke 7:4–5; Acts 10:2, 22; 13:6, 26, 43; 16:14; 17:4, 17; 18:7), but Paul is speaking here of what was typically the case.

[19]. See BDAG 24; PGL 44; and MacDonald 2004: 430–32.

[20]. Cf. 1 Cor. 8:4–6 and 10:20–22, where Paul assumes that the Gentiles’ gods do not exist but that their idolatrous sacrifices are actually sacrifices to demons.

[21]. It occurs sixteen times in the Pauline Letters, and apart from that, only twice in Hebrews.

[22]. Paul probably relies on the Hebrew rather than on the LXX. See on 2:17 below.

[23]. Other approaches include that of (1) Schlier (1957: 122) and Pokorný (1992: 118), who think that a piece of Christian tradition incorporated into the text (and not Isa. 57:19 itself) stands behind the language of “far” and “near”; (2) Lincoln (1982: 26–28, 30; 1987: 610–11; 1990: 138–39), who thinks that the author is using traditional Jewish terms for describing the conversion of proselytes (a change from his view in 1981: 137); and (3) Yee (2005: 113–19), who interprets the language in ethnic terms, assigning Jews a central position in society and Gentiles a position on the margins. For the perspective taken here, see Best 1998: 245.

[24]. God is the agent of the action described in the passive verb ἐγενήθητε.

[25]. Judg. 14:3; 15:18; 1 Sam. 14:6; 17:36; 31:4 [1 Chron. 10:4]; 2 Sam. 1:20; Isa. 52:1; Jer. 9:25–26. For the pejorative use, see, e.g., Judg. 14:3; 1 Sam. 17:36; Isa. 52:1.

[26]. “The term foreskin (הֶעָרְלָה) is applied only to designate [idolaters], For all the nations are uncircumcised, but all the house of Israel are uncircumcised in heart [Jer. 9:24–25]” (Blackman 1963: 3.225). Cf. Acts 11:3.

[27]. Cohen (1999: 45–46) argues that since many other peoples in the Eastern Empire practiced circumcision, it is primarily in the literature of the Latin West that non-Jews regard circumcision as distinctive of Judaism. The concern of both Philo (Spec. Laws 1.1) and Josephus (Ag. Ap. 2.137–44) to answer criticisms of the Jews with the news that many Eastern peoples practice circumcision shows, however, that even in the East people considered circumcision a distinctive marker of Judaism. It is perhaps also worth remembering that Paul wrote Ephesians from Rome, where, as Cohen says, circumcision was often seen as a Jewish distinctive.

[28]. Martial, Epig. 7.35 is sometimes thought to refer to a circumcised Jewish slave, but Cohen (1999: 351–57) has argued a persuasive case that this inference is mistaken.

[29]. Cohen (1999: 358–59) argues that Martial, Epig. 7.82 may not refer to circumcision, but see Hall 1988: 73–74. On the surgical procedure called “epispasm” and on the possible use of a pin or ring to pull what remained of the foreskin forward and disguise circumcision, see Hall 1988. On the disgust with which both Greeks and Romans viewed circumcision, see Hall 1992: 1027–28 and Gruen 2002: 51.

[30]. See, e.g., Josephus, Ant. 4.55; 15.324; J.W. 1.419, 420; 4.614; 7.176.

[31]. Cf. the use of ἀχειροποίητος of Christ’s resurrected body as a new temple in Mark 14:58.

[32]. The negative connotations of the term, moreover, tend to undermine Yee’s broader thesis that 2:11–12 is written from a Jewish rather than a Jewish-Christian perspective.

B. Christ Is the Believing Community’s Peace (2:14–18)

[1]. See, e.g., Aristotle, Rhet. 1367b.33, where Aristotle defines the encomium as focusing on a person’s achievements, and 1367b.38–40 and 1392a.18, where he describes the appropriateness of the strategy of “amplification” (τὸ αὔξειν) within an epideictic speech.

[2]. Lindemann (1975: 158) views the underlying text as exalted prose rather than a hymn.

[3]. Citing such texts as 1 En. 14.9; 3 Bar. 2.1; T. Levi 2.7; Irenaeus, Haer. 1.11.1; and Eusebius, Hist. eccl. 1.13.20, which speak of a wall, water, separation, or partition between earth and heaven.

[4]. For a similar verdict, see Stuhlmacher 1986: 185–87; Best 1997a: 60–63; 1998: 247–50; Schnackenburg 1991: 105–7; and Yee 2005: 127–40.

[5]. Christ rather than God is also the subject of the action in 4:7–13 and 5:23, 25–27 (cf. Best 1998: 249), and in each of these passages αὐτός is used of Christ. The style of the first part of the section, therefore, is consistent with the style of Ephesians generally.

[6]. Here Stuhlmacher (1986: 188) and Best (1998: 251) see a reference to Isa. 9:6, and this is certainly possible, but Paul’s identification of the church with Christ provides a more immediate explanation for the language.

[7]. HALOT 2:1507–9 refers to “prosperity, success, . . . intactness, . . . welfare, state of health, . . . friendliness, . . . deliverance, salvation.”

[8]. Λεγόμενοι (v. 11); ἀπηλλοτριωμένοι, ξένοι, ἔχοντες, ἄθεοι (v. 12); οἵ, ὄντες (v. 13).

[9]. It is sometimes said that neuter adjectives can be applied to groups of people, as in 1 Cor. 1:27–28 (BDF §138.1), and this is true, but it does not explain why Paul would use the neuter here and the masculine in the immediate context.

[10]. The καί therefore is not epexegetical (“namely,” “inasmuch as”; Alford 1857: 94; Eadie 1883: 171; Abbott 1897: 61) but coordinate (“and”), and λύσας does not modify ποιήσας adverbially but stands parallel to it. So, correctly, Best 1998: 253 and Aletti 2001: 147–48. For similar constructions, see Wallace 1996: 274–75. Note especially Matt. 27:40; John 6:33; and Acts 15:38.

[11]. The term never appears in the LXX, occurs rarely in classical literature and inscriptions, and appears only here in the NT. For its use in an extended metaphor that speaks of an outside wall separating the fields of two neighbors, see Vita Aesopi (W) 75.14–16 (translated into French in Aletti 2001: 149n120 and into English in Wills 1997: 202). For its use with reference to partitioning walls in houses, see MM 400 and the fifth-century AD lexicographer Hesychius, who defines the rare term κατῆλιψ as μεσοδομή, μεσότοιχον, δοκός, ὑπότονος βαστάζουσα τὸν ὄροφον (“something built between, a middle wall, a load-bearing beam, a support holding up roof thatch” [my trans.]). For the use of the term to describe an architectural feature of temples in Asia Minor, see Best 1998: 257n39. Clearly, the key elements of a μεσότοιχον are that it is an architectural term and that it separates.

[12]. Josephus says that the wall was punctuated at intervals with pillars inscribed in Greek and Latin threatening any Gentile who trespassed beyond it with death. A complete copy of this inscription was unearthed at the temple mount in 1871 and a fragmentary copy in 1934. On these inscriptions, see Bruce 1984: 297n115.

[13]. Bruce (1984: 297–98) is attracted to this interpretation but is also cautious about adopting it.

[14]. So a host of commentators, including Eadie 1883: 172; Dibelius and Greeven 1953: 69; Masson 1953: 165n1; Best 1998: 254; Aletti 2001: 149n120. Muddimann (2001: 128) argues against this objection, but, in my view, unsuccessfully.

[15]. Law observance was not an infallible guide to Jewishness, because, as Cohen (1999: 58–62) explains, some Gentiles occasionally kept the law, or parts of it, as matters of convenience or conviction.

[16]. Texts that speak of a fence around the law (e.g., m.ʾAbot 1.1; 3.14), sometimes cited in this connection (Pokorný 1992: 121), are not really relevant. As Best (1998: 255n37) and Muddiman (2001: 127–28) point out, these texts are concerned with the oral tradition that forms a fence around the law, not the function of the law in fencing off Israel from the Gentiles.

[17]. Cf., e.g., the placement of ἐν ἀγάπῃ in 1:5, the difficulty in understanding τὰ πάντα ἐν πᾶσιν in 1:23, and the broken syntax of 2:1, 5 and 3:1, 14.

[18]. E.g., Origen (Heine 2002: 135); Theodoret (R. Hill 2001: 2.40); Oecumenius (PG 118:1197); Theophylact (PG 124:1060); Alford 1857: 94; Ellicott 1859: 48; Abbott 1897: 62; Masson 1953: 165; Sellin 2008: 215.

[19]. E.g., Eadie 1883: 174; Robinson 1904: 63, 161; Gnilka 1971: 141; Lincoln 1990: 124; Schnackenburg 1991: 114; Hoehner 2002: 372.

[20]. The verb καταργέω is most often used in the NT in the negative senses of “invalidate, make powerless,” or “abolish, wipe out, set aside” (BDAG 525–26). At least in the NT, the negative nuance of the term seems intensified when it is in the active voice and God or Christ is the subject, as it is here (2 Thess. 2:8; 1 Cor. 1:28; 2:6; 6:13; 15:24; 2 Tim. 1:10; Heb. 2:14).

[21]. See also Eadie 1883: 177–78; cf. Yee 2005: 154–61. Despite Barth’s attempt (1974: 287–91) to distinguish his view from Calvin’s, it is difficult to see how the two views differ in substance.

[22]. Cf. the use of the term δόγμα to refer to the decrees of a king in, e.g., 4 Macc. 4:23–26; Dan. 6:13 LXX (6:12 Eng.); Luke 2:1; Acts 17:7; and to its probable use for the Mosaic law in 3 Macc. 1:3 (“ancestral traditions,” NRSV) and Col. 2:14.

[23]. Cf. Paul’s use of the terms γράμμα and γράμματα of the Moasic law in Rom. 2:27; 7:6; 2 Cor. 3:6–7.

[24]. So most interpreters, including Alford 1857: 94; Ellicott 1859: 48; Abbott 1897: 64–65; Westcott 1906: 37–38; Stuhlmacher 1986: 189–90; O’Brien 1999: 196–201; Best 1998: 260–61; and Hoehner 2002: 374–77.

[25]. A more detailed argument for this approach to Paul’s understanding of the Mosaic law appears in Thielman 1992; 1994; 1999: 7–46. Cf. O’Brien 1999: 196–201.

[26]. The eleven NT uses of κτίζω outside Ephesians all refer to God’s creative activity in Gen. 1–2 (Matt. 19:4; Mark 13:19; 1 Cor. 11:9; Rom. 1:25; Col. 1:16 [2x]; 3:10; 1 Tim. 4:3; Rev. 4:11 [2x]; 10:6), and Eph. 3:9 also uses the term this way. It is probable, therefore, that Eph. 2:10, 15 and 4:24 are all intended to recall God’s original creation of human beings.

[27]. Paul has shifted from the neuter phrase τὰ ἀμφότερα in 2:14 to the masculine expression οἱ δύο here, and this has led to discussion about whether he has also moved his focus from people groups in 2:14 (represented by the neuter) to individuals here (represented by the masculine). The shift in gender was probably dictated by the masculine ἄνθρωπος imagery, however, and so Paul’s focus remains on the two people groups. See Hoehner’s persuasive evaluation (2002: 378–79) of Best’s lengthy argument (1998: 261–63).

[28]. Some interpreters have taken the prefixed ἀπό to mean that Christ has restored an original peace between God and humanity that was disrupted (e.g., Calvin 1965: 152; Alford 1857: 95; Ellicott 1859: 49; Lightfoot 1879: 159–60; LSJ 201). As true as this is theologically, and as pertinent as it is to a context that emphasizes the new creation, the prepositional prefix ἀπό most often simply intensifies the words to which it is attached, and in such a rare word as this, it is safest to assume that this is all it is doing here (Abbott 1897: 66).

[29]. See the earlier commentators, such as Theodoret (R. Hill 2001: 2.41). Muddiman (2001: 135) sees a reference to the body of Christ in the hymn on which the editor relied and a double reference to both Christ and the church in the thinking of the editor himself.

[30]. Ἀποκτείνας is an adverbial participle of means. Its aorist tense does not indicate antecedent but contemporaneous action. On this, see Wallace 1996: 628–30 and the debate between Picirilli 2007 and Porter 2007.

[31]. Paul’s allusion is closer to the Hebrew than to the LXX, which has the herald announcing “a report of peace” (εὐαγγελιζομένου ἀκοὴν εἰρήνης) rather than “peace” itself. Paul’s use of Isa. 52:7 in Rom. 10:15, although it is concerned with a different part of the text, is also closer to the Hebrew than to the LXX.

[32]. Here too Paul seems to be dependent on the Hebrew rather than on the LXX, which disturbs the poetry of the Hebrew text’s שָׁלוֹם שָׁלוֹם (peace, peace) in 57:19 by inserting a preposition between the two words: εἰρήνην ἐπ᾿ εἰρήνην (“peace upon peace”). See also Lincoln 1990: 147.

[33]. Pace Moritz (1996a: 32–34), the “far” and “near” of Isa. 57:19 in their original context probably refer to Israelites in the dispersion and Israelites in the land (e.g., Westermann 1969: 300; Lincoln 1982: 27; Hübner 1997: 165; Hoehner 2002: 365). Moritz (1996a: 32–34, 45–52) is quite correct, however, that Paul’s theology of the eschatological inclusion of the Gentiles in the saving purposes of God is consistent with the earth-encompassing vision of Isa. 55–60. See especially Isa. 55:5; 56:6–7.

[34]. The causal use of ὅτι is common in Ephesians (4:25; 5:16, 23, 30; 6:12), whereas ὅτι only rarely indicates result in any literature. LSJ 1265 do not list result as a meaning, and BDAG 732 place it last. Since Paul has already given the content of Christ’s proclamation as “peace,” moreover, it is unlikely that ὅτι introduces another description of that content (so, correctly, Hoehner 2002: 388).

[35]. See, e.g., Lev. 7:8; 14:12; Tob. 12:12; 1 Macc. 5:54; 2 Macc. 3:32; 1 Pet. 3:18; and cf. Herodotus, Hist. 2.58.

[36]. Cf. Col. 1:20 in 𝔓46, א, A, C, D1, and Ψ, where the phrase διὰ τοῦ αἵματος τοῦ σταυροῦ αὐτοῦ is followed immediately by δι᾿ αὐτοῦ, a redundancy that makes it the more difficult reading and probably correct (R. Wilson 2005: 154–55). If retained, δι᾿ αὐτοῦ refers either to the cross itself or to Jesus in his role as the crucified one. In either case, the phrase refers to Jesus’s death as the means by which peace was made.

[37]. As with τοὺς ἀμφοτέρους in 2:16, the gender has shifted from neuter (v. 14) to masculine because of the intervening imagery of the “one new human being” in 2:15.

C. Gentile Christians as an Integral Part of God’s Household (2:19–22)

[1]. The phrase never appears in the LXX, and elsewhere in the NT only in 1 Thess. 5:6; 2 Thess. 2:15; Gal. 6:10; Rom. 5:18; 7:3, 25; 8:12; 9:16, 18; 14:12, 19, although it does occur in 2 Clem. 8.6; 14.3; Barn. 9.6; 10.2; and Ign. Trall. 10 (BDAG 127). Pace K. Clark (1972: 78–79), the context of Paul’s argument seems to dictate that the often-tentative nuance of ἄρα is missing here.

[2]. See Stählin, TDNT 5:30n203 and J. H. Elliott 1981: 25, 50n16. On the social and political connotations of these terms in the Greco-Roman world generally, see Zahn 1909: 2.139–40 and Cartledge, BNP 8:810–14.

[3]. Cf. the set of contrasts in Diogn. 5.5: “[Christians] live in their respective countries, but only as resident aliens [πάροικοι]; they participate in all things as citizens [πολῖται], and they endure all things as foreigners [ξένοι]” (trans. Ehrman 2003).

[4]. Although causal participles normally precede the verbs that they modify, they do occasionally come after them (e.g., Acts 16:34; Wallace 1996: 632).

[5]. This does not mean that τῶν ἀποστόλων καὶ προφητῶν is a subjective genitive (“the foundation laid by the apostles and prophets”), a position to which 1 Cor. 3:11 drove some earlier commentators (e.g., Ellicott 1859: 52–53; Eadie 1883: 196–98) and for which Sandnes (1991: 227–29) has more recently argued on other grounds. The phrase, as most interpreters now recognize, is a genitive of apposition (“the foundation, that is, the apostles and prophets”). This reading keeps the people in the passage (the Gentile Christian audience, the apostles, and Christ) together as part of the building and so provides a more consistent use of the architectural figure. Cf. Grudem 1982: 85, 88.

[6]. In recent times, the most convincing case for this position comes from Grudem (1982: 93–105), who recognizes that the case cannot be made on the basis of the single article.

[7]. Pace many earlier commentators, e.g., Chrysostom (PG 62:43–44); Theodoret (R. Hill 2001: 2.41); Jerome (Heine 2002: 139); and Calvin 1965: 155. The desire to refute Marcionism and other similar movements seems to have fueled this reading in antiquity. In more recent times, McKelvey (1969: 113) has suggested that this is the right interpretation.

[8]. See the link between knowledge of mysteries and prophecy in 1 Cor. 13:2; and cf. the comments of Percy 1946: 347–49.

[9]. Since the phrase αὐτοῦ Χριστοῦ Ἰησοῦ is part of a longer genitive absolute construction (ὄντος ἀκρογωνιαίου αὐτοῦ Χριστοῦ Ἰησοῦ), it seems unlikely that the αὐτοῦ is a genitive of possession referring back to θεμελίῳ in the previous clause (“Christ Jesus being its [the foundation’s] cornerstone”), a translation that Schnackenburg (1991: 123) thinks entirely possible (a change from his rejection of it in 1982: 259–60). Like every other word in the phrase, αὐτοῦ is genitive only because it is part of the genitive absolute construction.

[10]. Symmachus’s work comes, at the earliest, from the second half of the second century after Christ (Greenspoon 1992: 251). The date of the Testament of Solomon is very uncertain but probably falls in the first three centuries after Christ (Duling, OTP 1:940–43).

[11]. Aletti (2001: 163n165) has answered this objection by claiming that there is no need to think of Christ as being absent from the church as it grows. As the ἐν ᾧ of 2:21 and the use of the verb αὐξάνω in 4:15 indicate, the growth of the building follows the model of the growth of a body: the entire body is present as the body matures. McKelvey (1969: 118–19) acknowledges this connection but suggests that the image of a building under construction provided the conceptual link between a finished temple in which God dwells and a growing body: like a body and a building in process, the church is growing, but like a finished temple building, God already dwells in it.

[12]. Isaiah 28:16 LXX says twice that the stone is placed εἰς τὰ θεμέλια. At first, the significance of this would seem to be diminished if Lincoln (1990: 155) is correct that the author is alluding not to Isa. 28:16 but only to the Christian tradition that uses Isa. 28:16 as one of several stone texts. In 1 Pet. 2:4–8 and Barn. 6.2–3, however, the references to Isa. 28:16 are full enough that even someone relying only on them would know that they refer to a stone placed εἰς τὰ θεμέλια of the building.

[13]. Christus als Eckstein ist dann metaphorisch zugleich das fundamentum fundamentorum und der finis finium.

[14]. McKelvey (1969: 188–92, 203) points out that the foundation stone of Isa. 28:16 has a long and rich interpretive history in Jewish tradition as the first part of the earth’s creation and the portal of access to both the underworld and heaven. It is useful to know that Isa. 28:16 was not an obscure text in Jewish antiquity, but the literature in which these traditions are found cannot be dated with certainty, and there is no way to know whether they influenced Paul.

[15]. ἐν ᾧ πᾶσα οἰκοδομὴ συναρμολογουμένη εἰς ναόν ἅγιον ἐν κυρίῳ

ἐν ᾧ καὶ ὑμεῖς συνοικοδομεῖσθε εἰς κατοικητήριον τοῦ θεοῦ ἐν πνεύματι

[16]. See the discussion of Moule 1959: 94–95 and the use of the same construction in, e.g., Thucydides, Pel. War 2.43.3 (ἀνδρῶν γὰρ ἐπιφανῶν πᾶσα γῆ τάφος, the whole earth is the tomb of famous men [my trans.]); Matt. 3:15 (πληρῶσαι πᾶσαν δικαιοσύνην, to fulfill all righteousness); and 28:18 (πᾶσα ἐξουσία, all authority). J. Johnston (2004: 173) argues persuasively that the closest analogy to the idiom is the use of πᾶσα συναγωγή in the LXX without a genitive qualifier (Lev. 9:5; 16:33; Num. 27:2, 19, 22; 31:27).

[17]. The term seems to have entered the Greek language through its appearance in these two places in Ephesians. See Maurer, TDNT 7:855.

[18]. Συνεζωοποίησεν (v. 5); συνήγειρεν, συνεκάθισεν (v. 6); συμπολῖται (v. 19); συνοικοδομεῖσθε (v. 22).

[19]. For the eschatological inclusion of the Gentiles in temple worship, see also Isa. 2:1–2; 66:19–23; Tob. 14:5–7; 1 En. 90.29–34; and cf. McKelvey 1969: 118.

[20]. So, e.g., Hoehner 2002: 412–13; but pace, e.g., Tachau 1972: 137–38, 140–41, who believes that the relationship between Jewish and Gentile Christians is no longer in view in 2:19–22 but only the present existence of Gentile Christians in one, all-encompassing church.

[21]. A search of the TLG shows that prior to its use here in Ephesians, the term is used only of the dwelling place of a deity in the LXX, ten times of God and once of the gods (Dan. 2:11; cf. Rev. 18:2). It was not, in other words, a term used outside Judaism for the temple of a deity. This bolsters the case for seeing both κατοικητήριον here and its counterpart ναός in 2:21 as references not to just any temple but to the biblical temple.

A. Paul’s Role in the Administration of the Mystery (3:1–7)

[1]. Cf. the terms συγκληρονόμα, σύσσωμα, and συμμέτοχα in 3:6 with the terms συμπολῖται, συναρμολογουμένη, and συνοικοδομεῖσθε in 2:19–22.

[2]. Πάροικοι and οἰκεῖοι (2:19), ἐποικοδομηθέντες (2:20), οἰκοδομή (2:21), and συνοικοδομεῖσθε and κατοικητήριον (2:22).

[3]. Cf. ἐξῆλθον εἰς Μακεδονίαν (2 Cor. 2:13) with ἐλθόντων ἡμῶν εἰς Μακεδονίαν (2 Cor. 7:5); on this, see M. Harris 2005: 240.

[4]. Cf. Malherbe 2000: 184. The expression in Philem. 19 is part of a legal commitment (R. Wilson 2005: 358–59) and thus stands apart from these other uses.

[5]. Cf. Calvin 1965: 157, “And it must have been very moving for them to hear that it was for their sake that he was in trouble and peril.” Cassidy (2001: 96) says that the article may emphasize the way that Paul’s imprisonment now defines his day-to-day existence because he has been in prison for so long.

[6]. That the comparison is only an analogy and that Christ’s death has a unique, atoning significance for Paul also becomes clear in 1 Cor. 1:13, where Paul views as absurd any notion that he could take the place of the crucified Christ.

[7]. For the chronology, see 1 Cor. 16:8; Acts 20:3, 6, 16; 24:27; 27:9; 28:11, 30.

[8]. According to some interpreters, including BDAG 698, this is also the best meaning for οἰκονομία in 1:10.

[9]. Luke 16:2–4 illustrates how the meaning of the term can move easily between these two ideas (BDAG 697).

[10]. Cf. Lincoln 1990: 173–74; Hoehner 2002: 422; and especially Aletti 2001: 175–76.

[11]. Πάροικοι, οἰκεῖοι, ἐποικοδομηθέντες, οἰκοδομή, συνοικοδομεῖσθε, κατοικητήριον.

[12]. Cf. Epictetus (Arrian, Epict. diss. 3.22.1–5), where the philosopher says that acting out of accord with God’s design is foolish:

For in a well-ordered [καλῶς οἰκουμένῃ] house [οἰκίᾳ] no one comes along and says to himself, “I ought to be manager [οἰκονόμον] of this house”; or if he does, the lord of the mansion, when he turns around and sees the fellow giving orders in a high and mighty fashion, drags him out and gives him a dressing down. So it goes also in this great city, the world; for here also there is a Lord of the Mansion [οἰκοδεσπότης] who assigns each and everything its place. (trans. W. Oldfather 1925–28)

See Spicq, TLNT 2:574.

[13]. Cf. 1 Pet. 4:10, where all Christians are administrators (οἰκονόμοι) of the various gifts that God, in the diverse expressions of his grace (χάρις), gives to them.

[14]. Grammatically, the clause beginning with ὅτι forms a second object of the verb ἠκούσατε in 3:2, and this second object further explains the first object (τὴν οἰκονομίαν). Paul assumes that his audience has heard of the administration of the grace God gave to him, namely, that they have heard of the mystery made known to him by revelation. On this, see, e.g., Alford 1857: 100; Ellicott 1859: 57; Abbott 1897: 79; and especially Haupt 1902a: 97, who correctly observes that ὅτι introduces an explanation of οἰκονομία that stretches all the way to the infinitive clause in 3:6.

[15]. This use of the phrase differs, therefore, from its use in Rom. 16:25 or Gal. 2:2, where Paul speaks of the norm “according to” which God will strengthen his readers or “according to” which he and Barnabas traveled to Jerusalem. For the use here, see Justin, Dial. 78.2; and Eusebius, Hist. eccl. 6.11.1.

[16]. So, e.g., Abbott 1897: 80; Lincoln 1990: 175–76; and BDAG 875.3.e.δ; but not Eadie 1883: 215, who prefers the simpler meaning “in reference to.”

[17]. Cf. 1 Thess. 5:27; Col. 4:16; and the comments of Thomas (1992: 13), both on reading aloud in private and on the common practice in antiquity of reading texts aloud to audiences.

[18]. Cf. John of Damascus (PG 95:833): “The explanation is short, he says, and the teaching is concise, and the many things I have taught in seed form are brief, although I have revealed so great a thing, just as you are able to perceive; but [you are able] to perceive [it] by much reading, not by a cursory treatment or a hasty scan” (my trans.).

[19]. Pace Sellin (2008: 251–52), it is the author’s perspective that prevents ἀναγινώσκοντες from being superfluous even though it refers to material the readers have obviously read (or heard read).

[20]. See the texts that Aletti lists: Dan. 10:1; 2 Esd. (4 Ezra) 5:22; 14:40, 47; T. Levi 2.3; 18.7; 1QHa 10.13; 20.13; 2 Bar. 81.4.

[21]. E.g., Alford 1857: 100; Ellicott 1859: 59. Since the mystery in Col. 1:27 is not simply Christ, but Χριστὸς ἐν ὑμῖν (Abbott 1897: 80; Hoehner 2002: 436), a better analogy would be Col. 2:2: τὸ μυστήριον τοῦ θεοῦ, Χριστοῦ (cf. Col. 4:3).

[22]. Interpreters often call this an “objective genitive” (Eadie 1883: 215; Abbott 1897: 80; Haput 1902: 99; Masson 1953: 173n2; Hoehner 2002: 436). An objective genitive, however, must be related to a noun that has a verbal counterpart (Winer 1874: 185; MHT 3:210; Wallace 1996: 116–17). In this case the verbal counterpart would be μυέω, “initiate into the mysteries” (LSJ 1150; BDAG 660), and if τοῦ Χριστοῦ were objective, then Christ would be the initiate (cf. Phil. 4:12). It may be best to leave this genitive unclassified or simply to call it a “general genitive.” See Schnackenburg 1991: 133; the discussion in Zerwick 1963: 12–14; and Aletti’s acknowledgment (2001: 178) that the genitive here defies exact classification.

[23]. In the earliest extant commentary on Ephesians, Origen already expends much energy on the problem (Heine 2002: 144–46).

[24]. See, e.g., Pss. 22:27; 86:9; 96:3, 7–10; Isa. 2:2–4 (cf. Mic. 4:1–4); 11:10; 19:24–25; 45:14, 22; 51:4–5; 52:10; 55:5; 56:6–7; 60:11; 66:18–23; 54:15 LXX; Jer. 3:17; Amos 9:12 LXX; Zech. 8:20–23; 9:10; Tob. 13:11; 14:6–7; 1 En. 10.21; 90.33; 2 Bar. 72–73; T. Naph. 8.3–4; Sib. Or. 3.716–23; Philo, Moses 2.43–44. See Jeremias 1982: 56–62 and Donaldson 1997: 69–74.

[25]. It is sometimes said that Jerome adopted this interpretation (Barth 1974: 334; Best 1998: 306); however, not only are the relevant comments probably Origen’s rather than Jerome’s (Heine 2002: 144n6), but the author of the comments, whoever he may be, also appears to doubt that this interpretation is correct (Heine 2002: 145). Cf. Chrysostom, Hom. Eph., hom. 6; NPNF 13:76; Oecumenius, PG 118:1204.

[26]. Exceptions include Caragounis 1977: 102–3 and Bruce 1984: 314.

[27]. In 1 Thess. 2:6–7 and 1 Cor. 4:6–9 Paul uses the first-person plural and seems to include Silvanus, Timothy, and Apollos among the apostles, but there is no evidence that any of them had contact with Jesus during his earthly ministry.

[28]. Masson 1953: 173; Muddiman 2001: 155; pace, e.g., Lincoln 1990: 179 (tentatively); Hoehner 2002: 442–43.

[29]. For the translation “wisdom in a mystery,” see Bockmuehl 1990: 160–61.

[30]. A few commentators claim that the use of the phrase ἐν πνεύματι elsewhere in Ephesians and Colossians supports the attachment of the phrase here to the noun that precedes it (Schlier 1957: 150; Schnackenburg 1991: 133). This is certainly true of Eph. 2:22 and Col. 1:8, but as Best (1998: 308) points out, the phrase modifies verbal forms in 5:18 and 6:18. In 6:18, moreover, the verbal form is separated from ἐν πνεύματι by another phrase, just as it is in 3:5.

[31]. E.g., De Wette 1843: 119; Baur 2003: 2.32; Gnilka 1973: 167; Lincoln 1990: 179; Schnackenburg 1991: 28, 133; MacDonald 2000: 263.

[32]. See, e.g., 1 Cor. 1:2; 14:33; 16:15; Phil. 1:1; 4:22; 2 Cor. 1:1; 13:12; Rom. 1:7; 8:27; 12:13; 16:15; Philem. 5, 7.

[33]. A synoptic comparison of the two relevant phrases shows the plausibility of this reconstruction:

Col. 1:26b νῦν δὲ ἐφανερώθη τοῖς ἁγίοις αὐτοῦ

Eph. 3:5b ὡς νῦν ἀπεκαλύφθη τοῖς ἁγίοις ἀποστόλοις αὐτοῦ καὶ προφήταις

[34]. See, e.g., Merklein 1973: 164–67, 188–92; Pokorný 1992: 142; MacDonald 2000: 263; Strecker 2000: 569–70; and cf. Hahn 2002: 346–47. Dahl (2000: 54) comments: “One gains the impression [from 2:11–22; 3:5–7] . . . that our author sees the apostles and prophets more as ideal forms than as people of flesh and blood.” (Man gewinnt . . . den Eindruck, dass unser Verfasser die Apostel und Propheten eher als ideale Gestalten denn als Menschen von Fleisch und Blut ansieht.)

[35]. Dibelius and Greeven 1953: 74; Gnilka 1973: 179n6; Lincoln 1990: 179; Best 1998: 307–8; MacDonald 2000: 263.

[36]. Mark 7:24–30; 13:10; 14:9; 15:39; Matt. 28:16–20; Luke 24:47–49; Acts 1:8; 13:47 (cf. Isa. 49:6).

[37]. Gal. 1:12, 15, 16; 2:1–10; Rom. 1:5, 13; 11:13; 15:15–18; Col. 1:24–29; 1 Tim. 2:7; 2 Tim. 4:17; Acts 22:21.

[38]. Εἶναι could be an infinitive in indirect discourse (“as it is now revealed through the Spirit to his holy apostles and prophets: In the Messiah Jesus and through the gospel, the Gentiles are joint heirs”; Barth 1974: 326, 336). Most commentators, however, take the infinitive in apposition to the relative pronoun ὅ in 3:5 and its antecedent μυστήριον in 3:4, and this probably is correct. Cf. the similar constructions in Acts 24:15 and Rev. 2:14.

[39]. Συμπολῖται (sympolitai, citizens together, 2:19); συναρμολογουμένη (synarmologoumenē, being joined together, 2:22); συνοικοδομεῖσθε (synoikodomeisthe, you are being built together, 2:23).

[40]. See, e.g., Gen. 15:7–8; 22:17; 24:60; 28:4; 47:27; Exod. 23:30; Lev. 20:24; Num. 13:30; 33:54; 34:2, 13, 17–18; Deut. 1:39; 2:12; 3:20, 28; 4:1, 5, 14, 22, 26, 38; 1 Chron. 16:14–18; 2 Chron. 6:27.

[41]. This new creation is perhaps identical in Paul’s thinking with “the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:9–10; 15:50; Gal. 5:21; Eph. 5:5).

[42]. Indeed, during the Second Temple period some interpreters of the Scriptures found in their inheritance language a justification for the violent overthrow and subjugation of the Gentiles. See, e.g., the echoes of Ps. 2:8–9 LXX in Pss. Sol. 17.22–25.

[43]. We should not claim this too quickly. Σύσσωμος appears naturally in various contexts in Christian writers of later years (PGL 1348) and may not have been as unusual in Paul’s time as its absence in the extant literature could at first lead us to believe. The similar term συσσωματοποιέω (“incorporate, amalgamate,” LSJ 1734) appears prior to Paul in the second-century BC Stoic philosopher Posidonius (Fragmenta 341a 17) and then again in De mundo (396a.14), a passage that relies on Posidonius and is sometimes wrongly attributed to Aristotle (Abbott 1897: 83; Robinson 1928: 169). De mundo is dated variously from the mid-first century BC to the early second century AD (Ross 1923: 11; Forster 1931: preface). A term not unlike σύσσωμος was therefore in circulation around the time of Paul.

[44]. On the use of the genitive case with adjectives beginning with σύν, see BDF §182.1 and BDAG 958. Pace Abbott (1897: 83), the phrase must go with this last term rather than with all three terms because attaching it to σύσσωμα would involve “gross artificiality” (Haupt 1902a: 102).

[45]. See the comments on 1:13 and 2:12; and cf. Aletti 2001: 180.

[46]. It is true that we find a specific link between “servant” and “gospel” only here and in Col. 1:23, but it is difficult to see any substantial difference between this language and the concept of Paul’s apostolic “service” in the letters whose Pauline authorship is undisputed. Pace Merklein 1973: 223 and A. Weiser, EDNT 1:304, who find in both Col. 1:23 and Eph. 3:7 evidence of a post-Pauline development of the office of “minister of the gospel.”

[47]. Here the meaning of κατά slides slightly from its usual indication of the norm by which something is measured into an expression of the reason for something. Paul became a servant of the gospel because of the divine grace given to him. On this meaning for κατά, see BDAG 513.5.a.δ.

[48]. Most commentators agree (pace Westcott 1906: 47) that this second κατά clause does not stand parallel to the first κατά clause but instead modifies the participle δοθείσης. As Hoehner (2002: 451) observes, if the two clauses were parallel, they would probably be linked with καί.

[49]. See the discussion of these terms in the comments on 1:19.

B. How Paul Fulfills His Task (3:8–13)

[1]. Hoehner 2002: 452; cf. Muddiman 2001: 157; Hoehner and Muddiman cite Bruce in support of their position (cf. Lincoln 1990: 182), but Bruce (1984: 318–19) is much less definitive on this point in his later commentary than he was in his earlier one (cf. Bruce 1961: 63).

[2]. MacDonald (2000: 271–72) sees the increased emphasis on Paul’s preconversion sinfulness as part of a larger strategy to strengthen Paul’s authority as an apostle and thus strengthen the authority of contemporary church leaders by tracing their authority back to him.

[3]. Heron’s date can be firmly fixed by a reference in one of his works to a recently observed lunar eclipse that could have occurred only on March 13, AD 62, at 11:51 p.m. local time in Alexandria (Dioptra 35). On this, see the clever deductions of Neugebauer 1975: 846.

[4]. The term also appears in L.A.E. [Apocalypse] 16.2, but this document is difficult to date, and its text at this point is uncertain. See the note in OTP 2:277.

[5]. Ignatius is closest to 1 Cor. 15:9, whose sentiment is similar. The only significant overlap in the precise wording of the two passages, however, is the use in both of the adjective ἔσχατος:

1 Corinthians 15:8–9 Ignatius, Trallians 13.1

Ἔσχατον δὲ πάντων ὡσπερεὶ τῷ ἐκτρώματι ὤφθη κἀμοί. Ἐγὼ γάρ εἰμι ὁ ἐλάχιστος τῶν ἀποστόλων ὃς οὐκ εἰμὶ ἱκανὸς καλεῖσθαι ἀπόστολος, διότι ἐδίωξα τὴν ἐκκλησίαν τοῦ θεοῦ. Μνημονεύετε ἐν ταῖς προσευχαῖς ὑμῶν τῆς ἐν Συρίᾳ ἐκκλησίας, ὅθεν καὶ οὐκ ἄξιός εἰμι λέγεσθαι, ὢν ἔσχατος ἐκείνων.

[6]. MacDonald (2000: 270–71) suggests that a rhetorical convention described in Plutarch, Mor. 7, is operative in both Ignatius and Ephesians at this point. If so, then the convention may still have been the vehicle for genuine expressions of humility.

[7]. The few occurrences of this word in the extant literature cluster around texts concerned with the incomprehensible nature of God’s wisdom, especially as it is revealed in creation (Job 5:9; 9:10 LXX; 1 Clem. 20.5; cf. Job 34:24 LXX) and in his mercy to sinners (Pr. Man. 6 [Odes 12:6 LXX]; Diogn. 9.5).

[8]. Confusion on this point probably accounts for the absence of the term in some early witnesses to the text. See Metzger 1994: 534 and the additional note below.

[9]. For the use of the perfect tense to “intensify” the verb, see Campbell 2008a: 110.

[10]. For “aeons,” see, e.g., Dibelius and Greeven 1953: 75; Schlier 1957: 153–56; BDAG 33. Barth (1974: 344) and Best (1998: 320) think the term may have elements of both meanings.

[11]. Paul is still using the definition of “the mystery” that he developed in 3:6.

[12]. Lincoln (1990: 185) and Hoehner (2002: 459) basically adopt this second view but think that the purpose clause is ultimately related, beyond the infinitives, to ἐδόθη in 3:8 (so Lincoln; cf. Best 1998: 322) or to ἐγενήθην διάκονος in 3:7 (so Hoehner).

[13]. The thought, then, is similar to Rom. 11:33, where God’s “paths” of reasoning are “untraceable” (ἀνεξιχνίαστος). Cf. Col. 2:3; Sir. 1:6, 25; Bar. 3:15; Wis. 8:5; and 2 Bar. 54.13. In Wis. 7:22–23, the “spirit” of wisdom is described with a lengthy string of adjectives, including πολυμερές (manifold). On the relevance of this material to Eph. 3:10, see especially Schnackenburg 1991: 139–40; Dahl 2000: 355.

[14]. Critias was a fifth-century BC philosopher and playwright. This reference appears in a fragment on the invention of the gods and describes how someone came up with the idea that the array of stars in the heavens were “the beautiful embroidery [ποίκιλμα] of Time the skilled [σοφοῦ] craftsman” (trans. Freeman 1948: 158; cf. Schwindt 2002: 368).

[15]. See especially Dahl 2000: 355–56. Lincoln (1990: 186) believes that Dahl has read too much into the evidence, citing especially Dahl’s use of the second-century Christian apologist Theophilus of Antioch. Although Dahl (2000: 356) probably goes too far in suggesting that Theophilus’s use of πολυποίκιλος (Autol. 1.6.5, 16; 2.16.2; cf. παμποίκιλος in 1.6.12) was “dependent upon a Hellenistic Jewish interpretation of Genesis,” he has convincingly shown that Eph. 3:10 participates in a tendency in Hellenistic Judaism to speak of God’s creation of the universe as evidence for the vastness of God’s wisdom.

[16]. Ἵνα . . . κτίσῃ . . . ἕνα καινὸν ἄνθρωπον (2:15). Cf. Westcott 1906: 48–49.

[17]. The “rulers and authorities,” therefore, are not “saints and ministers of God” (Origen [Heine 2002: 149]), “the heavenly angels” (Calvin 1965: 163; De Wette 1843: 121; Alford 1857: 103; Ellicott 1859: 64; Eadie 1883: 234; Abbott 1897: 88), the angels who oversee the affairs of various nations (Masson 1953: 176), or a mixture of good and evil powers (Bruce 1984: 321; O’Brien 1999: 246–47; Hoehner 2002: 459–60). For the approach adopted here, see, e.g., Schlier 1957: 155; Gnilka 1971: 175; Arnold 1989: 62–64; Schnackenburg 1991: 140–41; MacDonald 2000: 266; Best 1998: 322.

[18]. See the section titled “The Circumstances That Prompted Ephesians” in the commentary introduction.

[19]. Here and in what follows I am especially dependent on Marrow 1982. See also Schlier, TDNT 5:871–86 and Fredrickson 1996.

[20]. O’Brien (1999: 249n114) also says (relying on Wallis 1995: 131) that “διά . . . followed by a reference to Christ in the genitive is often used in Ephesians to describe the means by which salvation is secured (1:5, 7; 2:8, 16, 18; 3:6, 16, 17).” It is true that three of these texts refer to the role of Christ’s death in redemption (1:7), reconciliation (2:16), or obtaining access (2:18), but the relevance of the others to the point being made is not clear.

[21]. Wallis (1995: 132) argues that this too may be a reference to Christ’s own faith. In 3:16, he says, Christians are strengthened διὰ τοῦ πνεύματος αὐτοῦ, meaning through Christ’s Spirit, and this stands parallel to 3:17, where Christ inhabits Christians διὰ τῆς πίστεως. Just as Christ’s Spirit strengthens Christians, then, so also Christ’s faith secures his habitation in their hearts. The antecedent of αὐτοῦ in 3:16, however, is not Christ but “the Father” of 3:14, and it seems likely that if Paul had intended the two διά phrases to parallel each other, he would have repeated the αὐτοῦ in the second phrase.

[22]. Theophylact, who is clearly relying on Chrysostom (cf. PG 62:50–51), is more explicit than Chrysostom about the meaning of the phrase. He paraphrases it αἰτοῦμαι ὑμᾶς ἵνα μὴ ἐκκακᾶτε (“I ask you that you not lose heart”).

[23]. By the time Paul wrote Ephesians, the indefinite relative pronoun was often synonymous with the simple relative pronoun (Zerwick 1963: 68–70), but it sometimes carried “a causal sense” (Zerwick 1963: 68). That is probably the case with ἥτις here (Best 1998: 331; Hoehner 2002: 469). Both ἥτις and the verb ἐστίν are singular because they have been attracted to the number of the predicate δόξα, an oddity that prompted comment as early as Origen (Heine 2002: 152–53) but was certainly not unprecedented. See Robertson 1923: 411–12.

[24]. Cf. Thompson 1960: 188; Lincoln 1990: 192; Best 1998: 332; O’Brien 1999: 250–52. Because this development from the undisputed letters is so natural, it should not figure in arguments about the letter’s authorship (so, correctly, Best 1998: 332).

[25]. Tischendorf (8th ed.), Westcott and Hort, and NA25 all reject πάντας, and the editors of UBS4 accepted it only with hesitation (Metzger 1994: 534; cf. Best 1998: 319).

A. Paul Prays for His Readers’ Inner Strength (3:14–19)

[1]. Schürer 1979: 449n106; HDCLA 1310, with illustrations; Greeven, TDNT 2:779; Versnel 2003.

[2]. Pace Bruce 1984: 325, πατριά should not be translated “fatherhood.”

[3]. Kraus (1993b: 557) comments on Ps. 147:4, “This calling is at the same time a creative act and a proclamation of the right of lordship.”

[4]. Unlike the ἵνα in 1:17, which introduces the content of Paul’s intercessory prayer (BDAG 476), this ἵνα introduces both the purpose of Paul’s prayer and its content. The ἵνα in 1:17 is followed by δῴη, which is optative, a mood that by the first century was a rarity in ἵνα clauses indicating purpose (see the additional note on 1:17). Here, however, ἵνα is followed by the aorist subjunctive, and so the connotation of purpose is probably still present. As Hoehner (2002: 477) says, “In the case of prayer, it is difficult to distinguish between purpose and content.”

[5]. Cf. PGM 4.1650–54, “Give glory and favor to this phylactery. . . . Give strength and honor to this phylactery.”

[6]. The parallels sometimes cited are not convincing. In Rom. 11:31, τῷ ὑμετέρῳ ἐλέει probably goes with the preceding clause, not with the following ἵνα . . . ἐλεηθῶσιν. Similarly, in 1 Cor. 9:15, the ταῦτα before the ἵνα . . . γένηται is probably not the subject of γένηται. The relative pronoun ἥν in 2 Cor. 2:4 serves as the object of ἵνα γνῶτε, making it unnecessary to take the preceding τὴν ἀγάπην as the object and demonstrating how unnatural it would be to do so. In Gal. 2:10; John 13:29; and Acts 19:4, the object of the subjunctive verb following ἵνα is in each case placed before the ἵνα for emphasis. Here, however, the participles carry no emphasis (Alford 1857: 106; Haupt 1902a: 115).

[7]. A few grammarians agree that the participles function independently but think that they are imperatives (BDF §468.2; cf. Moule 1959: 105; MHT 3:230). Imperatives directed toward Paul’s readers, however, seem ill suited to a prayer of intercession for them (Hoehner 2002: 483).

[8]. Among the examples in BDR §468n3, see especially the use of χειροτονηθείς and στελλόμενοι in 2 Cor. 8:19–20, πλουτιζόμενοι in 9:11, and δοξάζοντες in 9:13.

[9]. Paul mixed architectural and agricultural metaphors previously in 2:20–22, where he says that the whole “building” (οἰκοδομή), comprised of Jewish and Gentile believers, “will grow” (αὔξει). The same mixture of metaphors occurs in 1 Cor. 3:6–17, where the Corinthian Christians are both God’s “field” (γεώργιον) and his “building” (οἰκοδομή; v. 9). The language in Eph. 3:17b is especially close to Col. 1:23, where Paul assumes that the Colossian Christians are “founded and rooted” (τεθεμελιωμένοι καὶ ἑδραῖοι) in the faith, and to Col. 2:7, where they are “rooted in and built upon” (ἐρριζωμένοι καὶ ἐποικοδομούμενοι) Christ. The contexts of these expressions are so different in Colossians and Ephesians that it is very difficult to imagine direct literary dependence. Instead, the language of one letter must still have been in the mind of the author of the other, a situation easily explained if Paul authored both at roughly the same time.

[10]. Other uses of the verb from about Paul’s time and in the same sense of “prevail over” appear in Strabo (ca. 64 BC–after AD 21) Geogr. 6.3.4; 16.1.15; and 17.1.3. These examples, however, do not have a complementary infinitive.

[11]. Origen correlates the terms ὕψος and βάθος with Christ’s ascent and descent in 4:8–10 and explains the terms πλάτος and μῆκος as a reference to the wide reach of the proclamation of the cross (cf. Ps. 19:4; Rom. 10:18). Paul wants his readers to grasp what it means to be crucified with Christ, figuratively stretching oneself out (συνεκτεινόμενος, synekteinomenos) with him on his cross (cf. Gal. 2:19). Although certainly not the most convincing reading of the measurements, this explanation perhaps deserves better than the contemptuous dismissal it has often received (e.g., Calvin 1965: 168; Eadie 1883: 252; Abbott 1897: 101).

[12]. Theophylact is often listed in the commentaries as holding this opinion, but his view is a hybrid. Although he at first seems to support the view that Paul is referring to “the mystery,” he is then led by Gregory of Nyssa to say that Paul wants the Ephesians “to grasp the mystery of the cross” (PG 124:1076).

[13]. For these and other references, see Schnackenburg 1991: 150–51; Faust 1993: 35–39; and Dahl 2000: 367–75.

[14]. Photius of Constantinople (tenth cent.) takes a similar approach (Staab 1933: 617–18) and makes sense of the syntax by suggesting that Paul is using either “ellipsis” to refer to the “mystery” or “hyperbaton” to refer to “the knowledge of Christ,” expecting the reader mentally to transpose the term “knowledge” from the next clause.

[15]. Dahl (2000: 365–88) believes that the four measurements arise out of the environment of ancient speculation about the size of the universe and religious wisdom, but he thinks they function here in 3:18 as a “preamble” to Paul’s primary concern, which is the love of Christ.

[16]. The two clauses are tied tightly together with τέ, whose “commonest significance is combination or addition,” and which “denotes, on the whole, a closer connexion than καί” (Denniston 1950: 496). Cf. 1 Cor. 4:21, ἐν ἀγάπῃ πνεύματί τε πραΰτητος, where “love” and “spirit of gentleness” are basically synonymous.

[17]. See especially Barth 1974: 373–74; Lincoln 1990: 214; O’Brien 1999: 265.

[18]. This does not contradict Col. 2:9–10, which says that “all the fullness of the deity dwells bodily in [Christ], and you are complete in him [ἐστὲ ἐν αὐτῷ πεπληρωμένοι]” (2:9–10). The idea of growth toward maturity that lies beneath Eph. 3:19b also appears in Col. 2:19. Cf. O’Brien 1999: 265.

B. Paul Praises the God Who Is Able to Strengthen His Readers (3:20–21)

[1]. On the doxology as a liturgical and literary form, see Delling 1962: 62–66; Deichgräber 1967: 25–40; and Aune 1997: 43–46.

[2]. Most early Christian doxologies ascribe glory to God, but sometimes the glory goes to Christ (2 Pet. 3:18; Heb. 13:21; 1 Pet. 4:11[?]; 2 Tim. 4:18[?]) or to God through Christ (e.g., Rom. 16:27; Did. 9.4; 1 Clem. 58.2; 61.3; 64.1; 65.2). Rev. 5:13 ascribes glory to God and Christ, and Mart. Pol. 14.3 and 23.5 to all three persons of the Trinity.

[3]. E.g., ᾧ (4 Macc. 18:24; Gal. 1:5; 1 Tim. 6:16; 2 Tim. 4:18; 1 Pet. 4:11; Heb. 13:21; Mart. Pol. 21.1; 22.3); αὐτῷ (Rom. 11:36; 1 Pet. 5:11; 2 Pet. 3:18; Rev. 1:6). Pr. Man. 15 (Odes 12.15 LXX); Did. 8.2; 9.4; 10.5 are exceptions: all four begin with σοῦ.

[4]. BDAG 213. See, e.g., τῷ δὲ θεῷ (Phil. 4:20); τῷ δὲ βασιλεῖ (1 Tim. 1:17). Rev. 5:13 is an exception.

[5]. Pace Alford 1857: 108; Ellicott 1859: 74; Hoehner 2002: 92, δέ does not signal a contrast between the preceding intercessory prayer’s concern with human beings and the doxology’s concern with the praise of God.

[6]. Cf. 1 Tim. 1:17 and Jude 24–25, where an articular description of God in a doxology also receives elaboration.

[7]. The similar adverb ὑπερεκπερισσῶς appears in 1 Clem. 20.11 and in the text of 1 Thess. 5:13 in B, D, F, and G. It appears in the text of D and U in Mark 7:37 (BDF §116.3; BDAG 1033).

[8]. Cf. John Newton: “Thou art coming to a King, Large petitions with Thee bring; For His grace and power are such, None can ever ask too much” (“Come, My Soul, Thy Suit Prepare” [1742]).

[9]. E.g., Masson (1953: 183) picks the indicative, Caragounis (1977: 77) the imperative, and Hoehner (2002: 494) the optative.

[10]. Christian literature closest in proximity to Ephesians seems to use the indicative when a verb is expressed (1 Pet. 4:11; 1 Clem. 58.2; Did. 8.2; 9.4; 10.5), and so, if a choice must be made, it should probably be the indicative.

[11]. E.g., εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων (Gal. 1:5; Phil. 4:20; 1 Tim. 1:17; 1 Pet. 4:11; Heb. 13:21; 1 Clem. 58.2; Mart. Pol. 22.3); εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας (Rom. 11:36; 1 Pet. 5:11); εἰς πάντας τοὺς αἰῶνας (Jude 25; cf. 1 Clem. 64); and καὶ νῦν καὶ εἰς ἡμέραν αἰῶνος (2 Pet. 3:18).

[12]. Cf. Gal. 1:5; Rom. 1:25; 9:5; 11:36, where “amen” is Paul’s own utterance.

VIII. The Growth of the Church toward Unity and Maturity (4:1–16)

[1]. See Purves 1889: 258–70; Lightfoot 1896: 210; Barnard 1967: 130–34; and Beyer, TDNT 2:620.

A. Christian Unity and Its Theological Basis (4:1–6)

[1]. See Nauck 1958: 134–35 and Engberg-Pedersen 2004: 63.

[2]. As Engberg-Pedersen (2004: 54–59) and Starr (2004: 100–104) show, this same movement from doctrine to ethical precepts was much discussed in Stoic ethics. See especially Seneca, Ep. 94 and 95.

[3]. Cf. 1 Thess. 4:1, where Paul couples παρακαλῶ with ἐρωτάω (ask) to give his instructions a friendly nuance: “We ask [ἐρωτῶμεν] and appeal [παρακαλοῦμεν] to you in the Lord Jesus that just as you received instructions from us about how it is necessary to walk [περιπατεῖν] and to please God (just as you are doing), you do so even more.”

[4]. Royal decrees in antiquity, similarly, were often cast in the form of letters with their conventions of friendship, including the use of the phrase παρακαλῶ . . . ὑμᾶς, despite the lack of any personal relationship between the author of the decree and its recipients (e.g., 2 Macc. 9:19–27; cf. Bjerkelund 1967: 62–65).

[5]. Ephesians 4:1–6:20 is, therefore, a classic example of ancient paraenesis, which is a “concise, benevolent injunction that reminds of moral practices to be pursued or avoided, expresses or implies a shared worldview, and does not anticipate disagreement” (Starr 2004: 79). It appears in a wide range of ancient Greco-Roman ethical literature (Engberg-Pedersen 2004; Starr 2004).

[6]. This is not surprising, since the more-common adjective ταπεινός (tapeinos, lowly) and verb ταπεινόω (tapeinoō, humiliate), although they could be used positively, most often refer to servility, weakness, and breaking the spirit of others (Grundmann, TDNT 8:1–5; cf. LSJ 1756–57).

[7]. Cf. the use of the verb ταπεινόω and the noun ταπεινόφρων in Prov. 29:23 LXX.

[8]. A few interpreters have taken either both μετά phrases with both participles (e.g., Bengel 1860: 88; Theodoret [R. Hill 2001: 2.45]) or the second μετά phrase with the first participle (e.g., Muddiman 2001: 176, 179), but as Best (1998: 362) says, if the first of these options were correct, there would be no need to repeat the second μετά, and if the second option were correct, the symmetry of the two sets of phrases would be destroyed.

[9]. Cf. Mayer (2002: 61), who correctly identifies τοῦ πνεύματος as a subjective genitive.

[10]. Mayer (2002: 64–66) speaks of the unity portrayed in this passage as both “gift” (Gabe) and “task” (Aufgabe).

[11]. Pace Abbott (1897: 107), who says that “it is not by the bond of peace that the unity of the Spirit is kept” (cf. O’Brien 1999: 280; Hoehner 2002: 512). For the interpretation of the ἐν adopted here, see Schnackenburg 1991: 165; MacDonald 2000: 287; Aletti 2001: 210.

[12]. Τῆς εἰρήνης is, then, a genitive of apposition, as most commentators recognize. See especially the discussion in Alford 1857: 109.

[13]. Bruce (1984: 335, 337) refers to 4:4–6 as a “credo,” but his exegesis shows that he thought Paul had altered the original confession.

[14]. Cf. Lincoln 1990: 229, but not Best 1997a: 64–65; 1998: 358, who thinks that only 4:4b is the author’s own composition.

[15]. Cf. Paul’s statements elsewhere that believers were called ἐν . . . εἰρήνῃ (1 Cor. 7:15) and ἐν ἁγιασμῷ (1 Thess. 4:7; Ellicott 1859: 80; Abbott 1897: 108).

[16]. Ellicott (1859: 80), for example, thinks that there is one faith and one baptism because there is one Lord, and many commentators puzzle over why Paul mentions baptism but not the Lord’s Supper (e.g., De Wette 1843: 130; Alford 1857: 110; Eadie 1883: 275; Westcott 1906: 58–59).

[17]. On this, see Dunn (1998a: 96n31), who illustrates the point from Josephus, J. W. 4.137. There Josephus says that a crowd of outlaws poured into Jerusalem and that this influx ἐβάπτισεν τὴν πόλιν (overwhelmed the city).

[18]. The translation “irrigated” for ἐποτίσθημεν is from Dunn 1998a: 95.

[19]. See the extensive collection of Stoic and other Hellenistic religious expressions of God’s uniqueness and omnipresence in Norden 1923: 240–50.

B. The Gifts of the Victorious Christ Cultivate the Body’s Maturity (4:7–16)

[1]. Elsewhere in his letters, when Paul lists the gifts given to believers, he calls them χαρίσματα (1 Cor. 12:4, 9, 28, 30–31; Rom. 12:6), “favors bestowed” or “gifts” (BDAG 1081). Here he may have chosen to use χάρις instead specifically to make the link between his own powerfully transforming gift and the gifts that Christ gives to each believer. They are qualitatively alike. Cf. Best 1998: 377.

[2]. Schlier (1957: 191) also believes that the “us” of 4:7 refers to the offices of 4:11 but thinks that the letter comes from Paul himself.

[3]. These eccentricities should not, however, be exaggerated. Although the phrase διὸ λέγει does not occur in the undisputed Paulines, διό occurs more often in Paul’s undisputed letters than anywhere else in the NT, and Paul frequently introduces quotations with λέγει. Moreover, Paul twice uses λέγει to introduce a quotation from Scripture and seems simply to assume that his readers know its source (Gal. 3:16; 2 Cor. 6:2; cf. James 4:6). Philo often uses διὸ λέγει to introduce quotations of Scripture (Alleg. Interp. 3.172, 180; Agriculture 100; Drunkenness 138; Confusion 182), although mostly in the passive voice (Posterity 96; Drunkenness 166; Heir 58; 233; Flight 159; Names 17; Dreams 2.280, 296; Abraham 80; QG 97). Hebrews uses the same idiom, if not the precise phrase, to introduce Scripture quotations (Heb. 3:7, 10; 10:5).

[4]. NETS translates, “You received gifts by a person,” but for the use of ἐν ἀνθρώπῳ to mean “among humanity” or “in humankind,” see, e.g., Xenophon, Symp. 5.3; Plato, Resp. 2.376b; Aristotle, Gen. an. 770a; Eccles. 2:24 LXX.

[5]. Some of the wording in what follows is indebted to Thielman 2007: 819–25, where a more-detailed treatment of the relationship between Eph. 4:8 and Ps. 68:18 may be found.

[6]. Other strategies include taking “among humanity” to mean “by the virtue of Israel” (Pesiq. Rab. 47.4) or “because of the merits of the man,” meaning the pious Abraham (Soperim 16.10; Midr. Teh. 22.19; Exod. Rab. 28.1). Some interpreters claimed that Moses received the Torah as recompense for the insult that the heavenly angels gave to him when they called him a mere “man” (b. Šabb. 89a) or, moving in the opposite direction, that Moses received the Torah “as a mere man” (Pesiq. Rab. 20.4). Cf. the summary in Schwindt 2002: 404.

[7]. The Aramaic text with German translation is available in Schwindt 2002: 403.

[8]. See, e.g., Abbott 1897: 112–13; Robinson 1904: 180; Dibelius and Greeven 1953: 80; Barth 1974: 476; Lincoln 1982: 19; 1990: 243; Gnilka 1971: 207; Pokorný 1992: 170; W. H. Harris 1996: 64–122; Aletti 2001: 215–16; Schwindt 2002: 403–23.

[9]. On this second point, see especially Gombis 2005: 370–71.

[10]. On the history of interpretation of 4:7–11, see W. H. Harris 1996: 1–45.

[11]. Calvin (1965: 176) says that Paul was “dealing only with the condition of the present life,” although Calvin (1973: 350–51) also thought the phrase referred especially to Christ’s passion and death.

[12]. He was preceded, according to W. H. Harris (1996: 14–15), by Theodore of Mopsuestia in the fifth century and perhaps P. Abelard in the twelfth century.

[13]. As Bauckham (1992: 152) observes, there is some inconsistency in Od. 11 about Odysseus. The realm of the dead seems to be at the ocean’s edge, but then, in 11.475 Odysseus is said to have “come down” (κατελθέμεν) to the dead.

[14]. Dreams about descending into hades were common enough to merit a section on their interpretation in the Oneirocritica of Artemidorus Daldianus (Oneir. 2.55), a second-century-AD Ephesian.

[15]. Bauckham does not mention the ancient texts from which his list is constructed, but see, e.g., Aristophanes, Ran. 70; Plato, Resp. 10.614c; Virgil, Aen. 8.243–46; Lucian, Philops. 24. See also the texts mentioned in Kreitzer 1998b: 385–88 (Diodorus Siculus, Biblio. hist. 5.3.3–4; Pausanias, Descr. 1.38.5).

[16]. Paul did not need to use the term “hades,” therefore, to make a reference to the realm of the dead understood (pace, e.g., Eadie 1883: 292; cf. Best 1998: 384), nor did he need to use the superlative form κατώτατα (Pss. 62:10 LXX [63:10 MT; 63:9 Eng.]; 138:15 LXX [139:15 MT, Eng.]) to draw a contrast with the phrase ὑπεράνω πάντων τῶν οὐρανῶν (far above all the heavens) in 4:10 (pace, e.g., Lincoln 1990: 245).

[17]. See also Matt. 11:23 (par. Luke 10:15), where heaven and hades refer to the extremes of the universe and are used in this sense metaphorically.

[18]. On Hecate’s often-menacing nature, see Henrichs 2003b.

[19]. Αὐτός does not mean “same” here but instead is emphatic (Abbott 1897: 116; Muddiman 2001: 196; Hoehner 2002: 536). This does not mean, however, that the statement is about something other than the identity of the one who ascended with the one who descended (pace Barth 1974: 434). The emphasis on identity comes from ἐστιν καί (is also). For this reason, the translation “He who descended is the same one who ascended” (NRSV) is not incorrect (pace Muddiman 2001: 196; Hoehner 2002: 536). Cf. Westcott 1906: 61.

[20]. Cf. the role of the מבקר in the Qumran Damascus Rule. He is “the head of the community” (HALOT 1:151) and “will heal all the afflicted among them like a shepherd his flock” (CD-A 13:9; trans. García Martínez and Tigchelaar 1997; cf. Jeremias, TDNT 6:489).

[21]. I am assuming here that we can equate those who lead (προϊστάμενοι, proistamenoi) and admonish (νουθετοῦντες, nouthetountes) the Thessalonian believers with teachers (1 Thess. 5:12).

[22]. See the full taxonomy of views in Merklein 1973: 75.

[23]. One path around this difficulty takes the πρός phrase as the ultimate purpose of the gift of offices to the church and the two εἰς phrases as intermediate steps in accomplishing this goal (e.g., Alford 1857: 113–14; Ellicott 1859: 88; Eadie 1883: 308; Abbott 1897: 119). Another path that avoids the problem is to explain the πρός phrase as the work of the pastors and teachers and the two εἰς phrases as the work of all five groups (Masson 1953: 193). Both solutions seem too complex to be plausible, and neither has gathered much support. O’Neill (2001: 339) perceives the magnitude of the problem clearly, but his idea that the late minuscules 1, 242, and 1149 preserve the correct reading when they omit the article after πρός is not a viable solution.

[24]. This correspondence of language makes it unlikely that the assisting connections of the body in 4:16 are the “ministers” of 4:11 (pace Lincoln 1990: 263; Schnackenburg 1991: 189; Muddiman 2001: 209).

[25]. O’Neill (2001: 339–40) is more nuanced, recognizing that the view goes back at least as far as the early nineteenth century, but he still thinks that its current popularity has more to do with the spirit of the age than with sober exegesis.

[26]. This approach is also supported by a large number of more-recent exegetes from a wide variety of ecclesiastical contexts (e.g., Gnilka 1973: 213; Bruce 1984: 349; Best 1998: 395–99; Pokorný 1992: 175; O’Brien 1999: 301–5; Aletti 2001: 219–21; Hoehner 2002: 547–49).

[27]. It appears frequently in the first-century-BC commentary of Apollonius of Citium (ca. 90–15 BC) on Hippocrates’ treatise “On Joints” and twice in a medical text by the Ephesian physician Soranus, who flourished in the second century AD (cf. LSJ 910; Hoehner 2002: 549). Since figures from human development and physiology appear in 4:13, 14, and 16, it is tempting to read the term καταρτισμός as a medical metaphor: the five specially gifted groups of 4:11, like the ancient physician, are charged with setting the body in order so that it can grow and function properly.

[28]. Pace Page (2005: 33), who after a careful review of the evidence, nevertheless concludes that none of the nonliterary uses of the word closely parallels its use here.

[29]. Cf. Rom. 9:22, where the participle κατηρτισμένα is followed by the phrase εἰς ἀπώλειαν to indicate the purpose of the preparation (Aletti 2001: 221n69).

[30]. Pace Page (2005: 41), who appeals to the place of apostles and prophets at the foundation of God’s household in 2:19–20 as evidence that in 4:12 the author assigns the task of building up the body to those who hold the teaching offices of 4:11. The apostles and prophets of 2:20–21, however, are not portrayed as building up the church. Instead, they form part of the building, albeit an important part. Moreover, Paul is explicit in 4:16 that the whole “body . . . produces the growth of the body for the purpose of building itself up [οἰκοδομή] in love.”

[31]. The verb καταντάω and the preposition εἰς were commonly used together to speak of arriving “at” a particular point. See, e.g., 1 Cor. 10:11; 14:36; Phil. 3:11; Polybius, Hist. 4.1.8; 4.34.2; 6.9.10; LSJ 903; BDAG 523.

[32]. This reading of the three prepositional phrases in 4:13 might seem at first to require the same parallel understanding of the three prepositional phrases in 4:12. In 4:12, however, the prepositions at the head of each phrase switched from πρός to εἰς. In addition, the objects of the last two prepositional phrases in 4:12 (καταρτισμός and διακονία) contain verbal ideas that are naturally completed with purposes clauses.

[33]. Best (1998: 403) believes that both ideas are present.

[34]. The ἵνα clause (v. 14) is not, therefore, subordinate to the μέχρι clause (v. 13; pace, e.g., Alford 1857: 114–15; Ellicott 1859: 91) but stands parallel to it (e.g., Abbott 1897: 121; Westcott 1906: 63; Hoehner 2002: 560). Both clauses complete the verbal notion contained in the noun οἰκοδομή (v. 12).

[35]. As a search of the TLG suggests; cf. Hoehner 2002: 563.

[36]. The use of the term in Irenaeus, Haer. 1.1.19, seems to be dependent on Eph. 4:14.

[37]. Even in these places, however, it is debatable whether the word itself or the context in which it appears provides the negative connotations.

[38]. It could refer to an accounting error. See NewDocs 2:94–95, no. 69.

[39]. This phrase, then, goes with the participle ἀληθεύοντες rather than with the main verb αὐξήσωμεν (pace especially Abbott 1897: 123). Not only does this preserve the contrast with the manner in which “every wind of teaching” operates (cf. Lincoln 1990: 259; Schnackenburg 1991: 187), but it also is the stylistically more probable interpretation. As Best (1998: 407) points out, unless we take ἐν ἀγάπῃ with ἀληθεύοντες, the participle remains alone, unqualified by anything, whereas both the false teaching of 4:14 and αὐξήσωμεν in 4:15 receive generous qualification.

[40]. The phrase τὰ πάντα is an “adverbial accusative,” indicating that the growth takes place “in every respect” (“in jeder Hinsicht”; BDR §161.2). This probably corresponds to the statement in 4:13 that the edification of believers occurs until they arrive at “the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ.”

[41]. That idea would not quite “defy explanation” (Robinson 1904: 185), but it would certainly be odd.

[42]. The genitive phrase τῆς ἐπιχορηγίας is probably being use adjectivally. On this usage, see BDF §165 and Wallace 1996: 86–88.

[43]. Lightfoot (1879: 198–99): “joint”; Robinson (1904: 186): “ligament”; Hoehner (2002: 571–73): “contact”; van Kooten (2003: 57, 188–89): “cosmic bond.”

[44]. The reference is to Linguarum seu dictionum exoletarum Hippocratis explicatio (Kühn 1821–33: 19.87), attributed to Galen.

[45]. On ancient anatomical knowledge, see Vallance 2003: 82–85.

IX. A Reminder of How to Live as New Human Beings (4:17–5:2)

[1]. Cf. 1 Thess. 5:8; Gal. 3:27; Rom. 13:12–14; Col. 3:8–10; and, e.g., Philo, Drunkenness 7, 86; Let. Aris. 124; Plato, Resp. 5.457a.

[2]. There are conceptual and linguistic parallels between Eph. 4:17, 19, 22–24 and Col. 3:5, 7–10, and many interpreters (e.g., Lincoln 1990: 273; Schnackenburg 1991: 195; van Kooten 2003: 227–29, 268) see them as evidence that the author of Ephesians used Colossians as a source. There are also some odd differences between the two passages, however, if this is the case. Why are so many of the same words used, but in different forms (ἀκαθαρσία, πλεονεξία, περιπατέω, ἀποτίθημι, ἐνδύω, κτίζω)? Why the shift from νέον and ἀνακαινούμενον in Col. 3:10 to καινόν and ἀνανεοῦσθαι in Eph. 4:24? Perhaps one author simply had the other letter in mind when writing and did not follow it closely, but it seems at least as likely that Paul composed the two passages at about the same time and that the traditional language of one letter was still loosely in his mind as he composed the other letter.

[3]. Here too the correspondence between 4:25–5:2 and Col. 3:8–9, 12–14 has convinced some interpreters that the author of Ephesians was following Colossians (e.g., Lincoln 1990: 297–98; Schnackenburg 1991: 206; van Kooten 2003: 227–29, 270). But again, if this is so, the author of Ephesians has rearranged the material in curious ways. In Eph. 4:29, 31, for example, he has turned the admonition about anger, abusive speech, and shameful speech in Col. 3:8 into two separate admonitions, shifted the last admonition about shameful speech (αἰσχρολογία) to first place and changed its wording (πᾶς λόγος σαπρός), and then both changed the order and lengthened the list of terms describing anger and abusive speech (ὀργήν, θυμόν, κακίαν, βλασφημίαν becomes πικρία καὶ θυμὸς καὶ ὀργὴ καὶ κραυγὴ καὶ βλασφημία; Eph. 4:31). Why he did this is not clear. It is at least as plausible to ascribe both passages to Paul and to think of him as giving traditional ethical exhortation from memory in two separate letters composed at about the same time.

A. No Longer Walk as “Gentiles” but as a New Human Being (4:17–24)

[1]. Paul uses it in 1 Thess. 2:12 (alongside παρακαλέω and παραμυθέομαι) with somewhat different connotations.

[2]. The participle ὄντες could go with ἀπηλλοτριωμένοι rather than with ἐσκοτωμένοι (Eadie 1883: 329; Robinson 1904: 189). This would correspond to Col. 1:21, but here in Eph. 4:18 such a construction would destroy the symmetry of the two clauses, each beginning with a perfect participle whose last three syllables (ω-μεν-οι) match (cf. Clement of Alexandria, Protr. 83.11; Ellicott 1859: 97; Westcott 1906: 66; Best 1998: 418; Hoehner 2002: 585). Best takes ὄντες with both participles, but this introduces unnecessary complexity into the sentence.

[3]. Cf. Josephus, Ant. 9.57, where Josephus retells the story of how God blinded the Syrian soldiers so that they could not recognize Elisha and were led by him into the camp of their enemies (2 Kings 6:8–23). According to Josephus, God used a mist to obscure the vision of the Syrians, and so “they enthusiastically went, with the prophet in the lead, because their eyes and understanding had been darkened by God [τὰς ὄψεις ὑπὸ θεοῦ καὶ τὴν διάνοιαν ἐπεσκοτημένοι]” (my trans.). For the metaphorical use of this language, see 1 Clem. 36.2 and T. Dan 2.4.

[4]. Commentators often observe the contrast between the darkened understanding of Gentiles in this passage and the enlightened eyes that Paul prays for his readers to experience in 1:18. The use of light-dark imagery and of perfect participles (πεφωτισμένους, ἐσκοτωμένοι) in both passages is noteworthy, but there is an important difference in the imagery. The implied contrast in 1:18 is between believers who understand God’s blessings and discouraged believers (cf. 3:13) who do not understand them. In 4:18, however, the implied contrast is between unbelievers, who are completely in the dark, and believers, who have experienced the enlightenment of conversion (cf. 5:13–14; 1 Clem. 36.2).

[5]. Cf. L.A.E. 21.6 (OTP 2:281), where Adam exclaims to Eve in dismay, ἀπηλλοτρίωσάς με ἐκ τῆς δόξης τοῦ θεοῦ (You have estranged me from the glory of God).

[6]. Its other NT use (1 Pet. 1:14) couples “ignorance” (ἄγνοια) with “lusts” (ἐπιθυμίαι).

[7]. Cf. Epictetus (Arrian, Epict. diss. 1.5), who distinguishes between “two kinds of petrification [ἀπολίθωσις]: one is the petrification of the intellect [νοητικός], the other the sense of shame” (trans. W. Oldfather 1925–28). Intellectual hardness comes from the mental inability to understand (συνιέναι) an argument, but the petrification of shame recognizes the truth of an opponent’s argument and, simply to avoid embarrassment, refuses to acknowledge its validity. The latter is more culpable. The second-century-AD grammarian Aelius Herodianus equates πώρωσις with ἀπολίθωσις (Partitiones 113, l. 3).

[8]. For the same sentiment in connection with Jews who do not understand the true significance of the old covenant because they have not turned to the Lord, see 2 Cor. 3:14–16.

[9]. Οὐκ ἔχοντα σκοπόν, οὐδὲ τέλος, ἀλλὰ ματαίως φερόμενον.

[10]. BDAG 729–30 says that οἵτινες is used here “to emphasize a characteristic quality, by which a preceding statement is to be confirmed.”

[11]. For the use of εἰς to indicate result in the construction παραδιδόναι εἰς, see BDR §187.2. I have taken ἀκαθαρσίας as an objective genitive and the phrase ἐν πλεονεξίᾳ (literally, “with greediness”) as a kind of adverbial description of the action noun ἐργασίαν. According to BDAG 330, ἐν can be used as a “marker denoting kind and manner.” That is probably how Paul uses it here.

[12]. See the text and English translation of Düring 1979: 74–77. According to Düring (1979: 24), the fictional letters of “Chion” were written “in the second half of the first century A.D.”

[13]. BDF §173.1 could be understood to mean that ἀκούω followed by the accusative of a person is a regular idiom for hearing “about” someone. BDR §173.1n4, however, is somewhat clearer that, although the accusative of the thing(s) about which one has heard is normal Greek, the use of the same idiom for a person, as in Eph. 4:21, is less usual.

[14]. See Muddiman (2001: 216), who interprets αὐτὸν ἠκούσατε (you have heard of him) differently, but in commenting on ἐμάθετε τὸν Χριστόν, he uses the texts cited above to illustrate how authentically Pauline this unusual idiom is.

[15]. Barth’s idea (1974: 498, 505, 530, 533–36) that καθώς introduces the quotation “Truth in Jesus!” from a supposed body of early Christian teaching seems too speculative to be useful in interpretation.

[16]. Both Hort and Abbot recognized the oddity of this expression and, in apparent desperation, emended ἀλήθεια to the dative form ἀληθείᾳ (“as he [Christ] is in truth, in Jesus”).

[17]. “There is truth in Jesus” is, from the perspective expressed in this letter, a major understatement (Hort [Westcott 1906: 71]; Best 1998: 429). “He is in truth, in Jesus,” however, is (pace Hort [Westcott 1906: 71]; Abbott 1897: 136) a very complex way of saying that the true Messiah is the historical Jesus.

[18]. In grammatical terms, this is the use of the infinitive in indirect discourse, but the original discourse could have been either in the indicative or the imperative mood (see Wallace 1996: 605). The ὑμᾶς resumes the ὑμεῖς at the beginning of the sentence (v. 20). For this understanding of the Greek, see Alford 1857: 119 and Ellicott 1859: 100–101.

[19]. Cf. van der Horst 1973: 182; Lincoln 1990: 284; and Best 1998: 431.

[20]. See van der Horst 1973: 184–87. The phrase appears in the humorous story of a dog chasing the philosopher Pyrrhon in terror up a tree. As a Skeptic, Pyrrhon was supposed to remain calm in the face of such emergencies, and when confronted with the inconsistency between his touted philosophy and his behavior, he apparently responded that it was difficult to “put off the human being.” The account appears in Eusebius, Praep. ev. 14.18 [p. 763a] in a quotation from the third-century-BC artisan Antigonas of Carystus (cf. Diogenes Laertius, Vit. phil. 9.66). Van der Horst (1973: 186) has made a good case that Antigonas’s writings were popular in the first century AD.

[21]. On the use of κατά to mean “because of, as a result of, on the basis of,” see BDAG 513.

[22]. Cf. the use of φθείρω in 1 Cor. 3:17b and 2 Pet. 2:12 to mean eschatological ruin (BDAG 1054).

[23]. See, e.g., Ellicott 1859: 102–3; Masson 1953: 202n3; Schlier 1957: 220; Gnilka 1971: 230; Schnackenburg 1991: 200.

[24]. See, e.g., Theodoret [R. Hill 2001: 2.48]; Eadie 1883: 342; Calvin 1965: 190; De Wette 1843: 142; Alford 1857: 120; Abbott 1897: 137–38; Haupt 1902a: 178–79; Barth 1974: 508; Lincoln 1990: 287; Fee 1994: 709–12; Aletti 2001: 237; Muddiman 2001: 220; Hoehner 2002: 608–9.

[25]. Cf. Muddiman 2001: 220, although his “1 Cor. 1.12” should be 1 Cor. 2:11. The thought (if not the language) here is close to Col. 3:10, which speaks of “putting on the new man that is being renewed in knowledge.” Here, too, the renewal is inward and has a mental component. Cf. Lincoln 1990: 284, although the lack of verbal agreement does not seem to support Lincoln’s idea (1990: 273–74) that the author of Eph. 4:23 closely followed Colossians.

B. Living as Human Beings Newly Created in God’s Image (4:25–5:2)

[1]. For the syntax, cf. James 1:21; Heb. 12:1; and, less exactly, 1 Pet. 2:1 (BDAG 124).

[2]. Gnilka 1971: 234; Lincoln 1982: 43; 1990: 300; cf. Dibelius and Greeven 1953: 87.

[3]. Moritz (1996a: 88) is on the right track, then, when he argues that the author’s sensitivity to the language of the OT elsewhere in the letter makes unnecessary the theory that he simply took it over from Jewish ethical tradition. See also Thielman 2007: 826.

[4]. The LXX has interpreted the ambiguous Hebrew term רִגְזוּ, probably correctly, as a reference to anger.

[5]. Here I follow the interpretation of the Hebrew Psalm in Craigie and Tate 2004: 79–81. This interpretation works equally well for the LXX version despite the slight differences between the two texts.

[6]. Since God expresses anger against those who disobey him (5:6; cf. 2:3), Paul would not view anger as in itself wrong, but this does not decide the issue of whether the anger of people is justified on the basis that it imitates the anger of God. Paul would assume the complete purity of God’s motives in showing anger, but as 4:31 shows, he seems to align human anger with bitterness and to believe that it often results in violence.

[7]. 1 Cor. 16:1–4; Phil. 1:7; 2:25; 4:15, 18; 2 Cor. 8–9; Rom. 12:13; 15:25–28; Acts 2:44–45; 4:34–35; 1 Tim. 5:3–5, 16; 6:18; Did. 4.5–8; cf. Lucian, Peregr. 13, 16. See also Rosner 2007: 121–29.

[8]. On the “putrid” smell of death in the Testament of Abraham, see Allison 2003: 343.

[9]. Cf. Marcus Aurelius’s coupling of σαπρός with the adjective κίβδηλος (“fraudulent, dishonest”; LSJ 950) when referring to the person who is straightforward and honest in word only (Med. 11.15).

[10]. The oral connotations of κραυγή and βλασφημία are obvious. For πικρία, see, e.g., Rom. 3:14, and for θυμός and ὀργή, see, e.g., Pss. Sol. 2.23.

[11]. Cf. Rom. 2:8 and Col. 3:8, where they appear in the reverse of their order in Eph. 4:31 but with no clear distinction in meaning (Best 1998: 461). Pseudo-Phocylides reveals the influence of Stoicism when he defines ὀργή as ὄρεξις (desire) and distinguishes it from the stronger emotion μῆνις (rage).

[12]. Χρηστός is often used of God in the OT (e.g., LXX: Pss. 24:8 [25:8 MT, Eng.]; 33:9 [34:9 MT; 34:8 Eng.]; 51:11 [52:11 MT; 52:9 Eng.]; 68:17 [69:17 MT; 69:16 Eng.]; 99:5 [100:5 MT, Eng.]; 105:1 [106:1]; 106:1 [107:1]; 108:21 [109:21]; 118:68 [119:68]; 135:1 [136:1]; 144:9 [145:9]; Spicq, TLNT 3:512n6), and the Pauline literature uses χρηστότης of God in Rom. 2:4; 11:22; and Titus 3:4.

[13]. If this is correct, then the use of χαρίζομαι here is not a mere copying of its use in Col. 2:13 and 3:13. To the contrary, the use of the term is so natural in the context of Ephesians’ rich vocabulary of grace that Best (1998: 463) comments, “If we had to choose this would favour the priority of Ephesians.”

[14]. Cf. Lincoln 1990: 299; and see the additional note for the cultural background and probable origins of this phrase in Ephesians.

[15]. See also Deut. 10:17–19, where God’s love of the stranger provides the pattern for Israel’s love of the stranger. Cf. Houston 2007: 11.

[16]. The καί that introduces the clause “he gave himself for us” is probably used in an “explicative” way, to connect an explanation of something with what is being explained (BDAG 495).

[17]. Gal. 1:4; 1 Tim. 2:6; and Titus 2:14 all use δίδωμι rather than παραδίδωμι. Cf. Hengel 1981: 35.

[18]. A photograph of the relevant page of the damaged 𝔓49 is easily accessible in Comfort and Barrett 2001: 356.

[19]. On this text in Plato, see Michaelis, TDNT 4:662; on its relevance for understanding Eph. 4:24 and 5:1, see Wild 1985: 130.

[20]. Cf. Wild 1985: 127–43; Michaelis, TDNT 4:664–66. If Aelian is accurate, however, the use of the concept of imitating God in ethical discussion predates Plato: “Pythagoras used to say that these two things the gods had given to human beings are best: speaking the truth and doing good; and he added that each of these was like [ἔοικε] the deeds of the gods” (Aelian, Var. hist. 12.59, my trans.; cf. Colson 1939: 431).





X. Avoiding and Transforming the Deeds of Darkness (5:3–14)
