[1].Some interpreters think that Col. 3:5–8 was the primary source for Eph. 5:3–8 (e.g., De Wette 1843: 145; Lincoln 1990: 319; Schnackenburg 1991: 216; Pokorný 1992: 1998; van Kooten 2003: 190n74). There are certainly similarities in thought and expression: sexual immorality, impurity, and greed show up in both passages and in the same order; shameful speech appears in both; greed is identified with idolatry in both (the only places in the NT where the identification is this explicit); the wrath of God “is coming” (ἔρχεται); and the readers are reminded of what they “once” (ποτέ) were and what they “now” (νῦν) are (Lincoln 1990: 319). It is difficult to account for the many differences between the two passages, however, on the theory that Colossians was the source for Ephesians (Best 1998: 473). A common traditional vice list is possible (Best 1998: 473), and it is easy to imagine Paul using such a traditional vice list in slightly different ways in two letters written at roughly the same time.

A. Avoiding Sexual Immorality and Greed (5:3–7)

[1]. Πορνεία, ἀκαθαρσία (v. 3); αἰσχρότης, εὐτραπελία (v. 4); πόρνος, ἀκάθαρτος (v. 5); τὰ . . . κρυφῇ γινόμενα ὑπ᾿ αὐτῶν αἰσχρόν ἐστιν (v. 12).

[2]. Origen and Jerome (Heine 2002: 209–10). Cf. Abbott 1897: 148; Westcott 1906: 76; Lincoln 1990: 322; O’Brien 1999: 360.

[3]. Cf. Ellicott 1859: 113; Robinson 1904: 107; Best 1998: 476; Rosner 2007: 103–11.

[4]. Pace Osiek and Macdonald (2006: 109–11), who believe that πορνεία in the NT may not have included sexual relations between a married man and his female slave (cf. Glancy 2006: 57–70). This view is very difficult to square with 1 Cor. 7:1–9, where marriage provides the one legitimate context for sexual activity, or with 1 Cor. 6:19 (cf. Gen. 2:24; Eph. 5:21), where it is assumed that sexual relations establish a marriage bond. As T. Reu. 4 shows, moreover, Paul’s view was not unique among Hellenistic Jews. In the Testament of Reuben, πορνεία (1.6; 3.3; 4.6–7; 5.5; 6.1) is defined with reasonable clarity as a matter of occupying oneself sexually with anyone but a spouse (4.1).

[5]. So correctly, e.g., Dibelius and Greeven 1953: 89; Best 1998: 477; pace, e.g., Barth 1974: 561; Lincoln 1990: 322.

[6]. Cf. Alford 1857: 124; Ellicott 1859: 114; pace Hultin 2008: 179.

[7]. Syntactically, the construction is loose: there is no main verb for 5:4, which means that the main verb of 5:3 (ὀνομαζέσθω) carries the thought forward (Best 1998: 477).

[8]. Cf. the description of banquet singing in Gosnell 1993: 336 and the general description of Roman banquets in Slater 1991 and D’Ambra 2007: 55.

[9]. This common cultural background is a more likely context for Paul’s language in 5:4 than Kreitzer’s suggestion (1998a: 51–77) that this text refers specifically to the practices of the Demeter/Cybele cult in Hierapolis. The general nature of the three terms αἰσχρότης, μωρολογία, and εὐτραπελία allows them to refer to a far broader range of behaviors than the specifically religious practices that Kreitzer’s evidence reveals. Kreitzer’s article usefully demonstrates, however, that words beginning with αἰσχρ- frequently refer to obscene speech or behavior. It also provides helpful illustrations of the type of behavior that 5:12 refers to when it speaks of secret behavior that is shameful even to describe.

[10]. E.g., Aristotle, Eth. Nic. 8.3 [8.1156a.13–14]; 8.4 [8.1157a.3–6]; Eth. eud. 3.7 [3.1234a.4–23]; Plutarch, Ant. 43.3 (van der Horst 1978: 167–68, 171; Hultin 2008: 190–96). Hultin disputes van der Horst’s claim that the term is often used with negative connotations.

[11]. The verb is in the imperfect tense, which, according to BDF §358.2, is sometimes used “in expressions of necessity, obligation, duty, possibility, etc.” Cf. the use of καθῆκεν in Acts 22:22.

[12]. Symmachus (late second cent. AD) apparently used it to render תֵּדְעוּi יָדֹעַ in Jer. 49:22 (42:22 MT: “Be well aware,” NRSV; Robinson 1904: 199). Much later, Mark the Hermit (fifth cent. AD) also used the phrase in his Disputatio cum quodam causidico (16 lines 48–51): Τοῦτο οὖν ἀκριβῶς ἴστε γινώσκοντες, ἀδελφοί, ὅτι ἐὰν μὴ τὰς ἐπιφορὰς μετὰ πίστεως καὶ εὐχαριστίας ὑπομείνωμεν, τὴν ἐγκεκρυμμένην κακίαν εὑρεῖν οὐ δυνάμεθα. (“Be sure you understand this clearly, brothers, that unless we patiently endure calamities with faith and thanksgiving, we are not able to discover the evil concealed within” [my trans.].)

[13]. Paul used the neuter relative pronoun ὅ to begin his explanatory comment, a seeming anomaly since πλεονέκτης, its apparent antecedent (cf. Col. 3:5), is masculine. This lack of concord has led to confusion from ancient times to the present. The manuscript tradition represented by A, D, K, L, P, 0278, and 𝔐 “corrected” the grammar by changing ὅ to ὅς. Modern commentators are sometimes led by the problem to suggest that the neuter encompasses all three vices, which are together called “idolatry” (e.g., Schnackenburg 1991: 219n10). The phrase ὅ ἐστιν, however, was a common formula in Koine Greek for identifying one thing with another thing and was used without regard to the gender of the words that it links (BDF §132.2; BDAG 727; Metzger 1994: 539; cf. Mark 15:16).

[14]. Cf. also 1 Cor. 15:50, where inheriting the kingdom lies in the future.

[15]. See 2 Bar. 39.7; Pss. Sol. 17.21–46; 18.5–9; 1 Cor. 15:24; Matt. 16:28; Luke 1:33; 22:29–30; 23:42; John 18:36, where the Messiah or Jesus rules over God’s people as king. Cf. Eadie 1883: 375; Hoehner 2002: 661; Lincoln 1990: 325.

[16]. See Thielman 2005: 512–35 and the scholarship cited there; and cf. Calvin 1965: 198; Abbott 1897: 152; Schlier 1957: 236; Bruce 1961: 104–5; Barth 1974: 565–66; Best 1998: 484–85.

[17]. Pace, e.g., Lincoln (1990: 325) and Schnackenburg (1991: 220), who believe that the “empty words” come from unbelievers, and, e.g., Hoehner (2002: 663), who believes that they come from both believers and unbelievers.

[18]. On the phrase ἔρχεται ἡ ὀργὴ τοῦ θεοῦ in Col. 3:6 as a reference to God’s future wrath, see, e.g., Dunn 1996: 216–17 and R. Wilson 2005: 247.

B. From Avoidance to Transformation (5:8–14)

[1]. Pace Best 1998: 488 and Muddiman 2001: 237; the thought here is close to that of Matt. 5:13–16.

[2]. Cf. also the use of “fruit” in an ethical sense by John the Baptist (Matt. 3:8–10 [Luke 3:8–9]) and Jesus (Matt. 7:16–20 [Luke 6:43–44]; 12:33; 21:33–44 [cf. Mark 12:1–12; Luke 13:6–9; 20:9–18]; John 15:2, 4–5, 8, 16]). The metaphor was not uncommon in Jewish religious and Greek philosophical literature (e.g., Odes Sol. 8.2; 11.1, 23; Epictetus [Arrian, Epict. diss. 2.1.21]). On this, see Schnackenburg 1991: 224n27; Best 1998: 489; BDAG 510.

[3]. Cf. Acts Paul 1, line 4, where Christ’s ἀγαθωσύνη inspires Paul to refrain from doing harm and instead to show affection toward his enemies.

[4]. Cf. 1 John 1:5–7, where the imitation of God is developed specifically in terms of God’s character as light.

[5]. This is how most commentators take the syntax, although Barth (1974: 569) and Schnackenburg (1991: 215, 217) give δοκιμάζοντες an imperatival nuance.

[6]. This translation comes from the rendering of Did. 12.1 in Ehrman 2003: 437.

[7]. I have argued this case more fully in Thielman 1995.

[8]. Paul uses the noun συγκοινωνός to refer to those with a deep, spiritual involvement in God’s people (Rom. 11:17), the gospel (1 Cor. 9:23), or the work of the gospel (Phil. 1:7). He uses the verb with this positive sense in Phil. 4:14. Cf. the use of both the noun and the verb first in a positive then in a negative sense in Rev. 1:9 and 18:4.

[9]. It is difficult, then, to agree with Engberg-Pedersen (1989: 97–100) that the “single root idea” (1989: 97) of ἐλέγχω is to reveal a fault by means of confrontation.

[10]. Believers: e.g., Gnilka 1971: 255–56; Best 1998: 492–94; Hoehner 2002: 679–80. Unbelievers: e.g., Schlier 1957: 239; Lincoln 1990: 329–30; Kreitzer 1998a: 54–55; O’Brien 1999: 371.

[11]. Kreitzer (1998a: 55) astutely observes that “the use of personal pronouns ‘we’ and ‘you’ elsewhere in the letter is almost always inclusive language,” making it that much more likely that the αὐτῶν in 5:12 is “a group outside the bounds of the church” (italics in original).

[12]. There is no need to become more specific and identify the activity with secret, sexually oriented religious rites (pace many earlier commentators and, more recently, Schlier 1957: 239 and Kreitzer 1998a).

[13]. If we accept Rom. 7:14–25 as an account, from a believer’s perspective, of a moral unbeliever’s struggle with the power of sin, then in that passage we can find a more extensive analysis of what it means for hidden and shameful deeds to be exposed (cf. Engberg-Pedersen 1989: 107–9).

[14]. That Paul is quoting is clear from the introductory quotation formula διὸ λέγει and the sudden switch from singular to plural verbs (Noack 1952: 52). On the unusual quotation formula διὸ λέγει, see both the remarks below and the comments on 4:8 above.

[15]. See, e.g., Isa. 37:17 LXX; 1 Tim. 3:16; Matt. 6:9; Did. 10.2–6 (Norden 1923: 254–58).

[16]. See, e.g., Ps. 43:24 LXX [44:24 MT; 44:23 Eng.]. Cf. Noack 1952: 53–54.

[17]. See, e.g., Hippolytus, who in Comm. Dan. 4.56.4 simply attributes the quotation to Isaiah (although in Antichr. 65 he seems to assume that it comes from an unidentified “prophet” distinct from Isaiah; cf. Origen [Heine 2002: 222]); Alford 1857: 128; Ellicott 1859: 121; and Eadie 1883: 389–90 (who assign it to Isa. 60:1). For Isa. 9:2 and 26:19, see the accounts of Eadie (1883: 389) and Jacobus (1897: 13–14) of the history of interpretation to their own day. Jacobus (1897: 21–29) himself proposes Jon. 1:6.

[18]. This consideration also weighs against the theory that the quotation is from a Christian hymn, which, in turn, derived its language from Isa. 26 and 60 (Moritz 1996: 97–116; cf. Abbott 1897: 158).

[19]. Elijah: Epiphanius, Panarion (F. Williams 1987: 333); Jeremiah: Euthalius (Dahl 2000: 248; cf. Schlier 1957: 240); Enoch: Codex Boernerianus (G; ninth cent.), marginal note (ex secreto Henochi, “from secret Enoch”; Schlier 1957: 240).

[20]. Barth 1974: 575; see also Sir. prol.8–10, 24–25; Luke 24:44.

[21]. Theodoret knew of interpreters who took this view (R. Hill 2001: 2.51). Was Severian of Gabala (Staab 1933: 311) one of them? Cf. John of Damascus (PG 95:848).

[22]. E.g., Dibelius and Greeven 1953: 90–91; Gnilka 1971: 260; Fischer 1973: 140–44; Schnackenburg 1991: 229; Best 1998: 499; Aletti 2001: 257.

[23]. Noack 1952: 61–62; Wedderburn 1987: 81–82; cf. Muddiman 2001: 242–43.

[24]. Clement of Alexandria (Protr. 9.84.2) may reproduce the continuation of the fragment when he adds to his own quotation of it the lines, “the sun of resurrection, the one begotten before the morning star, the one who grants life by his own light beams” (my trans.).

[25]. Ἐπιφαύσκω is a rare word that in biblical Greek appears only here and three times in Job (25:5; 31:26; 41:10 LXX [41:18 Eng.]). It seems to refer primarily to the shining of objects in the sky either directly (Job 25:5; 31:26) or by analogy (Job 41:10). For the metaphor of Christ as a shining astral body who gives inward illumination, cf. 2 Pet. 1:19.

[26]. Wedderburn (1987: 81–82) argues that the quotation originally referred to the general resurrection of the dead on the last day but that the realized eschatology of the author of Ephesians has prompted him to shift its setting into the present. As others have observed, however, if the original quotation had referred to the general resurrection on the last day, we would expect its first two verbs to be plural and future (Fischer 1973: 141; Lincoln 1990: 319; Best 1998: 499–500). Muddiman’s reply (2001: 242–43)—that perhaps the singular present-tense verbs are analogous to Rev. 1:17—does not solve the problem, since the metaphorical use of death there differs from its use here. Ephesians 5:14b must stand as an interesting piece of evidence that early Palestinian Christianity could speak in terms of a realized eschatology not unlike what we find in passages such as Col. 3:1–3; Eph. 2:5–6; and John 5:24–25.

[27]. For Jerome’s account of the legend, see the translations in Robinson 1904: 119n1 and Heine 2002: 224.

A. Introduction: Wisdom and the Life Filled in the Spirit (5:15–20)

[1]. For the idiom βλέπετε ἀκριβῶς (watch carefully), cf., e.g., Thucydides, Pel. War 1.134.1, where the historian describes how the magistrates of Sparta departed from their place of hiding “after listening carefully” (ἀκούσαντες . . . ἀκριβῶς) to an incriminating conversation.

[2]. See the LXX rendering of Exod. 28:3; 35:10, 25; 36:1; 1 Chron. 22:15 (LEH 561); and cf. Prov. 1:5.

[3]. “Wishing because of his affection for her to purchase the girl’s freedom [ἐξαγοράσαι τὴν παιδίσκην]” (trans. C. Oldfather 1933–67). Cf. Origen’s interpretation of the phrase ἐξαγοραζόμενοι τὸν καιρόν as buying “‘the time’ for ourselves” (Heine 2002: 225).

[4]. Severian of Gabala, who shared Paul’s fluency in ancient Greek, explained the text this way: “The present time is enslaved to evil people; ‘redeem’ it to make full use of it for piety” (Severian of Gabala [Staab 1933: 311], my trans.).

[5]. The content of the filling can be expressed with an ἐν clause (Ign. Smyrn. prol.), but this is rare.

[6]. Similarly, it is not clear that the expression ἐν πνεύματι or its equivalent elsewhere in the letter (2:18, 22; 3:5; 4:30; 6:18) always means “in the Spirit” (Heil 2007b: 5:11–514). It surely means this in 2:18, but the other references are more ambiguous.

[7]. On λαλοῦντες as a participle of result (since it is present tense and follows the verb it modifies), see Wallace 1996: 639 and Hoehner 2002: 706.

[8]. Begg (2005: 288) restricts the reference in Josephus (Ant. 7.305) to 2 Sam. 22:2–51 and 23:1–7.

[9]. Pace, e.g., Lincoln (1990: 346), Schnackenburg (1991: 238), and Best (1998: 511), who think that the adjective πνευματικαῖς applies to all three nouns.

[10]. See 1 Cor. 10:30; 2 Cor. 1:11; Rom. 1:8; 14:6; Col. 1:12; Mark 8:6 (Matt. 15:36; John 6:11, 23); Mark 14:23 (Matt. 26:27; Luke 22:17; 1 Cor. 11:24); Luke 18:11; 22:19; John 11:41; Acts 27:35; 28:15; Rev. 11:17.

[11]. The rule states that two personal, singular nouns linked by καί, neither of which is a proper name, refer to the same person even though the first noun has the article and the second noun does not (Wallace 1996: 271–72).

B. Submission in the Believing Household (5:21–6:9)

[1]. See especially Darko 2008, who, however, seems to exaggerate the extent to which the Ephesian household code fits comfortably into the world of Greco-Roman moral discourse.

[2]. The term goes back to Martin Luther’s Small Catechism, which contains a section on “Die Haus Tafel” (Luz 1998: 233).

1. Wives and Husbands (5:21–33)

[1]. Cf. Merz (2000), who thinks, however, that Ephesians is a pseudonymous, post-Pauline response to ascetic tendencies arising from contradictions in the authentic Pauline tradition (e.g., 1 Cor. 11:3–6, 11–12). As 1 Corinthians shows, both sexual debauchery (5:1–13; 6:12–20) and sexual asceticism (7:5) could occur within Christian congregations well within Paul’s lifetime, and Paul’s supposedly contradictory statements on the relationship between men and women reflect the complexity of the situation he addresses in Corinth rather than confusion in his own thinking.

[2]. This is also clear from Origen’s comments on 5:21. He read the text in his native language and found no apparent difficulty in applying it to everyone (Heine 2002: 231).

[3]. Χριστοῦ should be understood as an objective genitive.

[4]. For the meaning of φόβος, I have depended heavily on BDAG 1062.

[5]. These two kinds of fear were well understood in Greco-Roman moral discourse and would have been fully intelligible to Paul’s readers, whatever their level of familiarity with the OT. See, e.g., Pseudo-Aristotle, Oec. 3.3 [3.144.25–145.1]:

For of fear there are two kinds. The fear which virtuous and honourable sons feel towards their fathers, and loyal citizens towards righteous minded rulers, has for its companions reverence and modesty; but the other kind, felt by slaves for masters and by subjects for despots who treat them with injustice and wrong, is associated with hostility and hatred. (trans. Tredennick and Armstrong 1935)



[6]. At this point Ephesians is closer to 1 Pet. 3:5 (ὑποτασσόμεναι τοῖς ἰδίοις ἀνδράσιν) than to Col. 3:18, a sign that the material in Ephesians and 1 Peter is probably based on preformed tradition and that Ephesians is not a literary revision of Colossians.

[7]. See Aristotle, writing in the fourth century BC (Pol. 1.5 [1.1254b.13–14]; 1.12 [1.1259b.1–2]); Arius Didymus, writing in the first century BC (Stobaeus, Flor. 2.7.26, trans. in Balch 1988: 42); and Josephus, writing in the first century AD (Ag. Ap. 201).

[8]. It is true that 1 Cor. 14:34 and 1 Tim. 2:11 require women to be silent and submissive (ὑποτασσέσθωσαν, ὑποταγῇ) in the context of corporate worship, that 1 Tim. 2:13 relates this requirement to the order in which the woman was created relative to the man, and that 1 Cor. 11:3, 8–10 relates the headship of the husband over his wife to the order and purpose for which the woman was created. All these comments, however, are closely related to specific pastoral problems in the communities to which they were directed, unlike the more sweeping descriptions of women generally in Aristotle and Arius Didymus.

[9]. See the discussion and rejection of this reading in, e.g., Ellicott 1859: 127; Meyer 1880: 290; Abbott 1897: 165.

[10]. On the energetic debate over the figurative use of the term in the NT, see the additional note on 1:22.

[11]. Paul has used κεφαλή of the husband’s relationship to the wife already in 1 Cor. 11:3 (κεφαλὴ δὲ γυναικὸς ὁ ἀνήρ), and there too one person is the “head” of another person in the sense that one person has authority over the other person. This is clear from Paul’s statement that “the head of Christ is God” (ἡ κεφαλὴ δὲ τοῦ Χριστοῦ ὁ θεός), which probably refers to Christ’s functionally subordinate position with respect to God (cf. 1 Cor. 15:28). The practical problem over head coverings in Corinth may have led Paul to use the metaphor in this unusual way (cf. I. Marshall 2004a). The use of the metaphor in Ephesians is perhaps less unusual since the wife corresponds to the church, which is a group of people.

[12]. I assume that Perriman (1994: 618) refers to this sort of consideration when he says that connotations may belong to the use of the term in Colossians and Ephesians that are unusual elsewhere because those texts develop a particular “theological conception of Christ as ‘head.’”

[13]. Plutarch’s approach to marriage may have been an attempt to reimpose the old standards of classical Greece at a time when upper-class women were flaunting traditional mores (Foxhall 1999). On the “new woman,” whose sexual standards flaunted tradition in the first century, see Winter 2003: 17–74. Winter’s analysis reveals the continued existence of traditional views alongside those of the “new women.”

[14]. The translations of Plutarch in my discussion belong to Babbitt 1927–36. See also Xenophon, Oec. 3.10–15; 7.1–10.13; Pseudo-Aristotle, Oec. 1.3–4 (1.1343b.7–1344a.23); Musonius Rufus (Lutz 1947: 84–97). Each of these texts holds mutuality and harmony in marriage in high esteem, but underneath each is the assumption that the husband fills the leading role in the relationship. In a lengthy discussion with Xenophon’s Socrates about his wife, for example, Ischomachus makes the offhand comment that “a word from me was enough to secure her instant obedience” (ἅπαξ ἀκούσασα ταχὺ ἐπείθετο; Xenophon, Oec. 10.1, trans. Marchant and Todd 1923). Cf., e.g., Euripides (Stobaeus, Flor. 4.22.2), “Every decent woman is a slave to her husband”; Philemon (Stobaeus, Flor. 4.23.20), “A good wife, Nicostrate, should be submissive to her husband, not superior” (both quotations from Goessler 1999: 106n18); and the Neo-Pythagorean “Melissa” to “Clearete,” “The modest woman should express her love of the good . . . in . . . pleasing her own husband . . . by fulfilling his wishes. For the husband’s will ought to be engraved as law on a decent wife’s mind and she must live by it” (P.Haun. II.13; from Winter 2003: 73).

[15]. Pace Darko (2008: 106), who says, “There is no novelty in the substance of the household instruction for the believers.” Darko’s case is largely persuasive that the household code in Ephesians seeks to promote harmony and unity among believers rather than the integration of believers into society, but I think he has overstated his argument that the substance of the Ephesian household code says nothing untypical of Greek and Roman moral discourse generally.

[16]. Ὡς καί here means “in the same way that” (cf. 2:3; and 1 Cor. 9:5).

[17]. Cf. Yoder Neufeld 2002: 258. The correlation between Christ as “head” and Christ as “Savior” also recalls the claims in 2:5, 10 that God graciously “saved” believers through Christ Jesus.

[18]. Robinson 1904: 124, 205; cf. Dawes 1998: 86–89.

[19]. I have used the text and translation in Lutz 1947: 100–107.

[20]. Cf. the comments of Jerome (Heine 2002: 242) on wives fearing their husbands (Eph. 5:33):

Wives are frequently found who are much better than their husbands. They rule over them, manage the household, educate the children, and maintain the discipline of the family while the husbands revel and run around with harlots. I leave it to the decision of the readers whether these women ought to rule their husbands or fear them.

[21]. As Dawes (1998: 92) comments, the καθώς in 5:25 introduces “not a motive, but a comparison,” a statement “not so much ‘why’ husbands should love their wives, but rather ‘how’ they should love their wives, namely, as Christ loved the Church.”

[22]. Dawes (1998: 94) claims that the only point of comparison between Christ and the husband is the love that each shows to others, not the precise ways in which that love is shown (i.e., by giving oneself, sanctifying, and cleansing; vv. 25–26). This is correct with respect to sanctifying and cleansing, but Paul gives special emphasis to the imitation of Christ’s self-giving love in 5:2, and that emphasis carries over to this passage.

[23]. See the continuation in lines 20–23. The translation “love” that Lutz (1947) provides for κηδεμονία, however, does not seem entirely accurate. According to LSJ 946, the term means “care, solicitude,” and LSJSup 176 adds that it could refer to “the position of a curator or tutor.” It seems to have more to do with the care and kindness that a person in authority should show for those who are subordinate to them than with the kind of lavish, self-sacrificing love Paul says that God (Eph. 2:4; 5:1) and Christ (3:17–19; 5:2) have shown for believers and that believers ought to show to one another (1:4, 15; 4:2, 15–16; 6:21, 23) and to the Lord Jesus Christ (6:24).

[24]. On the whole subject, see Dixon 1992: 61–97.

[25]. With respect to Xenophon and especially Plutarch, see Foxhall 1999: 145–50. See also Musonius Rufus, who argues that women ought to be allowed to study philosophy, but the purpose of this, to a large extent, is so that they can better serve their husbands (Lutz 1947: 42 lines 9–10, 48 lines 20–26).

[26]. Cf. the statement in 2:5 (“by grace you are saved”) that is then expanded in 2:8–9.

[27]. On the structure of the clauses, see Dawes 1998: 94–96.

[28]. Καθαρίσας is an adverbial participle of means.

[29]. Cf. Bruce 1984: 387; BDAG 488–89. In 4 Macc. 17:21, the fatherland is “cleansed” by the deaths of the Maccabean martyrs when they die as a recompense for its “sin.”

[30]. Καθαρίσας is an adverbial participle of means (cf. Wallace 1996: 629). For the translation “bath” for λουτρόν, see BDAG 603.

[31]. See Treggiari 1991: 163, 168; Oakley and Sinos 1993: 15–16; G. Williams 2003: 928; Spicq, TLNT 2:413n19.

[32]. Cf. Titus 3:5, where Paul speaks of “the bath [λουτροῦ] of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit.”

[33]. A long parade of commentators opt for this view, including Ellicott 1859: 131; Eadie 1883: 419–20; Abbott 1897: 168; Westcott 1906: 85; Barth 1974: 625; O’Brien 1999: 423; and Hoehner 2002: 757.

[34]. See, e.g., De Wette 1843: 151; Robinson 1904: 206; and Schlier 1957: 257.

[35]. Muddiman (2001: 264) astutely observes that the syntactical ambiguity of ἐν ῥήματι would be solved by the person who read the passage aloud through “phrasing and intonation.” It seems likely that this ambiguity would not only have to be resolved orally but that it also began orally when Paul dictated the letter aloud.

[36]. See especially Lev. 14:8, where the leper will “wash in water” (λούσεται ἐν ὕδατι) and become “clean” (καθαρός).

[37]. Plutarch, Mor. 789d describes people laughing at the gray hair and wrinkled skin (ῥυτίς) of old men who speak in public (cf. Origen [Heine 2002: 237]). The first-century-AD medical writer Pedanius Dioscorides (e.g., De materia medica 1.34.1; 4.181.1; 2.109.1) frequently uses the term σπίλος to refer to blemishes on the skin and gives a complex prescription with an almond-oil base for the removal of “facial blemishes [σπίλους], freckles, and wrinkles [ῥυτίδας]” (1.33.1, trans. Beck 2005; again, cf. Origen [Heine 2002: 237]).

[38]. Syntactically, the οὕτως could point forward to the ὡς that follows it, and the sentence could be read as a new thought: “Here is how [οὕτως] husbands ought to love their own wives: as [ὡς] their own bodies” (e.g., Alford 1857: 133; Schlier 1957: 260; Schnackenburg 1991: 252). The use of ὡς, καθώς, and οὕτως in the Christ/church-husband/wife analogy from 5:22 up to this point, however, makes it likely that Paul uses οὕτως in the same way here (cf., e.g., Lincoln 1990: 378; Aletti 2001: 282). Some manuscripts read καί in the text at two different places (and NA27 and UBS4 include it in brackets), but the variation in the placement of the word probably reveals that it was added at different times by scribes who wanted to make the backward reference of οὕτως clear (Best 1998: 547).

[39]. For a more detailed examination of this quotation, see Thielman 2007: 826–28.

[40]. For this meaning of ἀντὶ τούτου, see, e.g., Ezek. 28:7; 34:9 LXX.

[41]. For the idiom λέγω εἰς, see, e.g., Acts 2:25, where it is also used in the application of Scripture to Christ.

[42]. Cf. 3 Bar. 1.6; 2.6; and BDAG 624. Marshall is commenting on the phrase μέγα ἐστὶν τὸ τῆς εὐσεβείας μυστήριον in 1 Tim. 3:16, where the adjective is used predicatively, just as it is here. Best (1998: 554) comments that μέγας is used predicatively and not attributively in Eph. 5:32 and so cannot “refer to the degree of the mystery” (cf. Sampley 1971: 87; Hoehner 2002: 775). I agree that μέγας is used predicatively here, but it is unclear to me why the predicate adjective cannot also refer to the degree of the mystery.

[43]. As Jesus does in the Sermon on the Mount, the only other uses of the phrase in the NT (Matt. 5:22, 28, 32, 34, 39, 44).

[44]. Cf. Dionysius of Halicarnassus (first cent. BC), who describes how the remnant of an army eventually came back together after “every single member” of it had been scattered: συνελθεῖν ἔφθασαν οἱ λοιποὶ οἱ καθ’ ἕνα διεσκεδασμένοι (Ant. rom. 9.14.3).

[45]. MHT 2:95; Moule 1959: 144–45; BDR §388.4; Wallace 1996: 477.

[46]. It is certainly true that ἵνα + the subjunctive does not always carry this nuance (2 Macc. 1:9), but it sometimes does so, and the contrast here between the imperative used for the husband and the subjunctive used for the wife shows that Paul was reaching for a different tone when he addressed the wife.

[47]. See the thorough survey of earlier attempts to explain the phrase in Eadie 1883: 427–29.

2. Children and Parents (6:1–4)

[1]. See the discussion of Pythagoras in Balla 2003: 14–16, 22–24.

[2]. It is the fourth commandment in Roman Catholic, Lutheran, and Anglican reckoning. A longer treatment of Paul’s use of Exod. 20:12 here appears in Thielman 2007: 829, from which some of the wording of my comments on this verse is taken.

[3]. In Greek, this would simply involve inserting the phrase ἣν ἐμάθετε after πρώτη.

[4]. Ἔσῃ is the future indicative of εἰμί and represents a departure from the LXX of Exod. 20:12 and Deut. 5:16, both of which have ἵνα μακροχρόνιος γένῃ at this point (cf. Philo, Spec. Laws 2.261). Commentators usually understand ἔσῃ to be dependent on ἵνα and point out that there is precedent for a future indicative following ἵνα elsewhere in Paul (Gal. 2:4; 1 Cor. 9:18; Eadie 1883: 440; Abbott 1897: 177; Hoehner 2002: 792).

[5]. The two Hebrew texts of the command differ slightly. Deuteronomy 5:16 speaks of long days and of life going well in the land, but Exod. 20:12 speaks simply of long days in the land. Some scholars (e.g., Bruce 1984: 397–98) have thought that Paul was quoting Deut. 5:16, presumably because his quotation agrees more with the Hebrew text of that command than with the Hebrew text of Exod. 20:12. But it seems reasonably clear that Paul was following the LXX of Exod. 20:12 rather than any Hebrew text. In the LXX of Exod. 20:12, σου is missing after μητέρα, just as it is in Eph. 6:2. Σου is present after μητέρα, however, in Deut. 5:16. See Lincoln 1982: 37–38; Moritz 1996a: 154–55; Best 1998: 566; Hoehner 2002: 788; Thielman 2007: 829.

[6]. In Greek literature, including the LXX, the verb appears far more often than the noun. Paul was familiar with the verb’s common meaning “to provoke to anger” (LEH 473) in the LXX, as his quotation of Deut. 32:21 in Rom. 10:19 shows.

[7]. On the use of the term in Greek philosophy, see Urmson 1990: 121.

[8]. C. Oldfather 1933–67 notes that this proverb was thought to be from Aesop (Fab. 9.28).

3. Slaves and Masters (6:5–9)

[1]. On the brutality of Roman slavery, see especially Bradley 1987: 113–37; Saller 1994: 133–53; and W. V. Harris 2001: 317–36; for a review of the way NT scholars have treated ancient slavery, particularly in the context of their work on the undisputed letters of Paul, see Byron 2008.

[2]. See W. Wilson 2005: 109–11 and Sellin 2008: 468, who cite, for example, Homer, Il. 9.312–13; Prov. 26:23–25; Sallust, Bell. Cat. 10.5; Ps.-﻿Phoc. 48–50; Sib. Or. 2.120–24.

[3]. See BDAG 409. Both texts come from the mid-second century AD. Cf. also Xenophon, Oec. 12.5, where εὔνοια is the most important quality of the slave who oversees other slaves on an estate (Alford 1857: 138).

[4]. Εἰδότες is an adverbial participle of cause, modifying the main verb ὑπακούετε in 6:5.

[5]. Paul’s advice, then, would be fairly conventional, at least for a thoughtful Stoic. Cf. Seneca’s pithy summary of his view of the treatment of slaves: “Treat your inferiors as you would be treated by your betters” (Ep. 47.11, trans. Gummere 2006). Some interpreters think that Eph. 6:9 articulates a somewhat lower standard than this. Muddiman (2001: 281) thinks that the author “was not in the slightest degree interested in laying down rules for the behaviour of slave-owners.” Harrill (2006: 90) believes that 6:9 means Christian leaders should reward “good” slaves (cf. v. 8) as a way of shutting them up.

[6]. It was Gregory of Nyssa who finally, in the late fourth century, concluded from the Christian understanding of God’s creation of humanity that slave ownership was a sin and an affront to God (Homilies 4 on Eccles. 2:7, quoted and analyzed in Garnsey 1996: 80–83).

[7]. Ἀπειλή seems to have been a natural word to use of precisely the kind of physical violence with which slaves were frequently threatened. See Philo, Virtues 124; Diodorus Siculus, Biblio. hist. 37.13.2; Plutarch, Cohib. ira 459a.

[8]. Syntactically, the participle ἀνιέντες is probably an adverbial participle of result (“do the same things for them, with the result that you give up the threat of violence”), but the rhetorical effect is virtually the same as an imperative.

XII. Standing against the Strategies of the Devil (6:10–20)

[1]. See the introductory comments above on 1:3–14, 20–23; 2:1–10; 3:1–7, 8–13; 4:1–16; 4:25–5:2.

[2]. There is perhaps an echo of the military image in the theme of watchfulness (ἀγρυπνοῦντες). “Probably not,” according to Best 1998: 606.

[3]. Ephesians 6:18–20 and Col. 4:2–4 share a concern that their readers be watchful (ἀγρυπνέω/γρηγορέω) in their praying, that they devote (προσκαρτέρησις/προσκαρτερέω) themselves to it, and that they pray that (ἵνα/ἵνα) God might open (ἄνοιξις/ἀνοίγω) Paul’s mouth (τοῦ στόματός μου) or a door for the word (θύρα τοῦ λόγου) so that he might explain (γνωρίζω/λαλέω) the mystery (τὸ μυστήριον/τὸ μυστήριον) of the gospel (τοῦ εὐαγγελίου) or of Christ (τοῦ Χριστοῦ), for which he is a prisoner (ὑπὲρ οὗ πρεσβεύω ἐν ἁλύσει/δι᾿ ὃ καὶ δέδεμαι), as he is supposed to do (ὡς δεῖ με λαλῆσαι/ὡς δεῖ με λαλῆσαι).

[4]. Best (1998: 586) also believes that 6:10–20 has affinities with such speeches but cites 1QM 15 as his example. In both its brevity and its thematic elements, the 1QM passage provides a closer analogy to Eph. 6:10–20 than the lengthy and politically complex prebattle speeches of the Greek historians.

A. Wearing God’s Protective Armor (6:10–17)

[1]. For the first position, see, e.g., Eadie 1883: 455; Hoehner 2002: 819–20; for the second position, see, e.g., Robinson 1904: 212; Masson 1953: 218n5; Schnackenburg 1991: 271n1; Aletti 2001: 306n7; Lincoln 1990: 441; Best 1998: 589–90.

[2]. See MM 380; LSJ 1060; and LSJSup 198. For the full phrase, see Sophocles, El. 317; and for the short form, see, e.g., Herodotus, Hist. 1.189; Thucydides, Pel. War 4.98.1; Josephus, Ant. 1.101; 4.187; 7.145, 362. Paul uses the short form in Gal. 6:17, and there too “from now on” or “henceforth” makes good sense. The temporal use of τοῦ λοιποῦ is not merely a classical idiom. It also appears in the common Greek of the papyri from the third century BC to the second century AD with the meaning “henceforth” (MM 380).

[3]. This does not mean that we should follow Barth (1974: 759–60) and adopt an eschatological meaning for the phrase (“For the remaining time . . .”).

[4]. Cf. the similar metaphor, but without the imagery of armor, in Isa. 11:5 and 1QSb 5.24–25.

[5]. For a more detailed discussion of the debate, see Thielman 2007: 830–33.

[6]. On all this, see Harnack 1981: 35–40. Cf. Westcott 1906: 92.

[7]. See Malherbe 1977: 72–73, 142–43; 1989: 101, 103–5; and Dibelius and Greeven 1953: 96–97.

[8]. Τοῦ θεοῦ is probably a genitive of possession, since in the other uses of the tradition, God is wearing the armor.

[9]. The expression ἐνδύσασθαι τὴν πανοπλίαν seems to have been a normal way to speak of putting on armor. See Josephus, Ant. 13.309; Plutarch, Pyrrh. 22.8; Lucian, Dom. 17.

[10]. Πρός followed by the articular infinitive indicates purpose (BDAG 874).

[11]. Cf. 1 Tim. 3:7 and 2 Tim. 2:26, where he is called ὁ διάβολος, just as he is in Ephesians.

[12]. See BDAG 752; for the performance of tragedy in the first-century Roman Empire, see Beacham 1999: 233–37.

[13]. Cf. Heb. 2:14, which, like Eph. 6:12, uses the unusual order αἷμα καὶ σάρξ. For the more usual order, σὰρξ καὶ αἷμα, see, e.g., Sir. 14:18; Gal. 1:16; 1 Cor. 15:50; Matt. 16:17.

[14]. The term occurs in a fragment supposedly from the fifth-century BC “historian” Ctesius, but according to F. Jacoby, the authenticity of this fragment is doubtful (FGH 688 no. 69). On the term, see also Michaelis, TDNT 3:913–14; Arnold 1989: 65–68; and Schwindt 2002: 371–74.

[15]. The Testament of Solomon probably contains material from the first century AD but took its present form several centuries later. See the discussion in D. C. Duling, OTP 1:940–43.

[16]. The word “dimension” belongs to Hanson 1980: 138, as quoted in W. H. Harris 1991: 86. Harris (1991) has shown that when “heaven” and earth (or the earth’s “lower parts”) stand in contrast with each other in Ephesians, οὐρανός, rather than ἐπουράνιος, is the word of choice (1:10; 3:15; 4:10; 6:9).

[17]. Sellin (2008: 477–78) comments insightfully that in Ephesians this is the equivalent of the tension in the earlier Pauline correspondence between what has “already” been accomplished through the death of Christ and the believer’s faith (e.g., Rom. 3:21–26; 5:1–2a, 6–8, 11; 8:1–17, 31–34) on one hand, and the redemption that has “not yet” been realized (e.g., Rom. 5:2b–5, 9–10; 8:18–30, 35–39) on the other hand.

[18]. As with the expression “to put on” (ἐνδύσασθαι) one’s armor in 6:11, it was normal to speak of “taking up” (ἀναλαβεῖν) one’s armor (πανοπλία). See, e.g., Jdt. 14:3; Josephus, Ant. 4.88, 244; 20.110.

[19]. The term is characteristic of Paul. Of its thirty-five occurrences in the NT and LXX combined, twenty belong to the Pauline corpus, and of those, all but this occurrence are found in the undisputed letters.

[20]. Cf. the use of κατεργάζομαι in 2 Cor. 4:17 and 5:5.

[21]. Polybius (Hist. 6.23) gives a full description of “the Roman armor [πανοπλία].” This provides a helpful general picture of the soldier’s equipment, but Polybius was writing in the second century BC and describing the armor of soldiers during the Second Punic War (218–201 BC). There were some changes in the equipment during the intervening centuries. For a description that pays careful attention to dating and relies heavily on archaeological evidence, see Webster 1985: 120–33. For clear, accurate illustrations of fully equipped first-century Roman soldiers, see Warry 1980: 186, 191, and 193.

[22]. See the description and detailed illustrations in Warry 1980: 191; Webster 1985: 123–25; and Biship and Coulston 2006: 95–100.

[23]. See Webster 1985: 121; Bishop and Coulston 2006: 111–13. Cf. the illustration in Warry 1980: 191.

[24]. Polybius (Hist. 6.23.2), writing in the second century BC, says that the shield measured 2.5 × 4 feet.

[25]. The rhetorical imbalance this created may be responsible for the textual variant in the Western textual tradition (D, F, G) that left out δέξασθε in 6:17 and made the final two pieces of armor dependent on ἀναλαβόντες in 6:16 (“and [taking up] the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit”).

[26]. The relative pronoun ὅ, which introduces the phrase, is neuter not because its antecedent is πνεύματος but either because its antecedent is the entire preceding phrase (e.g., Fee 1994: 728n210; Best 1998: 603) or because it has been attracted to the gender of ῥῆμα (e.g., De Wette 1843: 159; Hoehner 2002: 852).

[27]. See, with slight variations, e.g., Haupt 1902a: 240; Westcott 1906: 97; Masson 1953: 222; Bruce 1984: 409; Best 1998: 604; Hoehner 2002: 853.

[28]. See, e.g., Ellicott 1859: 153; Meyer 1880: 339; Schlier 1957: 298; Lincoln 1990: 451; Schnackenburg 1991: 280.

B. Persevering in Watchful Prayer (6:18–20)

[1]. Cf. Jude 20–21, where Jude’s readers, in contrast to the false teachers who “do not have the Spirit,” should “keep” themselves “in the love of God by praying in the Holy Spirit.”

[2]. See Sudhaus 1892: 11 (col. 6, lines 36–37): οὔτε πρὸς ὄνυχα τὴν προσκαρτέρησιν πονεῖσθαι δοκιμάζομεν, which Chandler (2006: 22) translates, “We do not see fit to elaborate in detail.” Cf. Philodemus’s use of προσκαρτερητικῶς (“painstakingly,” LSJ 1515) in Sudhaus 1892: 92 (col. 54, lines 4–5).

[3]. IG 12.249.8. Cf. the use of the verb προσκαρτερέω in Rom. 13:6.

[4]. For more information on the meaning of both noun and verb, see the comments on that verse.

[5]. On the relationship between the imperial cult and Paul’s references to political power in Ephesians, see the section in the commentary’s introduction titled “The Circumstances That Prompted Ephesians.”

XIII. A Concluding Commendation and a Final Prayer-Wish (6:21–24)

[1]. Commentators often observe that Ephesians brings no greetings from Paul’s coworkers and has no instruction about greeting one another, but these elements are also missing from Galatians, and among the disputed Pauline letters, from both 2 Thessalonians and 1 Timothy.

[2]. According to Richards (1991: 70–72), Burrhus was the courier, not the secretary (pace Lightfoot 1890: 34, 281), for these two letters.

[3]. Colossians has neither the awkward opening clause ἵνα δὲ εἰδῆτε καὶ ὑμεῖς nor the redundant τί πράσσω but includes in the description of Tychicus that he is καὶ σύνδουλος. It is probably fruitless to try to decide which letter came first on the basis of these differences. Colossians 4:7 might be a more concise version of Eph. 6:21 (cf. Best 1997b: 78–79), or Eph. 6:21 might be an attempt (through the omission of καὶ σύνδουλος in Col. 4:7) to focus attention on Paul alone (e.g., Gnilka 1971: 322; Lincoln 1990: 462). Since the καὶ ὑμεῖς in Eph. 6:21 hints that it was written after Col. 4:7–8 (see the additional note), it is probably best to think of Col. 4:7–8 as the foundational text that is repeated with slight variations in Eph. 6:21–22. The Ephesians text is certainly less polished, but this accords with the style of Ephesians generally.

A. Tychicus and His Mission (6:21–22)

[1]. Ancient letters commonly referred to the circumstances of the writer or the recipient, even when the main purpose of the letter was something else. Cf. P.Eleph. 13.3 (223/222 BC) : “When Santos arrived, I received your letter, which having read, I rejoiced when I learned your circumstances [τὰ κατὰ σέ].”

[2]. Some interpreters think the plural refers to the people mentioned in Col. 4:9–14 and Philem. 10, 23–24 (Meyer 1880: 349; Westcott 1906: 99; cf. Ellicott 1859: 158; Eadie 1883: 481; Schlier 1957: 306), but since only Tychicus is mentioned here in Ephesians, this seems less probable. Those who think the letter is pseudepigraphic usually attribute the plural to the author’s use of Col. 4:8 (e.g., Lincoln 1990: 462; MacDonald 2000: 353; Sellin 2008: 492).

[3]. Supplementing a letter with vital information not mentioned in the letter itself was a common role of the letter courier in antiquity (Head 2009: 286, 289, 293, 295–98).

[4]. Although Luke does not mention the reason for the delegation, Barrett (1998: 947) views it as “certain” that at least one purpose was the conveyance of the collection to Jerusalem.

[5]. Tychicus was “Asian” (Acts 20:4) but may have had connections to Rome, since most occurrences of the name outside the NT come from Rome (Hemer 1990: 236). Perhaps a connection both to Rome and to Asia explains why Tychicus was available to Paul to carry Colossians, Philemon, and Ephesians, all of them probably written during the Roman imprisonment described in Acts 28:16, 30–31 and all of them intended for destinations in Asia.

B. Peace, Love, Faith, and Grace for the Letter’s Recipients (6:23–24)

[1]. On the use of figurative sibling language in Greco-Roman culture generally, see von Soden, TDNT 1:145–46 (from whom the statistical information is derived) and Malherbe 2000: 109–10.

[2]. See 1 Thess. 4:6, 10; 5:27; 2 Thess. 3:15; Gal. 1:2; 1 Cor. 5:11; 6:5–8; 8:11–13; 15:6; Phil. 1:14; Rom. 14:10, 13, 15, 21; Col. 4:15; Philem. 16; 1 Tim. 4:6; 6:2; 2 Tim. 4:21. Cf. Malherbe 2000: 150.

[3]. Philemon, although a later letter, follows the early group in speaking of “the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Philem. 25). See the useful table in Weima 1994: 80.

[4]. See, e.g., Epicurus, Epistula ad Menoeceum 123; Epistula ad Herodotum 76; “Philo,” De aeternitate mundi (Περὶ Ἀφθαρσίας Κόσμου, On the Eternity of the World); Plutarch, Arist. 6; Mor. 425d; Urmson 1990: 27, under the adjective aphthartos; and the use of the adjective ἄφθαρτος to refer to God in Rom. 1:23 and 1 Tim. 1:17. Cf. Robinson 1904: 217–18.

[5]. Bruce cites 1:4, 8; 3:12; 4:19; 6:2, 16 as other examples of the “comitative” use of ἐν. Lincoln (1990: 467) adds 2:7 to the list and notes that here too the first word is χάρις. See also, e.g., Gnilka 1971: 326; Pokorný 1992: 251; O’Brien 1999: 494–95; Muddiman 2001: 300.

[6]. Translations of Psalms of Solomon here are my own.

[7]. For other occurrences of the verb ἀγαπάω qualified adverbially by ἐν with an anarthrous noun, see 2 John 1 (ἀγαπῶ ἐν ἀληθείᾳ) and 3 John 1 (ἀγαπῶ ἐν ἀληθείᾳ). Cf. T. Dan 5.3 (ἀγαπᾶτε . . . ἐν ἀληθινῇ καρδίᾳ); T. Gad 7.7 (ἀγαπᾶτε . . . ἐν εὐθύτητι καρδίας); and Ign. Trall. 13.2 (ἀγαπᾶτε ἐν ἀμερίστῳ καρδίᾳ). Each of these expressions refers to sincere or pure love, which is probably what τῶν ἀγαπώντων . . . ἐν ἀφθαρσίᾳ in Eph. 6:24 also means.

[8]. The Psalms of Solomon are most plausibly dated sometime in the first century BC (OTP 2:641), and although probably not known to Paul, nevertheless reveal a form of piety with which Paul was probably familiar.

[9]. Cf. Calvin 1965: 224; 1973: 704; Eadie 1883: 484–85; Abbott 1897: 191; and Moule 1953: 197. Among translations, see KJV and ESV; among lexicographers, see LSJ 289.





Frank Thielman (PhD, Duke University) is Presbyterian Professor of Divinity at Beeson Divinity School of Samford University. He has written extensively on Paul’s view of the law and is the author of the NIV Application Commentary on Philippians and Theology of the New Testament: A Canonical and Synthetic Approach.
